FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace

Ars Technica Long form November 13, 2026

Airlines praised the AI tool, but the air traffic controllers’ union wasn’t involved.

The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.

“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.

However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system “cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft,” the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.

The previous FAA announcement included supportive statements from Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom.

But the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, also told Flying magazine that it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”

Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system’s coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News.

The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

Ars has previously covered the SMART system’s development and lingering questions about how it works, as well as the air traffic controller shortage and other challenges facing the FAA.

It’s a weird time to buy a laptop, but the new MacBook Pro doesn’t skimp on quality

Ars Technica Long form November 06, 2026

It has the best laptop screen we’ve used, but there may be reasons to wait.

Apple’s new MacBook Pro is expensive as hell.

Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.

But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.

We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”

Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.

It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.

It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.

For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.

And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.

The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.

According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.

Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.

Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.

Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.

Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.

The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.

The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.

As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.

It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.

We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.

I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.

Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.

With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.

Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.

Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.

From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.

When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.

Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.

When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.

The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.

I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.

This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.

Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.

A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.

As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.

That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.

Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.

If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.

There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.

Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.

For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.

It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.

As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.

If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!

If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.

If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)

All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.

But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)

For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.

Forensic expert says his analysis of autopsy photos suggest Epstein was killed

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 20:33:57 GMT

This article contains distressing details and references to suicide

A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.

The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.

Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.

Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.

He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.

Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.

Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.

He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.

Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.

He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".

He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."

The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General that Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.

Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.

According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.

Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.

When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".

"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.

Challenged on whether his views veered into conspiracy theory, Freeman said: "I have the luxury of being able to say, don't take my word for it, let everybody look at it."

"If you think I'm still a conspiracy theorist because I'm looking at something that looks like a strangulation and say, I think it is a strangulation and I don't think it could be a hanging, show me where I got it wrong."

"I'm wide open to that. I'm an academic. I'm quite happy to hear people's theories on things that are informed," he said.

Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.

Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:43:58 GMT

Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply gratreful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".

"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."

At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.

Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.

Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire,

He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.

Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.

He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.

But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.

His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:43:33 GMT

This video can not be played

You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career

Andy Robertson has become Scotland's most capped men's international after starting in Monday's Nations League game in Switzerland to reach 103 appearances for his country.

Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years.

After moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare.

But, in St Gallen, the spotlight shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he moves solo at the summit.

Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King

Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson

This video can not be played

Andy Robertson on his hero, Kenny Dalglish

For much of this year, Dalglish was the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.

'King Kenny' topped the list on 102 caps - earning his last in November 1986 against Luxembourg when in a player-manager role at Liverpool.

Few since have even come close to toppling him - and Robertson is keen to stress the throne is still reserved for Dalglish - but it is perhaps fitting it is the current captain, given their great friendship.

Which allows Dalglish to say he's not having any of it.

"He always says: 'You've got millions more games. Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.

"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.

"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."

Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.

But not out of John McGinn's - the midfielder's double against North Macedonia on Friday took him to within six of the legendary duo.

The Aston Villa captain is lurking only eight caps behind Robertson on the all-time caps list, too, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.

Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 33 times more than any other player.

At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.

Now he is the only man to have led Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.

Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.

"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."

One of those young players is 20-year-old Findlay Curtis, who told the media the night before Robertson's historic night that his captain has "probably been the biggest role model" he's looked up to since joining the international set-up earlier this year.

Perhaps that was because Robertson did him a turn back in the day. Unbeknownst to the skipper.

Rangers winger Curtis was only 14 during the Covid pandemic and was partial to playing a bit of Fifa, and Robertson was a star in his team.

"I was just thinking, I had him in my Fifa team," he explained. "[For] defending and he was just fast as well.

"What a servant he has been for the country."

This video can not be played

'I had him in my Fifa team!' - Findlay Curtis on going from fan to team-mate of Robertson

Robertson has played under four permanent Scotland team bosses in his 12-year international career.

It was Strachan who plucked him from the under-21s to hand him his debut as a 19-year-old in a win over Poland in March 2014.

McLeish made him captain in 2018, calling Robertson the "outstanding candidate" and an "inspirational figure" - and now he has played five times for new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.

He even played one game under interim manager Malky Mackay in a friendly against the Netherlands at Pittodrie in 2017 as the Scottish FA searched for Strachan's replacement.

However, it is Steve Clarke's seven-year stint that Robertson will be mainly associated with, as the pair led Scotland to three major tournaments.

Robertson played 68 times for Clarke, all of them as captain, and the recently departed head coach consistently praised his figurehead.

"He's been a fantastic captain for Scotland," Clarke said at the World Cup.

"He's worked ever so hard for the country and he leads the group like the leader he is - and he's very, very important to me and the squad."

This video can not be played

'An amazing moment for me'

Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.

Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.

Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.

He has started 101 of his 103 caps, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.

The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with?

At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.

Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:30:30 GMT

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.

The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.

Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.

Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.

Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.

Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.

The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.

A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.

Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.

The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.

Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.

It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.

The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.

The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.

Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:16:52 GMT

US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.

Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.

The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.

The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.

The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.

However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.

"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.

The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X.

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:22:22 GMT

A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable".

In a post on X, Norris wrote: "Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims.

"This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".

Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."

"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.

Victims' commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma.

"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

If Brand is found to have broken prison rules, possible punishments enforceable by prison governors can result in restrictions on social visits or loss of privileges such as access to additional time in the gym or loss of TV.

Governors can also impose proportionate restrictions on communications where justified.

This could include blocking specific phone numbers, increased monitoring of calls or restricting contact with individuals where necessary to protect victims or maintain prison security.

It come as Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy met with senior leaders in media, entertainment, arts and sports organisations as part of her call to end the culture of abuse in industries where there can be large power imbalances.

In the meeting, she asked the leaders what they were doing to create a culture where bullying, harassment and abuse are challenged, how they are empowering whistleblowers to speak out and how their safeguarding systems apply to freelance employees.

The attendees are due to report back to Nandy on the questions she asked them within the coming weeks, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said.

Over the weekend, Brand was moved from the category B HMP Wandsworth in south London to the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison that mostly houses sex offenders and has tailored programmes for them.

Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, told LBC he agreed it was not "a good look" that he'd been moved to a lower security prison.

"I think people want to see him facing the appropriate punishment for what are appalling crimes against women and others and I think the whole episode is shocking," he said.

Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.

Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.

She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.

Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.

In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...

"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."

But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.

She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".

Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.

Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".

Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.

"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."

Any change in the law would only affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which is also currently set at 16 in both nations.

The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.

The foreign secretary also apologised for having appeared on Russell Brand's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.

Miliband told Today if he'd known about the allegations then, he would not have done spoken to him, adding: "I deeply regret doing that interview and all my sympathies are with those victims."

How Frank can restore reputation and save Crystal Palace

"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.

That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.

"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.

Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?

Frank 'the perfect man' for Palace job

Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.

In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".

Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest.

Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., external

Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.

It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.

Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.

A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.

So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?

Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.

Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.

Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".

Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?

Would Thomas Frank be a good fit for Crystal Palace?

Frank, who places a major emphasis on set-piece organisation, will have to hit the ground running at Palace, who have lost their past four league games.

They have conceded more goals than anyone else in the Premier League (24) and have scored only 10 themselves.

"If you want someone to go in and restore some stability and defensive solidity while improving the set-piece element of the team, then Thomas Frank is the perfect man for the job," Times football writer Tom Allnutt told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.

With the Premier League season just 10 games old, Frank certainly has time to turn it around and will have targets in mind when the transfer window opens in January.

Palace sold France centre-back Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea for £52m and Colombia right-back Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest for £22m during the summer transfer window.

Allnutt added: "We know they have sold so many good players and so far I don't think they have really replaced them adequately."

Another challenge for Frank is getting midfielder Adam Wharton, who has not played for England since March, back to something like his best form.

These are all challenges the new manager will relish.

After his bruising experience at Tottenham - having established Brentford in the Premier League - Frank has decided to climb back on the hamster wheel with Palace.

"Crystal Palace and Thomas Frank feels like a very good fit," added Robinson.

This video can not be played

Crystal Palace fan calls Thomas Frank 'the perfect hire'

Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).

It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).

Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.

There is also one significant factor in Frank's favour. Although Palace may be bottom of the Premier League, they are certainly not cut adrift as they sit just two points from safety.

The side propping up the table at this stage have had an average of just three points in the past 10 seasons, but for as bad as they've been, Palace have seven - the most the bottom side have had after 10 games for 24 years.

Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:27:24 GMT

Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.

Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".

The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.

The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.

In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".

Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".

He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".

Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.

The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".

With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.

Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.

The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.

According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.

In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:40:16 GMT

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:02:41 GMT

Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.

He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.

His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.

Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.

"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.

"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."

He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.

Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.

He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.

"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.

"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."

In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world", saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".

After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.

He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse, saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird."

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'

"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."

The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.

By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men.

"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.

Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.

Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.

With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.

But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.

Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times.

"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.

"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."

Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:58:12 GMT

Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.

Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.

The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.

The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.

Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.

Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.

The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.

A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.

But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.

"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

Raye, Rosalía and Dolly Parton recognised in Grammy nominations

BBC News Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:48:55 GMT

British singer Raye leads the charge at the forthcoming Grammy Awards with 11 nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with three posthumous nods.

Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.

Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers.

Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.

The late country star also received a nomination for best audio book, for her narration of Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.

The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles.

Madonna's album Confessions II, a sequel to 2005's Confessions on a Dancefloor, was absent from the "big four" categories - including album, record and song of the year.

That will be seen by many as the Grammys continuing their tradition of snubbing the US singer, but the album did make it into the best dance category.

Rosalía's nine nominations for her widely acclaimed album Lux come after her huge success at last week's Latin Grammy Awards.

Langley's seven nominations include song of the year for her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas, which this year became the longest-running number one single in the history of Billboard's Hot 100.

There are five new categories being introduced, including best Latin song and best Asian pop music performance.

They have been added as part of the Academy's attempts to make the event "more inclusive" and represent a wider range of music genres.

Four of Korea’s five biggest entertainment companies withheld their music from consideration. Starship Entertainment, which bucked the trend, scored nominations for its girl bands IVE and KiiiKiii.

The other nominees were Babymetal, Japanese singer Lisa (not to be confused with the Blackpink star of the same name) and the Filipino bands BINI and SB19.

Elsewhere, Beyoncé picked up the 100th nomination of her career when Morning Dew (Donk) was shortlisted for best R&B solo performance.

Songs and albums had to be released between 31 August 2025 and 28 August 2026 to qualify for nominations.

Around 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy are eligible to vote for the winners.
