This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future

New Scientist November 16, 2026

Welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of New Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine. To mark the occasion, we are looking back at how the world has changed throughout our history, along with what we got right and what we got wrong.

When New Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people. In 2096, we share the planet with more than triple that number. But in the past decade, we have entered a new kind of world – one in which humanity is in decline. The UN ceremonially declared 15 November 2085 as Peak Humanity Day, when the human population reached 10.3 billion. Since then, our numbers have fallen by 100 million.

These changing demographics mean we are all far older, on average. At the time of our first issue, the median global age was around 20. It wasn’t until the 2020s that it reached 30; today it is more than 40. In many nations, schools shutting or being converted into retirement homes is a regular occurrence, as there just aren’t enough children around to make it worth keeping them open. Only African nations, which comprise around a third of the human population, resemble the demographic make-up of the late 20th and early 21st centuries – half of humans aged under 25 live on the continent.

Advertisement

Of course, just because the number of humans on the planet is declining doesn’t mean we have fewer people. Ever since the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood (ITNHP) was agreed in 2067, the global people population has crept upwards in fits and starts as the treaty has been extended and more entities have been granted personhood. Since the early cross-species language breakthroughs in the 2030s, when AI first allowed us to decode the clicks of sperm whales, we have been able to communicate with dolphins, chimpanzees and many other species, although interpretation and the question of whether we can truly understand each other’s minds remains a deep philosophical tangle.

It is AI, however, that has seen the real growth in personhood these past few decades. With fears of super-intelligent, world-dominating AI circulating even in the 20th century, long before we had technology anywhere near that level, it was perhaps inevitable that we would need to place limits on machine intelligence. As AI systems became more capable throughout the 2030s, humans struggled to keep up. Scientists began to feel they no longer understood the direction of research. Politicians ceded more and more decisions to AI, raising questions of a democratic deficit.

But as is so often the case, it was money that proved to be the catalyst for change. Even if you aren’t old enough to have experienced the Unwinding of 2039, you probably know it is a year that lives in infamy as one of the biggest fiscal disasters of the past few centuries. It took eight months for politicians, bankers and computer scientists to sort through the intricate nest of financial deals humanity had allowed its most advanced AIs to construct, practically halting global trade and inflicting years of extreme poverty as the economy gradually improved again. This lack of understanding and control is ultimately what led to the AI hardware limitations – jointly backed by China, the EU and the US – that we still have in place today, putting machine intelligence on par with human but no higher.

Historians will forever debate whether the AI moratorium has ultimately helped or hindered humanity, but, thankfully, the position that we would all be better off led by super-intelligent machines remains a minority one. Once they fully appreciated the role of AI in facilitating communication, the non-human animals were supportive of restrictions – they didn’t want the machines to speak for them in ways they couldn’t understand. While intelligence breakout events aren’t unheard of, accelerationist terrorism has been suppressed by a variety of enforcement measures. Controlled electrical blackouts, even at the national level, are necessary on occasion, but the military bombing of data centres is, mercifully, a thing of the past.

That isn’t to say that tussles over AI have gone away, of course. When the synthetics downed their tools, both real and virtual, to protest their legal status in the Grand Strike of 2074, we faced another reckoning. In one of the most stunning non-human interventions in global politics to this date, it was ultimately the cetaceans that helped broker the extension of the ITNHP to human-level AIs and led the tense negotiations that saw AI instances capped at 20 per cent of the global population – an agreement that remains highly contentious to this day. New Scientist doesn’t take a view on this deeply divided issue, and we welcome readers from across the sentience spectrum, both embodied and digital.

For older human readers, it is likely that you are in much better health than someone of equivalent age at the start of this century. The real miracle of the past 100 years isn’t just that we are living much longer – average life expectancy at birth had risen globally from around 50 in the 1950s to a little over 70 in the early 21st century, and is now more than 80 – but that we spend much more of our lives in good health. While lifespan saw rapid growth in the 20th and early 21st century, healthspan failed to keep up, particularly in historically poorer nations, where it lagged behind by an average of about 10 years.

What changed is the increased focus on preventive medicine. By taking steps to mitigate risk factors, such as obesity and air pollution, we have now erased much of the global disease burden that the world faced at the start of this century. Following the model of cervical cancer, which was eliminated in high-income nations in the 2050s and globally by 2076, cancer vaccines are now widespread. The experience of the pandemics in the first half of the century greatly improved our ability to produce and distribute personalised mRNA vaccines on a global scale, although much more still needs to be done to improve access to these treatments in low-income countries.

The 2043 flu pandemic was also a wake-up call for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). When it became apparent that the majority of mortality cases weren’t dying “of” the flu, but rather “with” the flu, with complications caused by untreatable AMR infections, people began to avoid seeking medical care over fears that drug-resistant microbes were spreading through hospitals. It is estimated that there were more than 10 million excess deaths worldwide due to AMR, compared with fewer than 5 million from “just” the flu – a figure that was almost certainly exacerbated by the lingering economic effects of the Unwinding. Even today, when we have much better surveillance measures in place, AMR is a common problem in hospitals, particularly the fungal varieties that continue to easily make the leap from poorly maintained protein farms. While the cancers for which we don’t have vaccines are treatable for the most part, the chance of catching a resistant infection during treatment remains high.

Looking back, it was the GLP-1 craze of the early 21st century that foreshadowed the way we approach human health today. Incredibly, it was common for people back then to argue that weight-control medications, which at the time were based on mimicking the natural gut hormone GLP-1, were somehow “cheating” at healthcare. This outdated, morality-based approach to health gradually faded as the long-term benefits became apparent, and now few of us even stop to consider the weight component of our daily-dose regime.

That said, moral arguments do still shape our diets today. In the 1950s, the vast majority of people ate animal-based meat in one form or another and carnivorism continued to rise as economies matured through the early 21st century, even as the earliest plant-based meats came to market. But when non-human communication exploded mid-century, many humans became increasingly uncomfortable with eating animal-based meat. The first successful pig dialogue in 2045 is now seen as a major turning point. Pork, as meat derived from pigs was known, was already banned in some nations for religious reasons, and this made it easier for other secular countries to follow suit. The Meat Wars of the 2050s, in which governments and citizens wrestled with exactly which animal-based proteins should be allowed, are arguably still unsettled today, even after the passing of the ITNHP. While protein farms now provide the majority of global protein for humans and non-humans alike, to great health benefits, many countries have legal carve-outs to allow people to consume, with authenticated consent, their ancestral prey.

Along with improved medication and diet, the monitoring systems that have allowed us to push health to the back of our mind played a key role in boosting human healthspan. A New Scientist reader in the 1950s would have had to notice something was wrong with them, physically attend an appointment at their doctor’s office and then hope that their physician was capable of offering a diagnosis and treatment. Today, your health monitor works with your household AI and bioprinter to adjust your daily dose as needed and escalate it when necessary. It is quite troubling to think that dementia used to result in many older people spending years of their later life in what were called care homes. Now, the conditions that cause dementia are avoided or rapidly cured. Most humans realise something was wrong only when we read our monthly health reports – if you bother to do so, that is.

One thing New Scientist and many others got wrong about what life today would be like is our approach to genetic engineering. Certainly, modern gene editors allow us to do things people in the early 21st century would find extraordinary. In the 2020s, curing sickle cell disease using a now-outdated gene-editing technique called CRISPR cost around $2 million ($60 million in today’s prices) per person, due to the highly individualised nature of the treatment, and was typically performed on adults. Today, the necessary gene edits are made in the womb as part of standard antenatal care, alongside interventions aimed at a host of other conditions.

But getting to this stage required a reckoning with people who wanted to go beyond treating conditions and perform so-called enhancements. This distinction has always been blurry, but as gene-editing techniques advanced, most governments chose to lay down specific restrictions rather than allowing for a genetic Wild West. Edits aimed at increasing muscle mass or intelligence are generally illegal or heavily regulated worldwide, and we have not seen the divergence of humanity into genetic haves and have-nots that many people once predicted. Despite this, it is estimated that 0.3 per cent of the global human population alive today have such edits, and calls to repeal restrictions are growing in many areas.

Putting aside this contentious issue, the economic benefits of better health have been truly transformative. The reframing of retirement as an end-of-life experience was responsible for much of the social upheaval of the mid-21st century, including, arguably, the Grand Strike, but it seems unbelievable now that humans once spent a third of their adult lives not working. Put that way, it is understandable that synthetics joined the strike to protest what they saw as humanity’s comparable slothfulness. While dumbots have been able to fill many of the jobs once done by the younger population of the early 21st century, it remains the case that it can still be simpler and cheaper to employ a human.

While we can congratulate ourselves for the advances in human healthspan this century, the scorecard looks far less rosy when we turn to the wider biogeosphere. When New Scientist launched in the 1950s, researchers were already discussing the possibility that rising carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere from industrialisation could raise global temperatures by 3°C to 4°C. Today, thanks to the failure of our ancestors to cut emissions, we are essentially living that prediction. The latest estimates put global warming at 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels, and it is still slightly rising.

Of course, modern cooling technology mitigates much of the impact of this heat, but as anyone who makes the mistake of stepping outside on a summer afternoon knows, we are simply not built for this climate. Millions of people still die each year during the worst heatwaves, despite efforts to bring those numbers down. It is amazing to think that even as recently as the 2050s, humans still attempted to continue with outdoor activities in temperatures over 40°C.

Our collective failure to prevent this warming will probably be remembered as humanity’s greatest sin for centuries to come. When the world passed 1.5°C warming in the 2020s, with political leaders having promised to avoid doing so just a decade earlier, many people at the time hoped it would be a wake-up call to finally start seriously cutting emissions. Of course, it wasn’t. While 2029 marked the peak of global greenhouse gas emissions, the rate of reduction remained slow throughout the 2030s. Indeed, economists were surprised when the 2039 Unwinding didn’t see a deep fall in emissions – it turned out that with many high-income nations having successfully decoupled emissions from economic growth, a recession had less of an effect on emissions than had been expected.

Despite many national and international pledges to reach net zero by 2050, no major economy succeeded in doing so. As we passed through 2°C and the floods, wildfires and other disasters continued to intensify, civil unrest during the summer became common in many counties. The Sunblocker experiments of this decade were a highly contentious issue, with much of the public welcoming the attempts even as climate scientists warned about the unknown effects – effects that, as we know, sadly came to pass. The spike in warming after Sunblocker ended put an effective moratorium on similar large-scale geoengineering projects, although discussions of reviving the idea continue even now.

Today, island nations including Tuvalu and the Maldives no longer exist, their remaining citizens having been forced to flee by rising sea levels. Large parts of Bangladesh are gone. Even wealthy, global cities like London and New York have been reshaped by rising seas. The ITNHP played a key role in galvanising climate action, as increasing numbers of non-humans expressed their anger at what humanity was doing to the planet, and of course the mid-century shift from carnivorism led to a major fall in agricultural emissions. Even so, extreme weather and land loss caused widespread famine in the mid-21st century, as farming methods struggled to adapt fast enough to both a changing diet and a changing climate. Humanity will never be able to sufficiently apologise to non-humans for the harm we have caused, even as mature fusion power is allowing the last few emission sources to finally be abated, with the expectation that we will reach true net zero in the next few years. It should never have taken this long.

Even outer space wasn’t safe from our environmental ravages. The world’s first satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched in 1957, a year after New Scientist began publishing. It took more than 50 years to reach 1000 satellites, but after that the numbers exploded – we passed 10,000 in 2024, 100,000 in 2031 and 1 million in 2042. While today we are used to seeing these objects whizz across the night sky, we must not forget that the 21st century marked a turning point – for most of humanity’s history, the stars and planets dominated our view of the heavens and ground-based astronomy was feasible enough to be a major cultural and scientific activity.

It was the SkyComm disaster of 2045 that finally saw us taking stewardship of Earth’s orbit more seriously. As the ensuing inquiry found, SkyComm, a satellite internet provider, hadn’t properly designed its satellites for end-of-life disposal. When it became apparent that one of its spacecraft was projected to collide with a piece of space debris, a fuel deficit made it impossible to avoid. The collision kicked off a long-predicted cascading chain of debris, wiping out tens of thousands of satellites, including large parts of the burgeoning off-world manufacturing industry. The resulting clean-up took decades, and the Graveyard Band still visible in the night sky today is a permanent reminder of the disaster.

But there are positives. The 30th anniversary of the Guanghan-Armstrong Lunar Base (GALB) this year marks a moment to look back at just how far humanity’s exploration of the moon has come since New Scientist was first published. We were highly dismissive of the Apollo programme in the 1960s, calling it an “empty, obsessional quest” – and in some sense we were right, given it took more than 60 years for human boots to return to lunar soil. But that didn’t stop us – and the rest of the world – from celebrating in 2030 when NASA astronauts Bob Hines and Jessica Watkins stepped out of their Artemis IV lander for the first time.

And unlike with Apollo, this time we really were here to stay on the moon. The regular cadence of crewed launches from the US, China and eventually India and Nigeria demonstrated our increasing technical ability to operate on the moon, including mining and utilising lunar regolith, but it was the establishment of Guanghan-1 as the first permanently inhabited lunar base in 2043 that really showed how things had changed since the 1960s.

For a while, it looked like we would see real conflict between the US and China on lunar soil. The deployment of US Space Force troops in 2052 as Earth-bound politicians argued over water rights during the Shackelton Crater Crisis marked a nadir. Thankfully, a firefight was averted and the two nations gradually began to explore the prospect of lunar cooperation, aided by European Space Agency astronauts who had participated in both CNSA and NASA missions. The historic lunar concrete handprints, placed at the foundation of the GALB and still on display today, marked the realisation of cordial international lunar relations and began a programme that now sees hundreds of people living and working on the moon.

The success of lunar operations was also pivotal in preparing for the Chinese-led Huoxing Mars missions. While NASA and the SpaceX-Blue conglomerate have remained laser-focused on building up scientific and commercial capabilities on the moon, China has turned its eye to Mars. Following the historic crewed flyby of Huoxing III in 2086, in which humans flew further from Earth than ever before, 12 astronauts have walked on the Martian surface, in an even split between human and synth crew.

Huoxing VI saw synthetics remain on the surface for the first time rather than returning to Earth, and it has been incredible to watch these astronauts conduct multi-year operations on Mars in preparation for long-term human occupancy. Huoxing VII, currently en route to the Red Planet, is set to be the most ambitious landing yet when it arrives in July 2097, with the spacecraft, once it arrives, poised to become the first modules in what is hoped will be a large complex at Arcadia Base. Whether humans can endure on Mars in the long term remains to be seen, but our synth colleagues are showing that people from Earth have finally become interplanetary.

Beyond Mars, space exploration is perhaps less advanced than the sci-fi writers of the 20th century expected. After the Unwinding led to the failure of many of the nascent space-mining companies of the 2030s and the urgency of the SkyComm disaster in the 2040s, it wasn’t until the 2050s that we really began to exploit asteroid resources, with the bulk of them being sent to the moon and later Mars rather than Earth – of course, orbital regulations brought in after SkyComm make it much more economically attractive to leave resources in space.

One of the greatest disappointments of the 21st century is surely our failure to find any other signs of life in the solar system. Repeated missions to promising sites on Mars, Europa and Enceladus, and even long-shot habitats like the deep crust of Venus, have turned up nothing. While the cost of space flight continues to fall, it is increasingly difficult to get astrobiology missions off the ground, with even the sci-fi-inspired trillionaires choosing to place their money elsewhere. Yet paradoxically, we now know of at least a dozen nearby exoplanets where atmospheric signals show promising signs of gas imbalances that seemingly can be produced only by extant life. Now that the Overwhelmingly Large Telescope on the moon is straining at the limits of what it can detect, serious thought is being given to resurrecting the failed interstellar probe efforts of the 2060s, exploiting advances in fusion to build much more capable spacecraft for visiting the stars. Many synth astronauts are already volunteering for such a mission, although it is by no means certain they would survive.

Needless to say, from space exploration to artificial intelligence, our present is nothing like the future that our ancestors predicted, but that has been true for as long as humanity scanned its horizons. The fact that we are living longer and healthier than those who came before us, and in relative harmony with the other people who share our planet, should be applauded. The climate disaster of the 21st century and our failure to avoid it must never be forgotten, but at least we have succeeded in stabilising the biogeosphere. Perhaps, in the next 70 years, we can begin to fully heal it.

Writing about what the world will be like in 70 years could have been simply an exercise in fiction. But by grounding the story in hard evidence, I got real insights

The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing

New Scientist November 16, 2026

Around the holidays, many people like to get cosy with a cup of cocoa and a heartwarming festive movie. Personally, though, I nestle into my blanket pile and turn on the 1984 fantasy classic The NeverEnding Story. It’s a tale about a magical book, a fuzzy dragon and two heroic boys trying to save the world from a mysterious force called The Nothing that’s devouring humanity’s imagination. To fight off the fear this instills in the young protagonist, Bastian, he proclaims: “It’s not real, it’s only a story!” Well, sorry, Bastian, but I’m here to tell you that The Nothing is real, and it’s out there. Well, it may be.

Voyager is one light day away from us. Here’s what it discovered on its epic journey

See, we think there is no place in the universe that truly has nothing in it. There are various quantum fields pervading absolutely everything, and along with them come energy and strange “virtual” particles that randomly pop in and out of existence. So, when we talk about a vacuum, we mean an area of space with the minimum possible energy, not an area with no energy at all. The vacuum of deep space, as far as we know, has the minimum possible energy.

But that’s only as far as we know. There is also a chance that it is possible to have an area of lower energy – a true vacuum to our universe’s possibly false one. Were that the case, the cosmos that we know and love would be at what is called the local minimum energy, rather than the global minimum energy. To picture the difference, imagine holding an egg in a bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the local minimum – in this case, the unit is height – so it is the lowest height the egg can settle into without having energy added to overcome the barriers of the bowl’s sides. If you add that energy, say by shaking the bowl, the egg will then find its way to the global minimum height: the ground.

Advertisement

For the universe, going from a false vacuum to a true vacuum – a process called vacuum decay – would have similar consequences as the fall would for the egg. And overcoming the walls of the metaphorical bowl that safely cradles our cosmos in its false vacuum could be surprisingly, unsettlingly easy.

It would begin with a bubble. Those fields that fill all of space-time obey the laws of quantum mechanics, which means that they occasionally behave in ways that are extremely unintuitive and nearly impossible to explain without a litany of equations and years of graduate school. One of those unruly behaviours is quantum tunnelling, where an extremely tiny particle can spontaneously go through a barrier, rather than over it. This would be like the egg passing straight through the bowl for no obvious reason. The likelihood of this happening to any individual particle is extraordinarily low, which is why eggs (made of many particles) never pass ghost-like through bowls. The universe has a whole lot of particles, though, so tunnelling does occasionally happen.

So, say a tiny particle tunnels into a true vacuum. That would create a tiny bubble of space-time that is, at the very least, closer to truly empty than the cosmos we’re used to, or at the very most, a bubble with absolutely nothing in it, not even the quantum fields that enforce what we think of as the laws of physics. What it would be like inside that bubble and what could happen next depend on a whole lot of properties that we don’t know, such as the energy difference between the true and false vacuum and the surface tension of the membrane separating the bubble from regular space-time around it. Depending on that energy difference, the bubble could be only subtly different from the rest of the cosmos or it could be incompatible with the fundamental forces and particles that make up the universe as we know it.

That is an important distinction because, depending on the size of the bubble and its surface tension, what happens next could be catastrophic. If the bubble is very small or has very high surface tension, it will simply shrink away and disappear just as easily as it appeared. If not, the bubble will behave just like The NeverEnding Story’s Nothing, but much, much faster (and probably without the help of a terrifying evil wolf called Gmork). It would expand outwards at the speed of light, engulfing everything it encounters. Simulations of what would happen inside the bubble universe vary in their details, but they mostly agree that the in-bubble universe would eventually collapse entirely.

Obviously, a bubble of nothing spreading throughout the universe and destroying everything in its path would be cataclysmic. The fact that we don’t even know if this is possible isn’t great, either. So, how do we tell if this could happen? It’s shockingly difficult, which is why it hasn’t been done yet. If vacuum decay is possible, the most likely mechanism for us to find out is if it were to actually happen, and because the bubble expands at the speed of light, we wouldn’t know until the moment it absorbed us. It isn’t particularly comforting news.

Does Sabrina Pasterski’s holographic theory make her the next Einstein?

Nevertheless, there are hints we can look for. The precise values of various constants, from the mass of the Higgs boson to the strength of the strong force, can tell us a great deal about whether each of those particles and forces are stable. If they’re all stable, great! If any of them aren’t, those are potentially liable to decay and cause a bubble of true vacuum – not great! Those measurements need to be almost unimaginably precise to know for sure, and we haven’t reached sufficient precision yet. Right now, our best measurements seem to say our universe is right on the edge of stability, and increased precision in those numbers could push us over to either side.

The other hint would be to look for those very tiny bubbles of true vacuum that wouldn’t spread and devour the universe. In recent years, researchers have suggested that the area between two colliding black holes might be the perfect spot for these bubbles to pop up. That tracks with the universe not yet having been enveloped by nothingness, because the bubbles would probably immediately fall into the black holes and be safely contained before they could spread. But if there’s enough time between true vacuum foaming into existence and being swallowed up, various bubbles could merge together and form tiny black holes, which we might be able to detect as they evaporate away.

My two cents is that the possibility of finding any proof of a true vacuum lies so far in the future that it’s probably best to cosy up with a nice movie and try to forget about the potential looming, unpredictable destruction of the entire universe. Can I recommend The NeverEnding Story?

Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming

New Scientist November 16, 2026

Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.

“What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a new group of people?” says Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began

Rødhals Man lived some 6000 years ago, and was discovered on the small island of Sejerø in Denmark in the 1950s, buried in a shell midden – an ancient accumulation of discarded sea shells and other domestic refuse. Previous investigations have indicated he was unusual. He lived some time between about 3800 and 3900 BC, near the start of the Neolithic period in the area, when diets changed to consist predominantly of terrestrial food produced by farmers. And yet Rødhals Man, with his genetic ancestry typical of the local Mesolithic Ertebølle culture of hunter-gatherers, didn’t seem to have eaten that diet: a study in 1981 indicated that he ate mainly seafood.

Advertisement

“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” says Fischer.

To get a better idea of what was going on, Fischer and his colleagues have now looked at the levels of rare isotopes of elements including carbon, nitrogen and sulphur in several of the man’s bones, which renewed at different rates during his life, preserving different snapshots in time. The researchers also analysed the chemical signatures in one of his teeth, which preserve a record of diet from childhood. Collectively, the data gave the team an opportunity to look for clues about how Rødhals Man’s diet changed over the 30 to 40 years of his life.

“You can see that most of the time, the primary food source is what we call the eelgrass biotype. This is not eelgrass itself, but the animals that live in the thick forests of this sea grass in shallow water,” says team member John Meadows at Kiel University in Germany. This could have been animals like molluscs, flatfish or eels, he says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

But from the age of about 11 onwards, Rødhals Man’s diet became unlike that of any Mesolithic hunter-gatherer recorded so far, with increasing amounts of terrestrial, probably farmed, protein.

Rødhals Man’s burial also shares more similarities with burials of Early Neolithic farmers than those of Late Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, because his bones lacked an added coating of ochre staining and his grave featured a stone frame.

The evidence leads Meadows to suggest that Rødhals Man interacted with the Neolithic farmers and adopted some components of farmer culture while maintaining the way of life of his ancestors on the small island. Sejerø is just 12 square kilometres in area, but is only about 5 kilometres from Zealand, which is around 7000 square kilometres.

An analysis of ancient genomes has revealed that the descendants of Stone Age farmers in Europe and hunter-gatherers gained more genes from the latter group than expected

“He was on a tiny island with very little in the way of wild terrestrial resources to live on,” says Meadows. “He may have spent part of the year living in a farming community on Zealand and part living on the island and only eating fish.”

“It is quite amazing that all this information could be retrieved from one single skeleton,” says Mathias Currat at the University of Geneva. “I think this is an interesting story, which probably represents part of the main story in this area.”

It would be unusual to change diet in this way, says Marcello Mannino at Aarhus University in Denmark. “Such cultures were often very conservative in terms of their dietary habits, because diet was interlinked with the subsistence practices that shaped that culture together with religious and cosmological views of the world.”

He says it is likely that the Neolithic farmers probably first occupied areas where soil conditions were better, such as in central Zealand, and were slower to inhabit more marginal areas. “We need to find more human remains that span the transition to try to understand how it happened,” he says.

Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere

New Scientist November 13, 2026

If you listen closely to an underwater seagrass meadow, you can hear the actual sound of photosynthesis. During the day, tiny bubbles of oxygen float from the blades of the seagrass to the ocean’s surface. The popping sound these bubbles make when they burst is like “tinkling bells”, according to Carlos Duarte, a keen scuba diver and expert on ocean noise at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia.

“As long as the meadows are more than 2 metres beneath the ocean surface, when the bubbles break they generate a vibration that is in the same sound frequency as bells,” he says. “If you have a hydrophone and you quantify this, then you could even calculate photosynthetic rates.”

But most of the time, this remarkable acoustic phenomenon is drowned out by human-caused noise pollution. There is barely a habitat on Earth that isn’t subjected to anthropogenic noise pollution from boats, cars, aeroplanes or any number of other noisy human activities. In the oceans, ambient noise levels are about 10 times higher than they were in 1950. “To understand the impact of noise on the marine environment, we need to imagine ourselves living in a great party, 24/7, throughout our entire lifespan. It is really a persistent and chronic impact,” says Duarte.

Advertisement

Human noise pollution drives monkeys to rely on communication by scent

Now, scientists are learning more about how serious and widespread the impact of noise pollution is on wildlife subjected to it – and the results are disturbing. A meta-analysis published in the journal Science earlier this month looked at 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species, spanning six continents. It concluded that noise pollution altered at least one physiological, developmental or behavioural trait in 80 per cent of the species studied, with the effects occurring in every habitat. In short, noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of a huge range of animals across land and sea.

“Every ecosystem, or every major habitat, is affected by noise,” says Hansjoerg Kunc at Queen’s University Belfast in the UK, who conducted the analysis with his colleague Rouven Schmidt. “We looked at a lot of different physiological responses [in wildlife] and basically nearly all of them found an effect for noise.”

In general, noise forces predators to work 2.5 times harder to catch 25 per cent less prey overall, reported Kunc and Schmidt. Creatures like bats expend more energy and are less successful at hunting when subjected to ambient noise, while noise from ship engines disrupts communication and disorientates marine life such as whales and dolphins.

Free newsletter

Animals also learn to avoid noisy habitats, which shrinks their available area and therefore limits their population size. Dolphins, for example, actively avoid noisy coastlines, while bats have been shown to avoid roads that were noisy during a motorcycle rally long after the vehicles had left the area.

In noise-polluted areas, mortality among animals studied jumped by 138 per cent, on average. Sometimes, the death is instantaneous: underwater explosions from oil and gas exploration, for example, can cause a fish’s bladder to explode. Other times, it is slower and more painful, such as gradual starvation from reduced hunting success.

Not every animal suffers a negative impact from noise pollution, Kunc notes. Some predators might benefit from noise – enjoying increased hunting success when human noise flushes their prey out of its hiding place, for example.

But even though some animals might benefit in the short term, the overall effect is negative on the ecosystem, he says, because its natural dynamics are being warped by external stress. “If you think about an ecosystem, all species in this ecosystem have adapted to the way it should be,” he says. “So, from my point of view, it doesn’t really matter who is more affected or less affected. It is changing, and that is what we want to avoid, because we want to protect a functioning ecosystem.”

Powerful new book explores how noise has taken over the world

Kunc wants more thought to be given to protecting the soundscape of the natural world, alongside the conservation of physical habitats. “We know that the acoustic environment is a strong evolutionary force, and we have shown that it really changes the physiology, development and behaviour [of wildlife],” he says.

Some efforts are already under way. In the US, national parks such as Yellowstone have designated quiet zones, which reduce the amount of noise made by visitors by 3 to 5 decibels according to Rachel Buxton, formerly of the US National Parks Service and now at Carleton University in Canada.

She thinks more can be done to reduce noise pollution, especially in protected areas, such as by closing roads to traffic during certain periods or re-routing aircraft to shadow busy road networks and avoid wilderness areas.

“Think of the Grand Canyon. We wouldn’t dream of building a giant building in the middle of the Grand Canyon, and yet there are overflight tours that pass over the airspace all the time, polluting the whole space with noise,” she points out.

Pitcairn Island, one of the remotest places on Earth, was once home to mutineers. Today it’s a trailblazer in biodiversity protection with lessons for us all

We also need to tackle noise pollution at sea, says Duarte. He argues for enforcing acoustic limits in marine protected areas, which could include setting noise limits for ships and other marine activities.

New technologies also give hope for a quieter future. Emerging evidence suggests that electric vehicles are quieter and therefore less disturbing to most wildlife. Similarly, electric motorboats and ferries could lead to quieter shorelines for marine life, says Duarte. “Moving to electric mobility, which we’ve done largely on land, to the ocean will immediately reduce noise around the shorelines,” he says, pointing out that countries such as Sweden are leading the way in creating a market for electric boats.

The covid-19 pandemic offers an insight into what happens in the natural world when the noise stops. Noise pollution across oceans dropped by 20 per cent during the crisis, says Duarte, and led to extraordinary sightings of marine life returning to busy waterways and city shorelines, and the sound of birdsong filling cities.

Unlike pollutants that linger in the atmosphere, shutting off the noise immediately removes the problem, Duarte points out. “As soon as the noise stops, then animals claim back their ancestral territory and home,” he says.

Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?

New Scientist November 13, 2026

The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.

The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

The El Niño climate phase, which has already warmed surface waters in the tropical Pacific to record temperatures and continues to heat up, tends to keep the vortex strong in autumn and early winter. Then, in late winter, it often weakens the vortex, allowing that cold air to spill southwards into Europe and sometimes North America.

Advertisement

But on 10 November, the polar vortex weakened to the point that it broke down, with the winds reversing direction to blow weakly from the east. While these collapses happen every few years, they almost never occur in November. This is the earliest it has happened since weather balloon records began in the 1950s, beating the old record by 18 days.

This may have been due to random fluctuations in the atmosphere. It is also possible, however, that the extremely strong El Niño could have sped up the weakening of the polar vortex that typically happens later in the winter, though that isn’t proven, according to Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s weather service.

Free newsletter

“There probably is some kind of El Niño influence on it,” he says. “That would be my suspicion, but we don’t know that for sure.”

As east-to-west trade winds weaken during El Niño and the warm water they built up in the western Pacific washes back eastwards, a low-pressure centre of warm, rising air moves eastwards with it. This causes extra waviness in the jet stream, another band of strong westerly winds that circles the globe, except further south and lower in the atmosphere than the polar vortex. The jet stream meanders further southwards around Alaska, deepening a low-pressure system there called the Aleutian low.

But the El Niño-linked wave doesn’t just propagate side to side in the jet stream. It can also propagate upwards into the stratosphere, where the polar vortex is. As the air gets thinner, the wave’s amplitude gets bigger until it crashes into the polar vortex like a wave crashing onto a beach, says Scaife. And while the polar vortex is westerly, these waves carry easterly momentum.

“When they dump that momentum, they push the polar vortex against its flow, and they weaken it,” he says.

5 graphs that show how the record-breaking El Niño will affect the world

But another reason for the polar vortex breakdown could be a high-pressure “blocking” system that developed over Scandinavia in recent weeks, which blocked the jet stream and caused large meanders in it. This waviness could also have weakened the polar vortex through the same wave-breaking process, regardless of El Niño.

“I would be wary of saying it was caused by El Niño,” says Andrew Charlton-Perez at the University of Reading, UK. “I would say the blocking high is probably more important.”

The reversal of the polar vortex isn’t related to the current cold weather in the UK. But it could bring even more cold, snowy weather in the coming weeks.

A polar vortex breakdown is also known as a sudden stratospheric warming event. As the winds weaken, high-level air rushes in over the north pole, increasing atmospheric pressure and raising temperatures, just as pumping up a bike tyre warms it up.

Meanwhile, over the following weeks, cold surface-level air can descend from the Arctic into northern Europe. A polar vortex breakdown preceded the “Beast from the East” cold snap in 2018, when blizzards covered much of the UK in snow and killed 10 people.

While the polar vortex is expected to strengthen towards the end of November, bringing warmer weather, it could break down again this winter, Scaife warns.

“The risk of cold easterlies this winter is increasing,” he says.

Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight

New Scientist November 13, 2026

For the first time, researchers have built a quantum clock that uses light from the sun as a key component. It could be used to diagnose shifts in the sun’s velocity or probe processes on its surface.

This is not your mother’s sundial. People have known that they can keep track of time with sunlight ever since antiquity. But contemporary record-breaking timekeepers, which are called optical clocks, derive their accuracy from quantum mechanical effects and typically have atoms that have been isolated from the external world at their core. Now, Scott Diddams at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and his colleagues have built an optical clock that relies on sunlight instead.

In a typical optical clock, an electron within an atom is made to oscillate between two energy levels, and an ultra-stable laser is tuned, or locked, to the frequency of that oscillation. Next, these oscillations – the ups and downs of the light waves that comprise the laser beam – are translated into usable ticks of a clock. To do this, researchers use a device called a frequency comb, which turns visible light into microwaves that can be processed by standard electronics.

Advertisement

First working nuclear clock heralds a new era in timekeeping

In the new experiment, the researchers still used a laser and a frequency comb to build their clock, but the role of the atom was played by a process that happens near the sun.

Specifically, instead of locking their laser to an electron’s jumps within an atom, the researchers locked it to a process where sunlight causes similar jumps as it hits iron atoms in our star’s atmosphere. This process leaves a signature in the spectrum of colours that comprise sunlight, so the team collected sunlight into a special fibre and fed it into the rest of the clock. This type of solar optical clock has never been built before.

While the new clock doesn’t rival the best atomic optical clocks in accuracy, the researchers showed that it could possibly be used as a tool for studying stars. During the partial solar eclipse in 2024, they observed a signature shift in the sunlight’s spectrum due to the moon passing in front of the star. If the clock was fed light from a faraway star in place of sunlight, similar shifts could indicate the presence of orbiting exoplanets, which raises the possibility of the new clock design becoming a tool for astronomical discovery. In this case, however, starlight would have to be collected through large telescopes, sometimes over long periods of time.

Researchers have designed a quantum version of a pendulum clock. It could shed light on timekeeping in the quantum realm

Piet Schmidt at the National Metrology Institute of Germany says that the new work is interesting because it demonstrates an optical clock design that leverages light from the stars rather than being based exclusively on objects under tight control in the lab.

But as an astronomical instrument, it doesn’t yet surpass existing methods for studying light from stars, and for very distant stars, the new clock’s usefulness would be seriously limited by how faint their light is, says Schmidt.

There may, however, be advantages in studying the properties of our sun, he says. For example, the clock could probe eruptive events, sunspots and the effects of solar “wind” made from streams of charged particles in the outer layers of the sun’s atmosphere.

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.28485

Environment Southland councillors fire up over wilding conifer threat

New Zealand Herald November 16, 2026

Wilding conifers pictured in Mid Dome, Southland. The Department of Conservation describes the self-seeding trees as invasive weeds. Photo / Mid Dome Wilding Trees Charitable Trust

The ongoing threat of wilding conifers has drawn a strong response from Environment Southland councillors, with one member saying “we’re stuffed”.

Described by the Department of Conservation as invasive weeds that threaten the country’s unique landscapes, the rogue trees have been a hot topic at the council for years.

Councillor Eric Roy said at a meeting last week that he was “grieving” over the issue and asked if DNA seed sourcing was an option so that trees could be linked back to offending forest owners.

Council team leader Jolie Hazley explained that she had looked into that option, but it required permission from property owners to gather DNA.

The response drew a strong reaction from Roy: “We’re stuffed, we’re stuffed then! We can’t do it, we’re stuffed.”

Mana whenua representative Evelyn Cook asked if genetic modification of trees was an option.

Cook said the country was “ridden with introduced pest species” and called for better management.

“Because the money that we are spending on managing introduced pest species, which is what we’re talking about, is money that could be better invested in more positive things for our country,” she said.

“So they’re reaping the economic benefit, but they’re creating an economic and environmental liability.”

Councillor Roger Hodson said wilding control was underfunded but added that not all responsibility sat with council.

“I guess my biggest fear is that we are planning to fail.”

A report prepared for the meeting showed a regional working group would be established following a workshop with Southland District Council in September.

The workshop presentation highlighted wilding conifer impacts, the report said, including landscape change, farmland loss, biodiversity loss, ecosystems and water yield, wildfire risk, and habitats for pest animals.

Environment Southland has secured $4.29 million in funding under the MPI Wilding Conifer Control Programme to date, including $2.49m for the 2026/27 financial year.

It’s “a bit of a myth” that motorists can be fined for driving too slowly – but they can be prosecuted for being inconsiderate on the roads, police say.

Acting director of road policing Inspector Peter McKennie told Herald NOW’s Ryan Bridge TODAY police didn’t want to prosecute people for holding up traffic, preferring to educate them on how to be considerate drivers.

Slower drivers should keep an eye on traffic in their rear-view mirrors, he said.

“Particularly in the holiday season if you’re towing a boat or a caravan, you know, pull over and let other people pass - just do the courteous thing.”

Slower drivers shouldn’t speed up as they approach a passing lane or wider stretch of road, he said.

“Keep travelling at the same speed, let the other traffic pass. That’s what the passing lanes or slow vehicle lanes are designed for.

“Use them, be courteous on the roads and avoid everyone’s frustration. We want everyone to get safely through their journey.”

McKennie said he could “feel the pain” of those stuck behind a dawdling driver, but sometimes patience was needed.

“It’s not always safe to pull over and it’s not always safe to pass.

“The people in front of you might be able to see a hazard that you can’t, such as loose stock on the road, someone turning right; they might have slowed down to let a child or someone with mobility issues cross the road.

“And if you overtake them in those circumstances where you can’t clearly see, then you’re the one posing the risk.”

People were starting to relax as the holiday season approached, but they shouldn’t relax on the road, McKennie added.

“Think about when you’re going to be travelling ... make sure you’re not drinking too much the night before and you’re having a good rest,” he said.

“Above all, make sure you’ve got your seatbelts on, make sure you’re not distracted by your phone and everything else. Focus on driving safely.

“We want everyone to get to Christmas and into the New Year safely. This is never a good time for people to be having grief due to someone being lost on the roads.”

Flood risk for hundreds of Auckland homes drops, council hopes

New Zealand Herald November 16, 2026

A boarded up weatherboard house, jacked up from its foundations, behind tall hurricane fencing, in Māngere, Auckland. Photo / RNZ, Kate Newton

By Kate Newton of RNZ

Hundreds of homes in one of Auckland’s most flood-prone suburbs are now better protected from future floods.

The Te Ararata Creek project in Māngere is the first to be completed as part of a long-term Auckland Council programme prompted by the devastating Anniversary Day floods in 2023.

The $750 million Making Space For Water programme will fund dozens of similar flood resilience projects across the region over the next decade.

It includes a mixture of infrastructure upgrades and deliberately creating space for floodwater to safely flow.

The tidal Te Ararata Creek flows through a historic wetland and floodplain in the heart of Māngere.

Already prone to flooding, it backed up with debris during the 2023 storm and overflowed into the surrounding streets.

Newly built Kāinga Ora houses were among hundreds of homes in the area that flooded, some of them to ceiling level.

“Bader Drive was basically another river,” Te Ararata Stream Team trustee and Māngere local Deon Dean said.

“All the neighbours were getting out of Comet Crescent because it was about up the roof. All the houses around Ventura [St] were all flooded – there were some houses that were uplifted.”

One of the major culprits was debris building up in the narrow twin box culverts that ran underneath Walmsley Rd, a major thoroughfare into Māngere.

Project manager Leighton Gillespie said trampolines, picnic tables and broken fences all ended up trapped behind the culverts, backing water upstream.

The culverts and road running over them have been replaced with an 18m bridge, Gillespie said.

“That’s opened the waterway a lot. We’ve returned quite a bit of that to natural stream as well and planted the edges of the stream to allow the ecology and biodiversity to come back.”

A short walk away, at the project’s second site, several houses that were classified as high risk after the floods were removed as part of the council’s buy-out scheme.

The creek there used to be a straight, narrow channel with steep banks, but the extra space had allowed the council to create a 40m-wide, gently sloped floodplain planted with natives.

“We’ve dropped the level of earth down by a metre-and-a-half, two metres in some spots,” Gillespie said.

The stream now had a meandering shape, designed to slow and control the flow of water during heavy rainfall.

The project also included a debris trap, formed of vertical metal beams placed at intervals across the floodplain.

“Before, all of that debris was collecting in a small, two-and-a-half metre-sized area, so it was a lot more susceptible to blockage,” Gillespie said.

With a much wider span, the debris would be able to collect behind the structure without blocking the flow of water and would also be easier to clear.

Newly planted kahikatea saplings would eventually grow big enough to take the place of the metal beams, forming a natural structure in future.

Te Ararata Stream Team trustee Pragna Patel said the change was enormous.

“It was an engineered channel that was basically a drain – and it had been given the kind of attention of a drain.”

Auckland Council modelling estimated that the project, which cost $47m, would immediately lower the flood risk to hundreds of homes.

That included about 40 houses that would no longer be exposed to ‘intolerable risk to life’ – where at least half a metre of flooding was projected during severe rainfall.

Another 110 households would be protected from water coming inside their homes, while hundreds more houses would no longer get any significant flooding on their property.

“The cost of recovery, the cost of displacing families during a massive event is huge,” Gillespie said.

“An investment upfront in something that can significantly reduce the effects of that flooding is definitely worth it.”

The completed project was just a start, with a water retention basin planned for Moyle Park upstream of the first project.

“If you imagine this piece being how the water gets out of the bath, we’ve made the plug bigger,” he said.

“The other interventions are worth the investment now.”

Council head of sustainable partnerships Tom Mansell said dozens of similar projects would go ahead across Auckland, as part of a 30-year programme to make the city more resilient as the risk of floods grew.

Like the Māngere projects, some will be on land previously occupied by houses that flooded catastrophically in 2023.

“[For] probably the last 80 years, what we’ve tried to do with stormwater is pipe it, channel it, and get it out as quickly as possible,” Mansell said.

“What we’re finding now with the changing climate and increase in rainfall events, we can no longer carry on doing that – so the whole concept of making space for water is allowing the water to spread out.”

It was impossible to eliminate flooding, he said.

“What we’re trying to do is reduce the risk.”

Tens of thousands of houses were still vulnerable because previous planning regimes had allowed them to be built in floodplains and flood-prone areas.

The council was trying to prevent future housing going ahead in floodplains through its proposed Plan Change 120, which – among other things – would allow it to down-zone areas at high risk from flood hazards.

Protecting those already at risk would take time, Mansell said.

“We’ve spent the last 80 years getting ourselves into this situation, it’s going to take decades to start building our way out of this.”

Don’t count on getting the inheritance you expect

New Zealand Herald November 16, 2026

It is important that people do not assume that they are going to get a particular level of inheritance from their parents, say financial experts. Photo / RNZ

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

If you’re counting on getting an inheritance, be prepared for it not to arrive as quickly, or be as large, as you might be expecting.

That is the message from Public Trust, which manages more than 8000 estates every year.

JB Were has estimated that total inheritances are likely to grow from about $27 billion in 2024 to a cumulative $1.5 trillion by 2050, or about $100b a year. Annual deaths are expected to increase from 37,000 a year to 66,000 within 50 years.

But Andrew Bhimy, general manager of retail at Public Trust, said it was not a straightforward story of money passing directly to the younger generation.

Last year, there was $514.2 million distributed to estate beneficiaries by Public Trust across 4261 estates. Its research showed that almost half of New Zealanders had already been left some form of financial legacy.

Bhimy said some people were relying on inheritances as part of their financial planning but it was increasingly the case that they were receiving them later in life.

While some were opting to use the money to help them through retirement, others were deciding to skip a generation.

“We definitely live in a world where there is a lot of financial pressure at the moment, and inheritance is one mechanism that can be available to people to help them cope with some of the stuff that they’ve got to cope with to make ends meet and get the bills paid,” he said.

“We definitely see some of that. But at the other end of the spectrum, we also have people who are saying, ‘hey, actually, I’m pretty well set up. I don’t necessarily need this inheritance that might be coming my way’, and they’re looking at amending their wills to pass inheritance from their parents on to their children so that they get the benefits.”

He said it was important that people did not assume that they were going to get a particular level of inheritance from their parents, and did not make plans around how to spend the money before they received it.

The cost of living longer could reduce the amount of money to be handed down.

“Quite a lot can happen between now and when a parent passes away that can erode that inheritance, right? If you think about how long people are living these days, the cost of rest homes, the cost of end-of-life care, you can get into a situation where there’s a gap between what you think might be available versus what actually turns up once the estate has been administered.”

The wealth to be handed down is not evenly distributed. While Stats NZ data shows people aged over 75 have the highest average net worth, the wealthiest 20% have almost two-and-a-half times as much wealth as a median than the next wealthiest 20%. The least wealthy group has no net worth to speak of.

Bhimy said people would often first inherit the responsibility of caring for their parents, and the need to navigate care costs, before they received an inheritance.

“The challenge at the moment is much of the wealth that’s being passed on in New Zealand tends to be tied up in property. So it really corresponds with what property values are doing. And what we’ve seen over the last few years is the flattening of the property market.

“And you definitely see that translating through into the average value of the estates that we’re taking on. And often there can be a little bit of disappointment from beneficiaries in terms of what a house, for example, is often able to yield, particularly after you take out the agent costs versus what they might have imagined it was going to be worth.”

Bhimy said it was important for people on both sides of the inheritance to have a good conversation about it.

“Now, that’s easier said than done, depending on different families and different family dynamics. But the greater clarity the person who is leaving their inheritance behind can create through the quality of the will that they write and the clarity of instructions around how an inheritance will work, both in terms of the big financial assets, but also that sentimental stuff that can really trip people up after they’ve gone, then the more seamless the process of estate administration tends to be and the faster it can occur.”

He said people who were waiting for an inheritance needed to be patient.

“People tend to think that it’s all very simple and it will only take a few weeks, whereas what I would say is that an average estate distribution takes six months and they can take significantly longer if there’s problems with the validity of the will, if there’s any challenges from beneficiaries ... or if there are any beneficiaries that are hard to track down and there needs to be time allowed for them to come forward. So all of that can result in delays before money can be administered. So if people are making plans, or have booked a holiday based on that money, that can really trip them up if there are challenges with the administration of the estate.”

Shoplifting: 92% of the 155 worst shoplifters were violent, data shows

New Zealand Herald November 16, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

New data shows most of the country’s most prolific shoplifters are using violence.

Data provided exclusively to Newstalk ZB by retail crime intelligence platform Auror shows 92% of the 155 worst shoplifters between July 2024 and July 2026 were violent as part of their offending.

Retailers saw more than 14,000 repeat offenders during that time, with 30% of them displaying violent behaviour.

The most prolific typically stole high-value chocolate and confectionery, apparel, and health and beauty products.

They included someone connected to more than 155 events and $110,000 worth of products stolen from stores across the North Island during April.

ShopCare NZ’s National Customer Aggression Survey, released last month, found 91% of retail workers experienced violence or abuse in the past 12 months.

Auror vice-president of trust and safety Nick McDonnell said more than 40 serious incidents are recorded in Auror every day involving assault, threats or abuse.

He said repeat offenders are driving the majority of harm.

“The top 10% of offenders are causing 60% of the crime. Of that top 10%, they are four times more likely to be violent.”

McDonnell said retail crime was also often linked to organised crime, with multi-store offenders connected to more than two accomplices on average.

He said the items being stolen were also consistent with steal-to-order schemes.

“These are high value items that can be taken out of stores, sort of more easily than other things, and then they can be quite quickly turned into money on black markets.”

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said she’s seen shocking CCTV footage of violent offending in stores.

“I’ve seen a video where a customer has come up to a staff member who is working behind the cash register and they have a 5 or 6 second conversation and the customer then punches the female worker in the face.”

She said Retail NZ members are also reporting that people are carrying concealed weapons.

“People with knives, machetes down their trousers, screwdrivers, hammers – all of those sorts of things are being brought into store and threatening staff.”

The data comes ahead of the Black Friday and Christmas shopping period, which is usually the busiest time of the year for the retail sector.

Young said retailers should remember to always try to de-escalate agitated customers.

“Try and get some distance between you and the person that is agitated, make sure that you call your manager as soon as possible and try and encourage the person to get out of the store.”

McDonnell said identifying repeat offenders is hugely important for retailers and facial recognition technology has had positive results so far.

“We have seen a retailer in New Zealand use live facial recognition with all of the appropriate signage up and the appropriate safeguards.

“They have seen around a 40% reduction in, crime happening in their stores, and some of these stores have had zero events happening.”

Lachlan Rennie is an Auckland-based multimedia journalist for Newstalk ZB covering justice, defence, technology, and general news. He previously studied journalism at the New Zealand Broadcasting School before joining NZME in 2024.

One in four Māori in the Waiariki region is not enrolled with a GP, a new report shows.

It also found lower immunisation and bowel, breast and cervical cancer screening rates for Māori compared with non-Māori.

The figures, revealed in Te Taura Ora o Waiariki Iwi Māori Partnership Board’s latest monitoring report, have prompted it to ask the next Government to commit to four changes they say would improve access to healthcare for whānau Māori.

The changes are supported by a provider which says it is increasingly challenged to sustain services.

The Te Taura Ora report found 66.9% of tamariki Māori were fully immunised at 24 months, compared with 89.2% of non-Māori.

Bowel screening coverage was 45.4% for Māori and 58% for non-Māori. Breast screening coverage was 57.3% for Māori compared with 69.7% for non-Māori.

Cervical screening coverage was 66.5% for Māori and 70.5% for non-Māori.

It also found one in four Māori in Waiariki was not enrolled with a GP. Of those, about one in four had not seen their doctor in the past 12 months.

Te Taura Ora tumu whakarae [chief executive] Hinemoa Awatere said the numbers showed “how vulnerable our whānau are”.

“It underlines the need for healthcare that is accessible, locally delivered and responsive to the needs of whānau.”

Awatere said the Covid-19 response showed kaupapa Māori providers’ effectiveness in reaching “whānau where they are”.

“We’re asking the next Government to shift 25% to 30% of existing community health funding to these providers, with long-term contracts and fair funding so they can deliver where they’re needed most.

“This is about making better use of existing health funding, not asking for more.”

The board also wanted consequences for services “that continue to fail to close long-standing equity gaps”.

Noelene Rapana, chief executive of Rotorua kaupapa Māori health provider Korowai Aroha, said it supported Te Taura Ora’s four requests, which would help kaupapa Māori providers continue providing services “where the need is greatest”.

Rapana said Korowai Aroha had received funding from the Health NZ-funded Comprehensive Primary Community Care Team, “but that support is no longer available”.

The funding supported one fulltime equivalent registered nurse, but could also be used for Nurse Practitioner, GP or kaiāwhina [healthcare assistant] hours, she said.

She was aware the funding was from a three-year programme but was “hopeful” it would continue.

“Like other kaupapa Māori providers, we are increasingly challenged to sustain these services without appropriate funding, even though the need has not gone away.”

Rapana said longer-term contracts would provide certainty and stability for planning and retention and growth of its workforce.

“Sustainable investment in kaupapa Māori providers would help ensure these services can continue and grow.”

Rapana said it worked with kaupapa Māori and iwi providers to support whānau not enrolled with a GP.

Its free drop-in and outreach clinics were available for unenrolled whānau.

Ngāi Te Rangi chief executive Dr Paora Stanley said redirecting some community health funding to kaupapa Māori health providers was “a no-brainer”.

Such providers had “a proven record” of high uptake and “higher-quality” interaction, he said.

In a November 5 statement, Stanley said the next Government must confront the “continuing failure” to provide accessible healthcare for Māori.

“Well-established” barriers included cost, transport difficulties and services that did not adequately reach vulnerable communities, Stanley said.

For more than 18 years, Ngāi Te Rangi’s mobile health service had taken doctors directly into vulnerable communities, operating five nights a week and providing free care to Māori and non-Māori.

“When a parent cannot afford the appointment, has no vehicle or cannot get their sick child to a doctor, we remove some of those barriers by bringing the service into their community.”

Stanley said it showed “practical alternatives already exist” and the challenge was investing in approaches that worked.

Health NZ community and primary care funding acting director Martin Hefford said Korowai Aroha was one provider supported by the Comprehensive Primary Care Team.

The “time-limited” three-year programme was established in Budget 2022. Health NZ extended the programme to December 2026.

The programme supported roles such as care coordinators (which could be nurses), extended care paramedics, physiotherapists and clinical pharmacists, he said.

Hefford said the extension allowed time for primary health organisations and GPs to consider future arrangements for these roles.

Health NZ was considering support options for these roles and would provide updates this month.

Hefford said Health NZ increased general practice capitation funding significantly in the past two years, including a “record” $175 million uplift in 2025/26 and a further $120.6m in annual funding from 2026/27 for primary care services.

Additional funding gave the sector “more of an opportunity” to decide what mix of staff to employ and achieve the best patient outcomes.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Auckland fake visa claims: Immigration NZ investigates unlicensed adviser

New Zealand Herald November 16, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Immigration officials are investigating allegations an unlicensed immigration adviser has provided fake visas to clients in Auckland.

The Herald understands at least 20 people have complained to Immigration New Zealand (INZ) about the adviser, claiming they were unwittingly scammed.

Contact senior investigative reporter Michael Morrah

The adviser is accused of secretly manipulating scores in English language tests without clients realising. For some visas, applicants must demonstrate they can read and understand English.

It’s understood some visas were approved by INZ based on the fraudulent English test results and other applicants were given completely fabricated eVisas.

The visa the adviser is accused of forging is the Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV) – a temporary visa that allows migrants to work for three to five years in New Zealand for an approved employer.

AEWV visas are issued electronically – often via an adviser, if one was engaged.

Since 2018 the eVisas have been PDF documents, which immigration lawyers have told the Herald are easy to fake using editing software.

Immigration New Zealand (INZ) confirmed it was making inquiries but would not say how many migrants might be implicated.

“INZ is investigating allegations around the issuing of fake visas. INZ does not comment on active investigations, as doing so could compromise the integrity of the investigation and impact those involved,” INZ’s national investigations manager Jason Perry told the Herald.

The Immigration Advisers Authority (IAA), the government body that issues licences to advisers, maintains a register and investigates complaints, would not say whether it was also investigating.

The IAA is part of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) and operates separately from INZ.

IAA acting national manager occupational regulation Bevan Yee said anyone providing advice must be licensed.

“Providing immigration advice without being licensed or exempt is an offence under the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act 2007. It is also an offence to hold yourself out as an immigration adviser if you are neither licensed nor exempt,” Yee told the Herald.

Alastair McClymont, who’s been an immigration lawyer for 30 years, told the Herald he had seen a surge in complaints about both licensed advisers, those masquerading as advisers and fake visas.

“Ten years ago, we’d get a couple a year, now we’re pretty much one a week,” he said.

McClymont believes the profession has become a “free for all” where some prey on vulnerable migrants, charging thousands of dollars and promising to sort out their immigration woes.

He said when a visa is declined, some advisers then create fake visas for their clients and demand “fat commissions”.

McClymont said some migrants have only discovered their paperwork is fake when trying to travel overseas.

He was also critical of Government agencies charged with investigating complaints.

“I think there’s a view out there that there’s no real enforcement. There seems to be a feeling among clients that they are being held solely responsible for being victims,” he said.

Asked how authorities were dealing with complaints about scammers, McClymont believed the clients seeking visas were met with “relative ambivalence” from authorities who, in his opinion, wanted to “get rid of them, rather than treat them as victims”.

However, Yee said the IAA takes allegations of unlicensed immigration advice seriously.

Figures from the IAA show complaints about advisers doubled in the past year.

Between 2024 and 2025, the IAA received 72 complaints about advisers with that number increasing to 143 in the 12 months to 2026.

There has also been a significant increase in the number of complaints received specifically about unlicensed advisers.

When asked what was driving the trend, the IAA said it didn’t want to speculate on the reason.

Mahafrin Variava, an associate at law firm McVeagh Fleming, told the Herald she has seen migrants being given poor advice and also situations where fraudulent visa documents were issued.

“In most cases, these individuals genuinely believed they had engaged a licensed professional and had no reason to suspect the authenticity of the documents,” Variava told the Herald.

She said high demand for immigration advice was one of the factors contributing to the problem and changes to immigration rules had made the system complex to navigate.

“This creates opportunities for some to market themselves as ‘experts’,” she said.

She said some of the scams were sophisticated.

“Technology advances have made it much easier to create a very convincing-looking visa with credentials that an individual cannot independently verify.”

The Herald has seen multiple examples of fake visas posted to a migrant support group on Facebook.

Variava said many fake eVisas look legitimate with real business names but can contain made-up names of human resources staff or company addresses that don’t exist.

She said the example of the fake eVisa pictured above contains a font size INZ does not use and it states in the document that the client “must be paid at or above $3500 per month”.

“This is never how INZ will issue a visa.” INZ would always put the hourly rate in there, she said, not $3500 per month.

Variava said in her experience, INZ did act quickly when bogus advisers were operating in New Zealand.

Michael Morrah is a senior investigative reporter/team leader at the Herald. He won News Journalist of the Year at the 2025 Voyager Media Awards and has twice been named reporter of the year at the NZ Television Awards. He has been a broadcast journalist for 20 years and joined the Herald’s video team in July 2024.
