Letters: Wales deserve praise and the All Blacks need to get to work before facing England

New Zealand Herald November 16, 2026

Rod Emmerson's cartoon of Simon Watts after New Zealand was awarded the Fossil of the Day award yet again at this year's COP31 in Turkiye.

Well done Wales; more work needed All Blacks

Congratulations to Wales on a well-deserved win over the All Blacks at the Principality Stadium.

Wales’ defence with more than 300 tackles was monumental. The All Blacks were held up three times over the Welsh line in the second half.

The All Blacks’ 10 player changes were clearly too many, so continuity and combinations were lost. The backline attack from the All Blacks was the poorest seen in years – no variation, no moves, no captaincy.

The three starting loose forwards were the only bright spot. Ratima’s slowness behind the pack gave the Welsh forwards all the time they needed to be all over the All Blacks’ backline. Mo’unga had a shocker, so did Beauden Barrett.

Training for next week’s All Blacks team against England must include how to go low and score tries, how to get the ball on the ground over the line. Kicks in play and penalties to the line were dreadfully executed against Wales; lots of practice needed there. The All Blacks coaches got a lot wrong in selections and strategy against Wales.

I suggest New Zealand Rugby fly Ardie Savea over to England just to talk to the boys, even if he cannot play. A lot must change to beat England and face France in the Nations Championship final the following weekend.

Gary Carter, Gulf Harbour.

Death-or-glory stuff

Being hungover after the election hangover is bad enough but to be beaten by Wales in rugby is the last straw.

However, one would have to say the defence by Wales was totally death-or-glory stuff, although the All Blacks were a bit one-dimensional when on the Welsh line.

Congratulations, Wales, well done. Having said that, should the All Blacks come up with the same result next week against England, they can kiss their Christmas pudding goodbye when they get back home.

Reg Dempster, Albany.

Where’s the depth?

The defeat by lowly Wales put paid to Dave Rennie’s claim of depth in his squad.

There is clearly an A and B team.

Without Cam Roigard to run the show, the All Blacks looked lost.

The Welsh defence in the second half looked amazing but in truth the All Blacks didn’t pose much of a threat on attack. They just ran straight and hard with no variation.

Reviewing their performance will really hurt.

The good upside must be the morale boost for Wales, who have been getting thrashed for years. Could this win over the All Blacks prove a turning point?

Jock Mac Vicar, Hauraki.

Great for the game

It only goes to prove that all things come to those who are patient.

Wale of a time!

After 73 years, they have now conquered the mighty All Blacks.

Great for the game!

Rob Buchanan, Kerikeri.

Gritty defence

I’ve been an avid All Blacks follower for 70 years and I’ve never seen a better 80-minute gritty defensive effort than what Wales showcased in this one. Three held-up All Black non-tries says it all.

Gary Hollis, Mellons Bay.

Climate hot topic

Rod Emmerson’s cartoon (Nov 15) depicting Simon Watts’ sniffling acceptance of the “Fossil of the Day” award at the COP31 conference in Antalya, Turkiye, on behalf of New Zealand makes a lot of interesting points!

Firstly, the fact that he is arrogantly accepting the award on behalf of New Zealand and yet most Kiwis would be appalled that we could be doing so badly when it comes to our commitments regarding anthropogenic climate change mitigation!

Secondly, that it is a conscious decision by the right-wing Government that we elected three years ago.

Thirdly, that they intend to continue dismantling our climate commitments, including those embedded in Fair Trade Agreements.

Fourthly, that they will protect polluting corporations from being prosecuted in New Zealand and the suggestion that the right wing is getting financial support from them.

Fifthly, the arrogance of travelling (using lots of fossil fuels) to Cop31 and crying crocodile tears about the possible future extinctions in Aotearoa without meaningful mitigation measures!

Well done again, Emmerson.

Dennis Worley, Birkenhead.

Spending what we earn

Johann Nordberg’s analysis (Nov 14) managed to ignore the one factor that really limits what people can spend their income on. If employers paid living wages, their employees could spend more and boost the economy.

Ian Pashby, Montsenelle, France.

Poor decisions

The tsunami of poor decisions, public, private and personal, by the CEOs of our government departments and SOEs demands an urgent independent commission of inquiry.

Bruce Tubb, Ngataringa Bay.

Refused UK asylum seekers to lose five-day grace period and face immediate removal

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 20:06:24 GMT

Home Office plans will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety, say refugee charities

Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow immigration enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice.

Currently, enforced returns for rejected claimants can only take place after a minimum notice period of five working days, which can allow people to launch other legal interventions or prepare themselves for removal.

Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, condemned the change.

“We must treat people with dignity. Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety,” he said.

“We also need to look at the evidence of what works. The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns. If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer.”

Louise Calvey, the executive director at Asylum Matters, said: “People deserve a fair chance to make their claim for help and sanctuary, but forcibly removing people from the country so they don’t get a chance to make their claims won’t fix that.

“Right now, 63% of the population don’t have access to an asylum legal aid provider. What that means is people are attempting to navigate a horrendously complex and hostile system in a new country, often in a second language. In that environment, many people may not have had the proper advice in initial claims, so many who make further claims are found to have a genuine need for support.

“Expelling people from the country to ensure we never get to hear their legitimate claims is nothing to be proud of – it will lead to real injustices.”

Mahmood has tabled an amendment to the immigration and asylum bill that will scrap the five-day timeframe.

Officials would instead be given a six-month period to remove refused asylum seekers and rejected migrants before further notice is required, the Home Office said.

The changes follow a similar approach to the system that Denmark successfully operates, the Home Office has said.

The number of migrants awaiting removal in Denmark was cut from more than 2,185 cases at the end of 2020 to fewer than 1,000 at the end of 2025.

The UK has increased the number of removals since Labour came to power, but faces huge backlogs in asylum applications. As of 30 June 2026, 40,168 people were waiting for an initial asylum decision in the UK. The number of refused applications hit more than 90,000 in the same month, breaking previous records.

There are currently exceptions to the five-day notice period for removals, such as where the removal was disrupted by the individual or was cancelled due to bad weather. In these scenarios, removal can be attempted again without further notice for 21 days.

This timeframe will now be increased to six months under reforms in the bill, which returns to the House of Commons for report stage and third reading on 17 November.

The bill will also introduce a new immigration appeals authority with the aim of speeding up removals and changes to how human rights and modern slavery laws are applied to asylum applications to root out what the government described as “vexatious” claims.

Ministers hope the bill will bring into force proposals that will create a firm but fair asylum system, and which will reduce the pull factors driving illegal immigration.

Under other reforms, the responsibility to make modern slavery decisions for children will be devolved to local safeguarding partners.

This will ensure professionals who already support the child, and are closest to the child, are making the decisions for their future, the Home Office said.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said: “This government is ramping up removals of those with no right to be here, with over 80,000 illegal migrants and foreign nationals returned since the general election. “Now we are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.”

Tuchel and England must learn lessons of history, Seville and Southgateism

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 20:02:09 GMT

Another 3-2 win in Spain brings the lure of a golden new hyper-future – but it did not pan out that way last time

I may have the body of a weak and feeble German, but I have the heart and stomach of a manager of England. And I think it foul scorn that Spain should dare to invade the borders of my realm. Or, for that matter, any one of 24 qualified teams for Euro 2028, because at the end of the day there are no easy games at this level, I’ve always said that.

The words, there, of Thomas Tuchel, England’s Faerie King, speaking to TalkSport shortly after the glorious 3-2 defeat of the Spanish possession armada at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

OK, Tuchel didn’t technically say any of this. He was instead wry and spiky. He made a joke about people moaning about his team on the radio, which just goes to show he’s a good lad and one of us (disclaimer: when he wins). But this is England. And beating Spain can do some strange things to you.

Not just because Spain are the defining team of the past 20 years, six-time international trophy winners and current world and European champions. But because Spanish football culture is the global template for tone, texture and tactics, the ultimate source of the Football Association’s slightly dog‑eared footballing blueprint.

Beating Spain is like beating your super-smart but slightly controlling younger brother. It’s getting one over on that other way of playing, punitive high technique, death by possession, patience over urgency. Even better, Tuchel’s team did so in Madrid with a performance based around the hard‑running physicality that English football sees as part of its deep sporting soul.

As such it will be tempting to see this Nations League victory as a springboard, a Rubicon crossed, a shattering of the Iberian ceiling. With some justification; England have the talent to win a home European Championship two years from now. But it feels just a little bit easier to visualise now.

There was something new in seeing Spain not just outmuscled but outplayed in the first half, reduced to whinging about fouls, unable to take the ball away. Not only because England’s pressing was smart and relentless but because of the players’ ability to keep possession in tight spaces.

It is also true that a quick glance back at recent history tells us exactly how much of a golden dawn a win such as this can be. Which is: zero, zilch, nothing. No golden dawn at all.

In reality there are no Rubicon moments, no decisive levellings-up, only staging posts and warning signs, even in victory. This is the most important point about a night such as this. It won’t tell you where you’ll end up. But it may tell you how to keep heading the right way, if you’re ready to learn from recent history.

As it happens, recent history is in the room with us right now, clearing its throat, rattling its chains, trying to shift the Ouija-board dial. Here is an interesting fact. Spain have only twice conceded three goals at home in a competitive men’s international. The second time was on Sunday night, when England won 3-2 in Madrid after going 3-0 up. And the first time was 15 October 2018 when England beat Spain 3-2 in Seville after going 3-0 up.

The parallels between those games are numerically improbable. At the time of win No 1 Gareth Southgate had been in permanent charge for 684 days and one narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was his 29th game. At the time of win No 2 Tuchel had been in charge for 683 days and another narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was Tuchel’s 28th game.

That Southgate moment was greeted with understandable optimism. You know the kind of language used because it’s out here now, too. New dawns. Statement victories. Rise of a Golden Generation. Not just a benchmark but a springboard as well, an astonishing feat of carpentry if true.

So was it that? Answer: no. In fact Seville 2018 was arguably the moment Southgate-ism reached a stylistic ceiling. England played a fast-paced game of counterattack that night. The team was an attacking mix, a midfield of Winks‑Barkley‑Dier, with Sterling‑Kane‑Rashford in front. England scored 27 goals in six games the following autumn, starting most with a back four and a double pivot, ending 2019 with a 6-0, a 7-0 and a 4-0. This felt like something new.

The Covid break pretty much killed that mini-era. Or rather, it was allowed to kill it, because coaches have choices too. England went 42 weeks without a game. By November 2020 they were losing 2-0 in Belgium with a back five and a deep defensive midfield.

The Euros had already been postponed for a year. In the summer of 2021 England started the final against Italy with another back five plus Declan Rice and Kalvin Phillips, and congealed into a kind of footballing rice pudding as the game reached its crisis point.

Here is an unprovable counterfactual. If football had rolled on, if England had not had an empty year to look down and get scared, they might have retained enough momentum to go harder against Italy in that final and win it.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

But then, the Southgate era was gruelling for many of those players. There is a separate study to be made of the way so many key early Garethistas disappeared or entered a slow decline. That October 2018 team turned out to be a pop‑up thing of shifting parts, evidence of the complex, zigzagging nature of team building.

The would-be golden generation included Ben Chilwell, Eric Dier, Joe Gomez, Ross Barkley, Harry Winks and Marcus Rashford. Nathaniel Chalobah made his only appearance as a sub in added time, and still has the second shortest England career, after Martin Kelly.

Rather than a golden dawn of ultimate glory, England entered a more talent-appropriate era of losing late-stage games against good opponents. If anything the Spain victory added to the ambient pressure around those tournaments, helping to create the sense it is now unthinkable for England to lose, because we have an image of them as winners, and English winning is the best winning, the only real winning.

The lesson remains the same now, the need to avoid both portents of doom and the lure of a golden new hyper-future. In this sense Tuchel is encouragingly restless both in defeat and victory. Even his new-season touchline look – tailored, sombre, all black – has an agreeably priestly, hair‑shirt energy; less Elizabeth I, author of the introductory quote above, more Martin Luther on his way to a business meeting in an out‑of‑town spa hotel.

Tuchel’s best quality is his obsession with analysis and objectivity. On Sunday night he was already talking about the need to improve. This can be an obstacle at times (see: process-based Argentina substitutes). But it is also a rejection of complacency, ornament, frippery. This England are better than their 2018 equivalent. That team had seven players from Leicester and Arsenal. This one has key parts from Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich, including the current Ballon d’Or winner and a £300m midfield tripod.

The balance of the attack in Madrid was good, not just the most seductively talented players but the best parts for the plan. Anthony Gordon is an interesting figure in this respect, an intelligent, culturally adaptable, tactically aware footballer, whose game is nonetheless basically running up and down. Elite teams seem to have a place for this role now. Flank-scurry energy node. Right-sided gallop unit. Lewis Hall was also very good again. Any team looks better with a genuine left‑footed full-back, like hanging a picture straight on the wall.

Mainly what Tuchel did in Spain was to select a team with no indulgences, full commitment to a tailored gameplan, no celebrity passengers. And that style is not fixed. See also: Trent Alexander-Arnold against Croatia, and some excellent passes against a deep block even on a middling night. Stick that behind your ear as well, Thomas.

Teams are hugely complex things. Tuchel had to get to know his players. The idea you can simply bolt on an elite manager and expect instant progress was always a bit silly. No dips or lulls, no adaptation. This might work if you come from the same cultural system. But plonking on a brain from someone else’s body is still a way of looking for shortcuts, the managerial equivalent of sticking it in the mixer and hoping for the best. There you go. Give us a final fix on 75 years of inherited domestic culture.

Tuchel is now a little further along with all this. He even did the backs-to-the-wall thing better, waiting to the last moment to press the defensive emergency button, the sight of Dan Burn rumbling out a signal to both teams that this really is the end of the night, like turning on all the lights and getting the DJ to play Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Sunday night was a wonderful game. It was England’s most complete performance under Tuchel. But the lesson hasn’t changed. Trust the process, not the results. Keep doing the ruthless, adaptive things that got you there. England will at some point have to beat the best. And the Nations League is a very useful tool. Win it next summer and taking that final step starts to look a whole lot less of an Arthurian fever dream.

Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:59:31 GMT

DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.

Ministers have come under growing pressure to end the NHS in England’s relationship with Palantir, which is run by the Donald Trump-supporting US tech billionaire Peter Thiel.

James Frith, a health minister, said Palantir’s role would end in 2029 to boost public trust in NHS tech, end its “over-dependence” on one supplier and let UK companies start providing crucial digital infrastructure. The DHSC will in the meantime select UK tech firms to replace it.

However, Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs criticised Palantir being given a further two years.

“My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS,” said Chi Onwurah, the chair of the Commons science and technology select committee.

“It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier.

Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat MP, said: “After months of campaigning by the Liberal Democrats, the government has finally admitted that the Palantir contract has to end.

“However, ministers have kicked the can down the road to March 2029. That leaves a company co-founded by Trump ally Peter Thiel, and criticised by human rights groups over its work with ICE [the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency], holding the keys to our health data for years to come.”

Campaign groups such as Amnesty International and Just Treatment have been urging ministers to activate the break clause in February in the contract that NHS England agreed with Palantir in 2023.

Many NHS care trusts have declined to use the FDP, amid widespread doubts in the service that it is as good as Palantir insists. NHS England last week deleted a claim from its website that 137 trusts were benefiting from the FDP after the Guardian disclosed that 29 were using it never or rarely.

“The current contract will remain for two years, before coming to an end,” Frith told MPs. The DHSC will soon invite British tech outfits to bid to be part of whoever replaces Palantir. “A process this important must command public trust as well as clinical confidence,” Frith added in a tacit admission that many hospital bosses and doctors are sceptical about Palantir’s claimed benefits.

Ben Coleman, a Labour member of the Commons health select committee, who last week urged ministers to replace Palantir with a group of British firms, said: “I’m glad the government is ending reliance on a single supplier and shaking off the Palantir albatross. This must be done without disrupting patient care or creating new dependence [on a new single supplier]”.

Amnesty International said the decision was “a victory for healthcare workers, patients and campaigners who refused to give up”.

“Doctors and nurses … should never have to work in a health service that partners with a company supporting a military committing genocide.

“Palantir has openly acknowledged supporting Israel’s military in ‘war-related missions’, while Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. ‘First, do no harm’ should apply not just to NHS staff, but to the companies the NHS contracts with,” said Tom Guha, its crisis campaigner.

Leave. EU and Vote Leave veterans launch rival campaigns to defend Brexit

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:38:45 GMT

Andy Wigmore says there will be no animosity this time between his Enough Official group and Michael Gove-backed Stay Out movement

The Brexit wars were a bitter period in political history, fraught with tension and badmouthing – and that was just between the different leave campaigns.

Now as a new incarnation of Dominic Cummings’ Vote Leave looks set to re-enter the political fray, so too does a rival anti-EU campaign from the team behind Leave. EU, who ran their own unofficial campaign backed by Nigel Farage.

This time, both have vowed to be cordial with each other, but in 2016 there were significant creative differences.

Many of the names are the same. Oliver Lewis, a veteran of Vote Leave who was a Brexit negotiator under Boris Johnson, will chair Stay Out, a new campaign group backed by the former cabinet minister Michael Gove and under the interested eye of Cummings, though he has no formal role.

The launch of the campaign video – which claimed the costs of rejoining the EU would be £750m a week, and featured footage of recent riots in France and Spain and warnings about unchecked migration – caught No 10 off-guard.

On Monday they were joined by the launch of a parallel campaign from Andy Wigmore’s Leave. EU, which will be called Enough Official. Wigmore told the Telegraph he wanted to work with Lewis’s group. “There’s no split camps this time,” he said. “We’re all going to support each other, and we will support anyone who’s going to fight this.”

A number of high-profile political figures seem to be willing to re-enter the fray from retirement, including Johnson. The former prime minister and leave campaigner told the Telegraph it would be “madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority … [Andy Burnham] won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

Johnson hinted to the paper that he would be willing to be part of a campaign to stay out of the bloc. “There are plenty of people who are only too happy to make the points I’ve made – but I will of course make the points that I’ve made,” he said.

One senior campaigner said it was an irresistible opportunity for many former political advisers who were now out of Westminster politics. “They’re very effective guys that have been sitting around waiting for a chance to make themselves useful. A lot of talent on the right is currently off making money or kicking their feet. Rejoining is the one thing that will bring them back,” they said.

Veterans of both Vote Leave and Leave. EU are split between those who are willing to campaign to stay out and others who believe the political landscape is now far more uncertain.

One senior figure said they “had PTSD” from the Brexit period and vowed to steer clear. “I think that is exactly the reason why the prime minister should not be reopening this debate, but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusion it would be an easy win for either side.”

Another campaign veteran said both pro- and anti-EU campaigns would find it more difficult to get businesses to pick a side or to get public figures involved. “I think that many are scarred from previous involvement, but this would work in both directions,” they said.

Several of those involved in the campaigns said they expected serving politicians to be kept at arm’s length – including Farage.

At a press conference on Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said she would not engage with campaigning on Brexit. “We need to stop obsessing about Europe and whether to be in or out, and actually get on with doing the things that we are elected to do,” she said.

“Sort out the economy, fund our defence, cut welfare, get jobs for people, make sure that businesses can create those jobs. We don’t need to be in the EU to do any of that.”

Speaking on Monday before a crunch EU summit where Burnham hopes to clinch a new deal with the EU on food and drink and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility deal, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the government respected the 2016 result.

How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:16:19 GMT

Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis

In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.

The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.

Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill.

That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable.

On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people.

Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work.

In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line.

After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity.

Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them.

“Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.”

He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard.

Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead.

Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market.

Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment.

His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”.

The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term.

The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have.

His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs.

So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR.”

Glenn Close cries! John Malkovich weeps! But it’s Nathan Fielder everyone wants to talk to at the honorary Oscars

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:47:42 GMT

All of Hollywood’s biggest stars are in attendance for the Governors’ awards, but nobody gets drunk and the biggest draw is an awkward documentarian

Timothée Chalamet was seconds away from getting into trouble. It was just after 6pm in Hollywood and Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was trying to corral a crowd of 700-odd people into sitting down so she could begin the Governors awards ceremony. She jokingly threatened to start calling out anyone still standing by name if they didn’t sit down imminently. Chalamet was the only one left on his feet, circling the table where he was due to sit next to his girlfriend, Kylie Jenner, opposite Tom Holland and Zendaya. Howell Taylor gave him a few seconds’ grace. He looked like the popular kid testing how far he could push a headteacher.

The Governors awards had a curiously school-like atmosphere this year. Even the carpet in the Ray Dolby Ballroom was faded and striped. The social structure was much the same: closed-off and insular, with cliques, alliances, legendary enmities and intricate hierarchies of popularity and influence. There were those who seemed entirely comfortable – Chalamet, Holland, Tom Cruise, Matt Damon, Willem Dafoe, Seth Rogen – and others still angling for a better table.

Two hours earlier, I had arrived in a Toyota hybrid, almost certainly the worst car in the lot, wearing a jacket from Goodwill. At 4pm, the reception was still relatively quiet. There was a bar, a s’mores station and a playlist of default office-party songs: Timbaland, Rihanna, that sort of thing.

Among the first people I spoke to were Jordan Firstman, whose debut feature Club Kid was released in the US earlier this month, and Curry Barker, the 27-year-old film-maker behind Obsession. Firstman told me he was most keen to run into Parker Posey. Barker, dressed in a gleaming white suit, was hoping the night would finally be the one he met Christopher Nolan. Nolan’s wife was trying to arrange an introduction but Barker was hesitant. “Everyone’s talking to him, of course.” It was his first time at the Governors awards. “I like it,” he said. “I just don’t really know what it is.”

The Academy’s annual ceremony honouring careers and contributions to cinema are an unusual Hollywood gathering. Unlike the Oscars, it is not televised, and there is no suspense about who will win. Instead, the Academy assembles the people who make, finance, distribute, promote, preserve and perform in films to recognise five people whose work has helped shape the medium. This year’s recipients were Glenn Close, whose eight competitive Oscar nominations are yet to yield a win; Floyd Norman, Disney’s pioneering first Black animator; Ridley Scott, who was unable to attend; and Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, the independent producing partners behind Killer Films and champions of new queer cinema.

It was funny to see the raw material that would soon be repackaged as Vogue spreads and elevated to headline news: in reality, a fairly drab event. By 4.30, waiters were rolling out hors d’oeuvres, including truffles, although nobody seemed especially interested in eating them. I overhear an executive say, “I’m beating my own drum, but her films just aren’t going to make enough.” Christa, a bartender who has been working the event for 10 years, tells me she no longer gets starstruck. Some people are nice, she says; others not so much.

Nathan Fielder, for the record, was nice. He stopped to talk to practically everybody, displaying a degree of social ease that almost seemed a betrayal of his onscreen persona. His Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, was one of the films people were keenest to discuss. Several approached him to say how “genius” it was. Fielder seemed graciously to accept the praise, before eventually slipping into the figure more familiar from his television work: hands clasped together, trotting away with a wobbly, timid gait.

He was frequently in the company of Lance Oppenheim, his co-director on the documentary and the filmmaker behind Primetime. Executives approached Oppenheim to tell him how much they loved his movie. “Which one?” he asked. Later Seth Rogen stood with them, wiping away a tear from beneath his glasses as they laughed.

At 5.30, Willem Dafoe arrived, gliding slowly up the stairs. David Byrne appeared at around the same time, looking sweetly awkward and a little forlorn. An executive told him, “Thank you for being you.” Edward Norton was pouring red wine. Matt Damon had an arm around his wife. John Malkovich was chatting with Robert Eggers. Rashida Jones blinked with awkwardness. Charles Melton made a particularly slick flick of the wrist to retrieve a tiny hamburger slider. Travis Knight, director of Wildwood, offered me nicotine gum, apparently relieved to have found somebody who looked as lost as he did.

Tom Cruise was obviously the most intense person in the room. He wrapped his arms around whomever he was talking to and drew them into his extraordinarily concentrated gaze, as though he were about to impart something earth-shattering. Tom Holland arrived holding Zendaya’s hand, walking right past.

At 5.43pm, I overheard security say that Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet were five minutes away. When they arrived, Jenner smiled cordially at everyone who approached her, and I found myself counting how long she held the smile for: one, two, two-and-a-half. When she and Chalamet eventually took their places, the room began to settle.

Howell Taylor took the stage to introduce the evening. Her five-minute speech was so abstract and platitudinous that I struggled to follow it. She spoke about artificial intelligence and uttered phrases such as “It’s not just a celebration, it’s an endurance”. I later put the speech through Pangram, an AI-detection programme. Its verdict: “100% likely generated by AI.”

Mercifully, the evening went on. The first award went to Floyd Norman. Mahershala Ali presented the Honorary Oscar to the man who joined Disney in 1956 as its first Black animator and worked on Sleeping Beauty and One Hundred and One Dalmatians. The room rose to its feet.

Glenn Close followed. John Malkovich, her friend and co-star in Dangerous Liaisons, took to the stage to celebrate her, beginning with a joke about the mark of a great actor: dying on screen. He recalled Close’s crushed-chandelier demise while fleeing alien invaders in Mars Attacks! The chandelier, he explained, belonged to Nancy Reagan. Malkovich praised Close’s willingness to play “the more complex, darker characters”. Then he lost his footing. He began to cry as he sang her praises.

It was moving to see Close with an Oscar in her hands. She cried, too. She veered away from the teleprompter, took a breath and tried to correct herself: “Oh, I see what I meant to say.”

Matt Damon introduced Ridley Scott’s award. The two men, Damon said as a montage of clips from Scott’s films began to play, were forever sending each other books and scripts in the hope of working together again.

Finally, Todd Haynes and Julianne Moore presented the Irving G Thalberg Memorial award to the producing partners Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler and surprise guest Neil Patrick Harris performed a number from Hedwig and the Angry Inch, the 2001 film the pair produced.

Vachon and Koffler were the first female producing team and the first independent producers to receive the Thalberg award. In their speeches, they thanked the people who were rarely credited: their lawyers, distributors and, most emphatically, their assistants.

By 8.45pm, the party had begun to resemble a school disco at which the teachers had announced that the buses were waiting. Nobody was drunk or disorderly. This was very disappointing. The evening was remarkably civilised. Kylie, Timothée and Zendaya were nowhere to be seen; they had been among the first to depart. Tom Cruise was the last man lingering. Most people were in a rush to get home. Parker Posey and Julianne Moore chatted while in line for their limousine.

It had been an unremarkable four hours. Marco, an usher who sent me down in the lift, told me how hard he and the hundreds-strong team had worked to put the event together. “We’ve been doing this all week,” he said. When I told him I hoped he got to enjoy some of the night, he laughed and looked away sheepishly. Everyone had cleared out by 9pm.

Devon police renewed shotgun licence of known abuser who later killed his wife

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:46:53 GMT

Ex-marine John Perkins, who also killed himself, had been violent to Kathryn Perkins over 42-year marriage, Exeter inquests hear

A “controlling and violent” former Royal Marine who shot his wife dead after she told him she was leaving was allowed to keep two licensed shotguns despite police knowing he had a history of domestic abuse.

John Perkins shot Kathryn Perkins at their home in Devon with a double-barrelled shotgun before killing himself with his second weapon.

The couple’s inquests in Exeter were told that Perkins, 66, had repeatedly been violent towards Kathryn Perkins, 67, during their 42-year-old marriage, beginning when he head-butted her during their honeymoon.

The coroner, Alison Longhorn, area coroner for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay, concluded that Kathryn Perkins had been unlawfully killed and John Perkins killed himself.

Perkins’ violence towards his wife and his anger issues were recorded in his medical records and passed to Devon and Cornwall police when Perkins applied for his shotgun licence to be renewed.

Even so, police approved his application and Perkins was allowed to keep his shotguns, which he said he wanted for pheasant and deer shooting.

Longhorn said she was concerned that when someone applied for a shotgun licence, the scrutiny of any history of domestic abuse did not appear as “thorough, considered or as carefully and accurately documented as it should be”. She said she would write to Devon and Cornwall police and the Home Office about the case.

The relationship continued to deteriorate and shortly before he shot his wife in May 2025 Perkins searched the internet to find out if it was possible to get a silencer for a shotgun.

Devon and Cornwall police’s handling of firearms applications came under intense scrutiny for allowing Jake Davison to have the pump action shotgun he used to kill five people in Plymouth in 2021.

In a statement read out at the inquest, the couple’s son, Bradley Perkins, described his father as violent, controlling and unpredictable.

He said that when he was 11, his father punched him in the face, leaving him with a black eye and prompting social services to become involved. He also spoke about a time when Perkins punched his wife in the head as they drove home from a ski trip.

By May 2025, Bradley Perkins said his mother had decided to leave her husband and went to their house in Exmouth, Devon, to tell him.

Bradley Perkins said when he failed to hear from his mother, he went to their home and found his parents’ bodies. “I was screaming and could not believe what I was seeing,” he said.

Kathryn Perkins’ sister, Barbara, described Perkins as a bully and an “egotistical narcissist” who had head-butted his wife on their honeymoon.

She said her sister had contacted domestic abuse support at one point and that in 2010 John Perkins had attended an NHS anger management course but did not complete it because he thought it was “rubbish”.

The inquest was told that Perkins’ medical records recorded that he was referred on to the course because he had “smacked” his wife.

Police were told about this by Perkins’ GP when he asked for his firearms licence to be renewed in 2023.

An experienced officer was sent to the couple’s address and spoke to Kathryn Perkins but she said she had no concerns about her husband having shotguns.

Police also knew that in 1995 Perkins had had an altercation with a neighbour but this was disregarded as irrelevant.

The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:37:44 GMT

Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing

At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “welcome back” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “Breturn” has yet to catch on.

By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to avoid pre-empting the broader “conversation” that he desires on relations with the EU.

They are right to be wary, and not just because that debate will come with domestic political risks attached. Some form of closer relationship with the UK’s largest trading partner is desired by a majority of the British public. But however warm its rhetoric, Brussels is going to have other matters on its mind during a momentous period of elections that will test the EU’s internal unity.

Mr Macron will be gone by the spring. It seems increasingly likely that his replacement will be a far‑right president committed to national preference policies that are contrary to EU law, and the cutting of support for Ukraine. Pedro Sánchez, the leader closest to Mr Burnham’s own centre-left politics, could be gone by the end of the month. Polls suggest that Spain’s snap election is set to deliver a coalition government including the far right for the first time since Franco. Poland, beset by constitutional turmoil, could also lurch to the far right in 2027.

Such political storms breaking would limit EU headspace for Mr Burnham’s overtures and may give the prime minister himself pause for thought. But volatile times also offer political opportunities. Russia’s war in Ukraine, and the wider threat posed to the EU’s eastern flank by Vladimir Putin’s revanchism, mean that a big British offer on defence would be well received and possibly open doors on other issues. Similarly, the febrile geopolitics of energy contributed to five European leaders this month calling for Britain’s re-entry into the bloc’s internal electricity market. On both sides of the channel, the rapid emergence of an unforgiving multipolar world has served to underline the need for strengthened cooperation.

Should the UK seek to rejoin the single market, recognition of that reality will not alter Brussels’ red lines in relation to core principles such as the free movement of people. But we are no longer in the world of 2016 and its aftermath. Covid, Ukraine, Donald Trump and Chinese competition have altered the landscape of EU politics and shifted priorities. Possible far-right breakthroughs threaten imminent further disruption. The direction of travel chosen by Mr Burnham is the right one. But predicting the final destination is, for now, a futile exercise.

The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:36:12 GMT

From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible

The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “war minus the shooting”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday?

Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart the domestic rugby set-up in Wales; and the growing appeal of football. Until Saturday, Welsh sports fans looking for a winning finish were better off watching the darts champion Gerwyn “The Iceman” Price than Steve Tandy’s rugby team.

Wales hadn’t beaten New Zealand since 1953; not even the great Welsh teams of the 1970s managed it. Little was expected of a side that had laboured to beat Japan the previous week. The 55,000 crowd at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium was 20,000 short of capacity. Most would have settled for defeat by fewer than 20 points. Instead, Wales won 35-28, with magnificent first-half attacking rugby and a heroic defensive rearguard in the second. It was beyond Welsh supporters’ wildest dreams. Bread of Heaven indeed. A decade from now, 500,000 will claim to have been there.

It feels like a watershed for rugby in Wales – the team and the fanbase believe again. But such is the metaphorical power of sport that romantics hope it can be more than that. Cynics will scoff, but sport can capture a moment. It is not by chance that David Kynaston concluded his recent survey of mid-1960s Britain, Deep into the Sixties, with a detailed analysis of England’s win over West Germany in the 1966 World Cup final. That victory helped define the decade – energised, forward-looking, optimistic. The 2012 London Olympics conjured an impression of the same upbeat mood, even if it was shattered four years later by Brexit.

After Saturday, Wales can dream again. So will English football fans after Sunday’s triumph against Spain, which took place in the World Cup winners’ Madrid back yard and ended the hosts’ historic run of unbeaten matches. Wales have just overcome 73 years of anguish that had witnessed 34 successive defeats to the All Blacks; could England now put an end to 60 years of hurt and counting? English cricket supporters, too, will take heart not just from their one-day win in Adelaide at the weekend but, even more, from the Australian national nervous breakdown following the re-emergence of the “Sandpapergate” scandal.

Orwell would have recognised the tribalism. But sport really is more than just the drama unfolding on the pitch; it is the expression of a shared history, identity and ritual. War minus the shooting – but sometimes in a good way.

Woman accusing David Walliams of grooming her backs staggered age of consent call

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:30:20 GMT

Comments come after Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Russell Brand, had said she wanted a change in law

A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggered age of consent.

Walliams, 55, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found.

Alex has alleged she was 15 and studying for her GCSEs when she first met Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors. She has alleged they began having sex when she was 17 and Walliams was 34.

Alex said she would have saved herself “a lot of trauma” if a staggered age of consent had been in place when she was a teenager.

“As a parent myself now, I would absolutely love for there to be a change of law. It’s something that is incredibly close to my heart, and I would feel very, very proud and happy if this could get over the line,” she told the Guardian and ITV News.

“It would protect everyone … from people that can abuse the law as it currently stands. I think it’s really important that teenagers are able to have relationships with each other. I think that the staggered element to it, I think works really well.”

Alex was speaking out after a woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent. Mia Latter told the Sunday Times she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16.

She has called on the UK government to introduce a law that would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Last week, Alex told the Guardian and ITV News that she was “groomed” by Walliams. “I never said no … but I felt unable to say anything or have any control in that situation once I was with him,” she said.

“OK, it’s legal to have sex when you’re 17, 18, 16 even, but the context of who you’re having sex with – if that person is double your age, if that person has known you from a young age and promised you things and is in a much bigger position of power than you, both in age, in work, in finance, in stature and size, like, everything, I really don’t think that’s OK.”

On Monday, Alex backed calls for a change in the law to “make it a lot harder for predators to act”.

She said she would have had a different perspective on Walliams’ behaviour had the law already been in place when she was a teenager.

“I grew up in a culture where it was normalised,” she said. “There were people saying to me at the time that this feels really wrong, but it was a bit more accepted, and it still happened more. And I think if I grew up in a world where [I] knew that that was illegal, and it was more clear that that shouldn’t have been happening, and that was wrong, then I think that I would have been a lot more wary of that and scared by it, and probably seen it more clearly for what it was at a younger age.

“I feel like if we can make the children of today know and understand from a young age that’s illegal, that’s against the law, that that person shouldn’t be talking to you in that way, shouldn’t be engaging with you in that way, and certainly shouldn’t be acting on it, it would make you pause and hope and I think it would definitely stop a lot of incidents happening.”

Walliams’ lawyers have said the suggestion he groomed Alex is false and that she did not raise, and he did not believe, that she had any concerns about the sex at the time. The lawyers add that Walliams was mortified to learn that their brief, consensual relationship had caused her sadness. Walliams has denied all the allegations against him.

Ministry of Justice investigating Russell Brand message from prison claiming he is not guilty

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:24:49 GMT

PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.

Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.”

If found to have broken the rules, Brand could face sanctions ranging from an extension of his sentence to loss of privileges such as access to a telephone for a limited period.

It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published.

Asked about the comments, the prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “This is clearly appalling and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules.

“Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments … This is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if the rules have been broken.”

Brand, 51, is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

In his message, Brand said he had been moved from the category-B Wandsworth prison in south-west London to the category-C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison for men convicted of sexual offences.

Reading the message from a notebook, Laura Brand said: “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.

“I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.

“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for and forgive one another as God forgave us.”

Prisoners are allowed to protest their innocence, meaning that no criminal offence has been committed in the release of the podcast. They are not, however, allowed to make statements from jail that cause distress to victims, and heavy restrictions apply to speaking to the media.

According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”

The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.

Mia Latter, who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and has waived her right to anonymity, said his message was an “insult” to his victims and questioned why YouTube had allowed the video to be shared.

She told The Jeremy Vine Show on Channel 5: “I was shocked that YouTube put it out, because I feel like they have some kind of responsibility not to let these things be broadcast.

“And, it was an insult to all the women that stood trial, and it was an insult to the jurors that gave their time. It’s an insult to the criminal justice system.”

In July 2022, prisoner Charles Bronson said he was given a 28-day phone ban after sending an unauthorised voice note from his cell at HMP Woodhill.

Prison sources said it was not yet clear whether Brand had broken a rule because the message was posted by Brand’s wife, not by him, and the material may have been written before conviction. “There are a lot of possible scenarios, and the full facts are still to emerge,” a source said.

Responding to the video on Monday, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.”

According to official guidance, prisoners are expected to make a formal application through their governor if they wish to contact the media.

Allegations against Brand and fellow comedian David Walliams have prompted conversations about introducing a staggered age of consent.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said there was “some common sense” in the idea, but expressed doubts about how it could be enforced.

“I do think that there’s some common sense there in terms of a staggered age of consent. My issue is with how we will enforce it,” she told a press conference. Walliams denies wrongdoing.

Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job?

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:18:57 GMT

The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration

Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes.

This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words.

It was only when the likes of Google (now Alphabet) and Facebook (now Meta) appeared with their “mission” statements that dual class structures – and unequal voting rights – got a fresh lease of life. The corporate missions, went the argument, were so important that the founding geniuses needed to be able to pursue them in free-wheeling, risk-taking style without distraction from the tiresome short-term demands of ordinary shareholders.

In an extreme example, Snap, the Snapchat company, was even able to pitch its overblown ambition of “reinventing the camera” as so vital that shares could be issued with zero voting rights, as opposed to merely weakened rights.

Now we come to Anthropic, the Claude AI developer whose $1.4tn blockbuster listing happens this week. The governance setup here is, to put it mildly, different. In essence, there are two centres of power and neither is the ordinary shareholders.

One is the seven founders, who collectively have one vote that commands 50.1% of the ultimate voting power – the collective aspect is designed to force them to come to a consensus. The other is a financially disinterested trust, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which nominates four of the seven directors and looks out for the balance between making money and benefiting humanity. The trustees are a cast of the great and the good, including Ben Bernanke, former chair of the US Federal Reserve. And the whole structure is given an overlay as “public benefit corporation”, nodding to Anthropic’s commitment to develop AI responsibly and safely.

There are two positive things to say about this setup. First, the motivation is plainly more complicated than a simple power-grab by the founders, led by Dario Amodei. Rather, Anthropic’s backing for the Long-Term Benefit Trust seems to be designed to create some form of constitutional balance of power.

Second, Anthropic probably has a stronger justification than most to divert from the norm of equal rights for equal economic risk. If the development of AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the listing document puts it, a few unconventional governance structures are probably in order. We’re not talking about Snap’s fluffy videos for social media.

All the same, Anthropic is offering an untested experiment. For all the fine words, the company may simply have recreated an inward-looking “trust us” setup, just with more elaborate clothing.

Here’s a nuanced point from Stuart Riddick, sustainable investment manager at fund manager Aberdeen. “Agreement with a mission in principle does not equate to agreement over how it is interpreted and implemented by the directors.”

Riddick notes that Mustafa Suleyman, the chief executive of Microsoft’s AI division, even as he acknowledged Anthropic’s seriousness about AI safety, has made strong and detailed criticisms of the company’s thinking on so-called “model welfare”, arguing that AI models must not be trained to act as if they have rights or consciousness.

How, in practice, are such challenges handled within Anthropic’s supposedly responsible governance arrangements? It’s hard to tell unless the Long-Term Benefit Trust starts to throw its independence around, or not.

What happens if the trustees are at loggerheads with the founders on a basic safety question? Will they tell the outside world? Or will they reflect that ultimate voting still sits with the founders, so best not to rock the boat? If the shareholders are denied any role in holding the executives to account, what is the true level of challenge?

It is surprising after events at Nvidia that Anthropic’s governance has received so little attention. Yes, the setup is supposed to be high-minded and responsible. But it still represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals.

Ineos wanted £10m for alleged refusal to return yacht

Out-of-court settlement ends plan for a 2028 trial

Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos Group has reached an out-of-court settlement with Sir Ben Ainslie over the £180m yacht their companies built for the 2024 America’s Cup.

Ratcliffe and Ainslie worked closely together during two cycles of the America’s Cup, culminating in Ineos Britannia becoming the first British crew to win the challenger series two years ago. But they fell out over plans for a third bid, with Ineos announcing last year that it had “reluctantly withdrawn its challenge” for the 2027 event in Naples.

Ineos launched a legal action in March after expressing “surprise” that Ainslie’s Athena Racing had opted to keep using Britannia, which was beaten 7-2 by Emirates Team New Zealand in 2024, in the 2027 challenge.

Court documents filed this year showed Ineos was claiming more than £10m for Athena’s alleged refusal to return the boat. The dispute had been set for a trial in January 2028 in the admiralty division of the court of England and Wales, but the claim has been withdrawn.

“Ineos has reached a settlement with Athena Racing and considers the matter now closed,” the statement read. No further details, such as whether the yacht has been returned, were provided.

In a statement issued to members of Ainslie’s club, Royal Yacht Squadron Ltd, its chair, Michael Grade, said: “Members will no doubt be aware of the ongoing commercial dispute between Ineos and Athena Racing/GB1.

“I am delighted to announce that this dispute has now been settled, with any and all claims between the parties now withdrawn. This is excellent news indeed as GB1 prepares to challenge for the 38th America’s Cup in Naples next year. We continue to offer Sir Ben Ainslie and his team our full support as they look to build on their great success in Barcelona in 2024.”

Ineos had claimed when withdrawing from the partnership last year that delays in reaching an agreement with Athena Racing had “undermined its ability to prepare” for the event, adding that it had spent £180m on Britannia on top of £170m on the boat used in the 2021 America’s Cup campaign. In response, Athena claimed that they had always owned the assets and intellectual property from the two campaigns and that Ineos had been a sponsor.

In a defence filing in June, Athena alleged that Ainslie was warned on the eve of the 2024 America’s Cup by Rob Nevin, Ineos Sport’s chair, that Ratcliffe would “burn his house down” if he failed to give the billionaire what he wanted.

“We have a phrase at Ineos: ‘scorched earth’,” Ainslie claimed Nevin warned him in the defence filing. “It means that if you don’t give Jim what he wants, he will burn your house down.”

An Athena Racing/GB1 spokesperson told the Guardian: “Athena Racing/GB1 have always been, and remain, the owners of the assets, including the AC75 race yacht.”

Samaritans old and new will, I’m sure, have been just as shocked as I was by your article (‘Is anyone up for a fight?’: The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November). Many, though, will not be surprised. I was a volunteer for 26 years in three branches. The work was demanding and life-changing; the experience is so transformative that it gives every part of society people who are strong enough to bear others’ burdens and able to share their pain. We don’t stop being listeners when we stop being volunteers.

During my time, I found that the people at the top were detached from what went on at branch level. It is not news to me that they cannot understand how central to the work each local branch is and how important every human contact is to those who need to talk.

One phrase in the article struck an especially harsh note – the strategy will apparently enable the organisation to attract more “call handlers”. This is not a customer-service business. It is one flawed human being giving up their time to really listen to other human beings whose lives have fallen apart.

As it is so hard to do, it is not easy to find volunteers. When I became the director of my branch, recruitment was first on my to-do list. Difficult as it was to do, we managed it, but branches need to have the support and resources to do it well. Providing those should be the main job of the national team. I would say to them: stop counting the beans and start appreciating that this is one service that is too important to stop being small and local. Start doing what volunteers do – listen. Name and address supplied

I volunteer at a Samaritans branch not affected by this first wave of closures. Volunteers do not feel this process of change is collaborative and are gravely concerned about the approach being taken.

Our first concern is for callers, and we share the concerns of the chief executive, Julie Bentley, that in 2025 “some callers still didn’t get through, especially in crucial overnight hours”. In the past five years, answer rates have significantly improved, and they continue to do so.

The 13 branches facing closure or merger answered about 84,000 calls in the year to June. The future-proofing plan relies on scaling up selected branches and offering remote volunteering to replace that capacity. Neither of these has got off the starting blocks, let alone recruited and trained the volunteers needed to fill the gap.

If the management shared plans on how it will improve answer rates without losing ground through these changes, volunteers would be far less anxious for the future of the service. We have repeatedly asked for these, to no avail.

I have also taken calls from ambulance crews and police officers asking us to speak to the person they are with. Calling Samaritans the “fourth emergency service” is no exaggeration. Nobody would close a fire station before the new one had a crew. Our callers deserve a plan, not a leap of faith. Name and address supplied

Your article prompts despair at the effects of managerialism and arrogance. Decades ago I was a Samaritans volunteer in Cheshire, then in the leadership team for three years, and later branch director for three, responsible for around 100 volunteers. The lessons I took were that the population of volunteers is always ageing, and that the service offered is, in essence, local.

Branches are sustained by loyalty and familiarity, and most callers are conscious that they are talking to someone not too far away. The idea that volunteers will, for example, travel from Worthing to Brighton for shifts is so unrealistic as to be delusional, and mega-branches offering a call-centre experience will be ineffective. Why Alan Milburn’s Pip plan is a mistake

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:02:40 GMT

Savitri Hensman says financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest

Alan Milburn has a track record of so-called cost-cutting measures that waste billions of pounds in public money while making health worse. The private finance initiative was an expensive mess, though it did help huge companies and rich people get richer. It is less surprising that he wants more benefits for young sick and disabled people slashed than that the government might go along with this (Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund, 12 November).

Financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest. The high number of young people not in education, employment or training is probably largely due to past top-level decisions. Austerity, making life tougher for claimants while favouring multimillionaires, fewer youth clubs, underfunded mental health care, long delays in providing assessments and equipment, and making school and university more stressful have not only caused suffering but also been expensive.

In a few years, as parent-carers end up in hospital with heart attacks or strokes, and maybe inquiries ask why young people whose mental health went downhill after abuse or exploitation in the workplace dared not leave, Milburn’s latest bright idea will have lost its shine. But the public will keep paying, in money and hardship. Savitri Hensman London

Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest

You report (11 November) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock.

It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggle.

Our helpline already hears from too many older people on low incomes having to cut back on essentials to pay their bills.

With poverty in later life on the rise, and healthy life expectancy reversing (with lows of 50.9 years for men and 51.8 years for women, both in Blackpool at the last count, according to the Office for National Statistics) we need to think very hard indeed about how to mitigate these impacts if we contemplate further rises. Joanna Elson CEO, Independent Age charity

Police ‘retreating from streets’ due to major funding crisis, chief constables say

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 18:00:50 GMT

Forces across England and Wales struggle amid financial pressures described as worst for decades

Police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government.

Paul Sanford, the chief constable of Norfolk police and the finance lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), said exceptional financial support was needed if forces across England and Wales were to remain operationally viable.

He named the nine forces as Durham, Cleveland, Greater Manchester, Wiltshire, Bedfordshire, South Yorkshire, Gloucestershire, Lincolnshire and Norfolk.

The Home Office, which will decide whether or not the forces will get extra money – or whether the relevant councils will be allowed to charge taxpayers more – declined to confirm how many forces had applied for support.

The government argues it has already given forces extra money in real terms, but police chiefs say demands on them have risen, as have population numbers.

When Labour came to power in July 2024, officer numbers stood at 148,536, according to June 2024 figures. By March this year, the figure had fallen to 147,822, and senior officers expect it to fall further.

Sanford told the Guardian: “Demand has gone up, population has increased. There is a growth in complex cases, sexual offending and historic inquiries, and civil orders. All of those are the right thing to do, but they’ve not come with the funding required.

“That is why you see the retreat from the streets. Policing is in worse financial shape now than it has been for decades.

“Those forces who have applied for EFS believe that they are close to the tipping point where the ability to deliver core services can no longer be sustained.”

One of the factors affecting forces’ budgets is the government’s early release scheme for prisoners, intended to ease the overcrowding crisis in jails. The NPCC has predicted this will lead to a rise in crime of up to 6%, with a consequent need for officers to respond.

Police chiefs now say the projected funding gap for forces by 2030 has rocketed from £3bn to £4.3bn.

They point to the use of reserves worth £300m by 43 forces in the last year as a sign of increasing financial distress, saying that while some of this was used for investment, some was needed to maintain services.

Trevor Rodenhurst, the chief constable of Bedfordshire, said of the application for additional government support: “If I don’t get the money, the impact would be to degrade services.”

The Bedfordshire force has 1,486 officers, which Rodenhurst believes is hundreds fewer than it needs. He says it is getting a thousand more 999 calls a month this year compared with last year.

Catherine Roper, the chief constable of Wiltshire, said: “We’ve taken the efficiencies we can out of the system. The wiggle room we have is leaner.”

“But there is no point in the service being seen to whine about what we haven’t got when it is a racing certainty, given the state of our public finances, that no great slug of additional general funding is going to drop into policing anytime soon. Nor is the Treasury likely to be keen on directing even targeted investment into an unreformed service.”

A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “Since the election, we have increased funding to policing by £2bn. Police force funding this year is at a historic high of £18.5bn.

“We have established the financial resilience framework to ensure a consistent approach to assessing financial resilience in policing.

“We are also reviewing the police funding formula to ensure the system is fair and continues to prioritise public safety. The new approach to funding will be brought in as part of our reforms to police structures.”

The Conservative-led government that came to power in 2010 cut police funding as part of its austerity programme, with 20,000 officers lost before ministers reversed course.
