‘Near-philistine’: fury greets Shakespeare Institute plan to leave Stratford-upon-Avon

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 17:45:02 GMT

Renowned centre of Shakespeare studies, which is part of University of Birmingham, to move to its Edgbaston campus

“Near-philistine”, “ignorant”, “unbelievably stupid”, “terrible”, “extraordinarily sad and shortsighted”, “an appalling act of cultural vandalism”, “a disaster” and “an absolute disgrace”.

Such has been the furious reaction to news that the Shakespeare Institute, a much-loved and internationally renowned centre of scholarship, is to leave its home in Stratford-upon-Avon, the playwright’s place of birth, and move to Birmingham.

Established in 1951 to push the boundaries of knowledge about Shakespeare studies and Renaissance drama, the institute has worked with scholars from around the world, as well as leading actors and directors from its near neighbour in Stratford, the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC).

When Paul Mescal was researching for his role as William Shakespeare in the recent hit film Hamnet, he was shown around the Bard’s home town by the institute’s deputy director (education), Prof Abigail Rokison-Woodall.

Earlier this year, in a short video to mark the institute’s 75th birthday, the RSC veteran Judi Dench paid tribute to its work. “In all the seasons I did at Stratford at the RSC, what would I have done without the Shakespeare Institute?” she said. “I hope you go on for another 75 years because the help you’ve given me and so many other people is inestimable.”

Last week, however, staff and students were told that from next September the institute – which is part of the University of Birmingham – would operate out of the university’s Edgbaston campus, prompting a torrent of protest from academics on social media.

The director of the institute, Prof Michael Dobson, has said he will resign in protest if the move goes ahead. Many honorary doctorate holders are considering returning their doctorates, and the actors Samuel West and Janet Suzman are supporting a fast-growing petition calling on the university to halt its plans.

“For 75 years, the Shakespeare Institute has stood at the heart of Stratford-upon-Avon, moments away from Shakespeare’s home, his church, and the stages where his plays live on,” the petition reads.

“Housed in the historic Grade II*-listed Mason Croft, the institute is a world-leading centre for Shakespearean scholarship, bridging the gap between academic research and live theatrical practice. Now, the University of Birmingham plans to abandon Mason Croft and move the institute away from Stratford-upon-Avon to an as yet unspecified location. To sever the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon and its home at Mason Croft is to destroy the very thing that makes it unique.”

A former artistic director at the RSC, Greg Doran, told the Guardian: “It’s a catastrophe. I just think it’s such an out-of-touch decision.” He said it would “sound the death knell for the institute itself” and could have severe implications for the economy of the town.

West said the institute had helped him “hugely” in his preparations for his RSC work and in return he has donated his scripts, diaries and research to add to the riches of the institute’s 60,000-volume library.

“We should be proud that the greatest writer of dramatic English who ever lived is celebrated in his small Warwickshire home town with a world-class theatre company and a world-class research institute, a hub for studies of every sort and in many languages,” he said.

Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 17:43:57 GMT

The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country

This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old.

There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service, careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation, scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold, the leisure centres closed, the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back. That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here.

It is the central purpose and the meaning of Tuesday’s report by Alan Milburn, commissioned by Keir Starmer and keenly adopted by Andy Burnham. This is the hardest of social projects, yet the government nonetheless sets itself to be judged by it, despite the high upfront cost, with no payback for years.

How will this land? There will, no doubt, be protest from right and left. But never has a policy been so pitch-rolled to flatten critics and sceptics with undeniable evidence that it will be to the good. There is a cornucopia of plans for schools, colleges, the NHS, councils and early years education. Ideas come from visits to see what works elsewhere, notably the Netherlands and Denmark. Seeing proportionally far fewer Neets in those countries, Milburn asked what they did about school and college drop-outs. “They didn’t understand that term,” he tells me. In those countries, if children start to struggle with school attendance, “they go straight round to find them and work out their problem. Here they disappear.”

Politically, this duty will fall on local mayors (or councils, where mayors have not yet been introduced). Their colossal task is to pull together schools, FE colleges, jobcentres, NHS services and local employers. Heaving them out of their silos to collaborate will test mayoral devolution to its limits. With extra funding comes accountability for creating a continuous decline in the number of Neets in their area.

Everywhere, this will be delivered through youth hubs – welcoming places, “not jobcentres where they’re met by security guards, but places only for young people,” Milburn tells me. Last week he visited a model hub in Liverpool, Merseyside Youth Association. Hiring and training a new cohort of work coaches and advisers has begun, so hubs can offer supported internships, short flexi-jobs to ease people into work and experience for those with none on their CVs. Incentives to employers to hire them may include cuts to employers’ national insurance contributions for those aged 21-24 in retail and hospitality. Ordinary earners under 21 are already NI-free.

GPs will not mourn the passing of the “fit notes” with which they were expected to sign people off work. That task goes to hubs’ community teams of occupational therapists, work coaches, mental health and job advisers, who offer counselling and personal “return to work plans” instead. Neets will be fast-tracked through NHS mental health queues.

Milburn is searching for obstacles to knock down. Care leavers will get back the education maintenance allowances (EMA) for staying in school or college, with plans to spread this to all who used to qualify before the Tories axed them – that is, every sixth-former on free school meals. “Just paying for buses to stay in college is £4 a day, £20 a week: too much for those families,” he tells me. Abolishing another obstacle, the government will end young people’s loss of 55p from their benefit for every £1 they earn when they do get a job.

A good omen is the optimism of FE colleges, after years of despair at turning away 16- and 17-year-olds for lack of spaces and teachers. These neglected gardens of second chances for all those failed by Gove-stricken schools are the mainstay of this whole plan. Today, they celebrate being told they can now take as many students as they want. David Hughes, head of the Association of Colleges, closely involved in the Milburn plan, expects colleges to be funded to take tens of thousands more. He wants funding for colleges to do their own social outreach to missing young people. “We can go and find them,” he says. “Many have no adult to ask what to do.” Will this at last be FE’s phoenix moment, after years of neglect of the half not destined for university?

New FE pre-apprenticeship courses will prepare young people for twice as many apprenticeships on offer. The government will redirect existing subsidies to companies hiring new young starters, banning employers from using these funds to upskill existing staff by, for example, paying for managers to take business degrees. But they get big new incentives to take on Neets, with up to £5,000 for each Neet apprentice.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The price to be paid is thoroughly forewarned. Cuts to health benefits for all but the young with the most severe lifelong disabilities will fund this hoped-for youth revival, leaving them with the pitiful standard universal credit of just £80 a week. But here’s the difference from the Treasury’s previous disastrous attempted £5bn welfare heist. This cut won’t take effect until the new offers and supports are in place. That’s confirmed by the PM, Milburn and, on Sunday, by Pat McFadden who, as secretary of state for work and pensions, is the keeper of benefits. “That short-term change is going to be very difficult,” he told Sky. But “it’s really important that people don’t have benefit changes before support is in place. That’s the right way round to do this.”

Is that convincing? It helps that Milburn warns not to expect a financial payback from welfare cuts for a decade. This is not about saving money but saving young life chances. Ministers stoutly defend the young against those who brand them idlers and snowflakes. And that is the political dividing line the Tories relish, as they brandish a £36bn benefit axe at young people while rewarding the old with tax cuts. The public do want benefit cuts, but they also know the damage done by the last Tory assaults on the young. There’s the battle line.

It’s for Labour and Milburn, who will remain in post to oversee all of this, to prove, with falling Neet numbers, the value of good social investment. If even half these plans work, that will be a great social advance – a generational shift from appeasing the old to finally directing hope and resources towards the young. And it will be about time.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

The BBC has confirmed Emma Barnett is stepping down as a presenter of Radio 4’s Today programme, setting off the broadcaster’s latest search for a new name to co-host its flagship news programme.

The official announcement came after months of speculation about Barnett’s future on the show. Her last appearance will be broadcast on Wednesday.

Her departure comes just months after fellow presenter Amol Rajan left the show, opting instead to launch his own project, Amol Rajan Connection, on YouTube.

However, Barnett will be staying with the BBC, fronting a new show that will also be available on YouTube, as well as BBC iPlayer and the corporation’s BBC Sounds app. Exact details have not been announced, but it is expected to be a longform interview format.

Barnett said it had been “incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners” over the last six years.

“Having proudly hosted Woman’s Hour and now the Today programme I’ve had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network,” she said. “But it’s not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives.

“Over the last nine months, we have been creating a bold new BBC show which will launch at the start of 2027. Watch this space and look ready. I am.”

Barnett joined Today in 2024. Her short tenure had been the subject of rumours about clashes with fellow presenters – denied by her co-host Nick Robinson. Some insiders also believe she suffered from indecision at the BBC about the direction of the show.

Barnett’s previous success at BBC Radio 5 Live came from creating a show driven by her personal style, but she has also faced criticism for bringing personality to the Today programme.

A renewed search will begin for a new face to present alongside the rotating line-up of Robinson, Justin Webb and Anna Foster. Attempts to replace Rajan were ended after bosses decided to reduce Today’s presenting roster as part of BBC cuts.

Katie Razzall, the BBC’s culture and media editor, is thought to be well placed to take on the job. BBC executives have been impressed with how the Media Show, which Razzall presents on Radio 4, generates stories and works on digital platforms.

Katya Adler, the BBC’s Europe editor who has stepped in as a guest presenter of Today, is also seen as a possible replacement.

ITV’s Julie Etchingham and Sky News’s Sophy Ridge have recently been cited as potential outside candidates for the show.

Etchingham moderated the first election debate between Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer and was regarded by many viewers as the real winner from the encounter. Ridge was named presenter of the year at the Royal Television Society awards last year and has previously worked with John McAndrew, the director of programmes for BBC News.

Despite the fact that audiences have fragmented as a result of the rise of digital platforms and the draw of social media, the Today programme has retained its status as one of the BBC’s prize assets. It has more than 5 million listeners a week.

Rebecca Keating, the editor of Today, said of Barnett: “Emma has brought enormous energy to Today and a keen focus on our listeners.

“She has a track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate but is also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench. We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture.”

Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 17:35:46 GMT

The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe

So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser.

For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never be wrong. Except when they are.

Even the loudest cheerleaders for Brexit find themselves mumbling that it hasn’t gone as they had planned. Not that they had planned anything. Which was half the problem. The whole deal with Brexit before the referendum was that it could mean whatever you wanted it to mean. Sovereignty. Not sovereignty. Leaving the single market. Staying in the single market. Leaving the customs union. Not leaving the customs union. Everyone could have a Brexit in which they could believe.

It was only after the referendum that things began to fall apart as the Brexiters tried to pin down what leaving the EU meant. Only the UK could have chosen a prime minister as hopeless as Theresa May, whose main contribution was to say “Brexit means Brexit”. She was sacrificed on the altar of her own futility, to be replaced by Boris Johnson. Perhaps it was always going to take a liar and a chancer to get some kind of Brexit deal through parliament. It was only later that the Brexiters came to understand that lowering immigration actually meant increasing it exponentially.

But now we have a prime minister who is prepared to say the previously unsayable. In his Mansion House speech on Monday evening, Andy Burnham is expected to reveal that the emperor has no clothes. Whichever way you cut it, Brexit has been a failure. The UK is worse off now than it was before the referendum. Now is the time to abandon our traditional British reserve.

There would be no truth and reconciliation committee. Just a clean slate. Tabula rasa. No one will be judging anyone. Much. Simply take the plunge and try to find a way to reset the UK’s relationship with Europe. It can be whatever the people want. Rejoining the EU. Single market and customs union. Or just kisses and cuddles. The people would decide. Given that the people had got it so spectacularly wrong last time, this wasn’t a huge comfort. But needs must. You have to start from somewhere.

Mind you, not everyone was willing to put all their reservations to one side. In the 8.10am interview slot on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson was determined to give Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, as hard a time as possible. “You seem to think that any fool can see it’s a good idea to get closer to Europe,” he said. It was like entering a time machine again. Conjuring nightmares of David Cameron and Boris. Both of whom have declared that we should stay as distant from the EU as humanly possible. Which rather suggests Burnham is right. Lord Big Dave and Boris have rather been proved wrong on almost everything so far.

Miliband is too long in the tooth to be caught out like that. You could sense he was dying to say: “Of course any fool can see it’s a good idea to get closer to the EU,” because that’s what almost every listener was thinking. Instead, he said: “The prime minister was more nuanced than that….” Before going on to as good as say you’d need to be a complete halfwit to imagine we are better off now than we were before Brexit. Because what else was there to add. You can’t find a thinktank anywhere that believes Brexit has benefited the economy, immigration and national security.

It was now becoming obvious that Robbo’s heart wasn’t really in the interview. He’s the one who likes to have politicians on the ropes, not the other way round. And now he was left to play devil’s advocate by mentioning the five carrot growers in the UK who might be worse off if we did reset food regulations with the EU. But Ed was nothing if not generous. Plus, he might be needing a favour from Nick some time in the future. So rather than laugh, he nodded earnestly. He was very conscious that the five carrot growers might find life tougher, but maybe we should be thinking of the many thousands of food producers whose business would be markedly improved. Call it honours even.

Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 17:00:49 GMT

About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them

Naming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions.

That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years.

At first glance, it looks a little like a pie chart: three concentric circles sliced into colored sections, with each region representing a different category of emotion. The innermost circle lists broad core feelings (sad/happy/angry), which split off into gradually more specific sub-emotions in the outer rings (remorseful/proud/humiliated).

Created by US psychologist Dr Gloria Willcox during the early 1980s, the feelings wheel is a tool designed to help people identify and clearly name their emotions, by moving gradually from broad blanket terms to more nuanced ones. The wheel has surged in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its visual appeal – you can get it as a laminated office poster, as a wooden desk chart on a spin-stand or even stitched onto a cushion.

But do people really need this much help with the seemingly simple task of naming everyday feelings? Experts say that in many cases, the answer is yes – and behind this difficulty is an evidence-based scientific concept known as emotional granularity.

First identified by neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett in 2004, emotional granularity is the ability to recognise and name your emotions in a precise way, rather than lumping them into broad, general categories like “bad” or “sad”. You might think of it as the difference between seeing only primary colors, and seeing a full color gradient.

“I think of it as being able to experience and articulate your emotions in very nuanced, context-specific ways,” says Dr Katie Hoemann, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Kansas. While on one level it’s about precision, what actually makes emotional granularity useful is the level of insight it can provide. “It’s accompanied by a meta awareness of not only what you’re experiencing, but why. Do you have a sense of where this feeling is coming from, and do you have a sense of what you should therefore do about it?”

The extreme opposite of emotional granularity is alexithymia, a trait whose Greek translation literally means “no words for emotions”. Affecting roughly one in 10 people, it describes either an extreme difficulty or complete inability to identify and label one’s own emotions. It’s not a diagnosis in itself, but is commonly associated with autism and can also be a feature of mental health conditions like depression and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Research indicates that higher emotional granularity is associated with a range of positive outcomes, including lower levels of mental illness, more efficient emotional regulation and reduced chances of relapse for substance users in recovery.

“The findings are robust,” says Dr David Kimhy, associate professor of psychiatry at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and director of the Experimental Psychopathology Laboratory. Kimhy and his colleagues recently published a sweeping review of the existing research, which showed that “across the board, higher emotional granularity has been linked with better mental health outcomes and social functioning”.

The exact reasons for this link aren’t known, but experts have some theories. Emotions act as an internal feedback system, helping us to evaluate what we like and dislike, avoid danger and react appropriately to whatever is around us. “More specific emotions are more informative,” Hoemann explains, “and you can take that information and use it to select and regulate your behaviour.”

For instance, you might start out only knowing that you feel sad, but when you get more granular you realize that what you’re actually feeling is loneliness. That could in turn prompt you to reach out to a friend, or finally join that running group you’ve had your eye on. But a person with low emotional granularity might never move past that non-specific feeling of sadness to reach solutions.

after newsletter promotion

“If you feel anger, that calls for one strategy. If you feel guilt or anxiety, that’s a different strategy,” says Kimhy. “But if all you know is that you feel bad, it’s hard to know what strategy to use.” In that scenario, people tend to default to whatever coping strategy is familiar or accessible, which could look like avoidance (scrolling through social media, or putting off a difficult conversation), aggression (cutting someone off in traffic, or picking a fight) or self-medicating behaviours (substance use or over-eating).

Granularity also has interpersonal benefits, Hoemann adds. “Your words aren’t just for yourself, so if you can tell someone: ‘Hey, I feel frustrated,’ or: ‘I feel disappointed,’ that’s more informative. You’re communicating in a way that tells the other person how they can help you, and maybe how you can move forward together.”

The good news is that emotional granularity is not a fixed trait, but a skill that can be learned and cultivated. Tools like the feelings wheel can help by providing the vocabulary and basic skills to get started, but just like learning any new language, it only really sinks in with practice.

The goal isn’t just to learn a bunch of new words, but to use the wheel in the context of some kind of practice like journalling to reflect on experiences that you’ve had. “I think it’s a useful tool to the extent that people can use it to identify and make meaning out of moments in their life,” Hoemann says.

Experts have hypothesized that tools like mindfulness, mood-tracking and structured therapy can also build emotional granularity. In particular, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) highlights the interplay among thoughts, emotions, physical sensations and behaviors, and can help to develop more awareness of all four. When Kimhy works with patients using CBT, he often sees a blurring of the lines among those four areas. “Usually at the beginning of treatment, you’ll get: ‘Well, I felt like running out of the room,’ but that’s a behavior. Then they might say: ‘I thought I was going to have a panic attack,’ but that’s a thought. So you have to work with them to develop that understanding of what a feeling is first, and then to start labelling emotions.”

If somebody is really struggling to articulate how they’re feeling, or they’re experiencing alexithymia, it’s particularly important to consult a mental health professional who can provide guidance, rather than using a self-help tool like the wheel in isolation. Hoemann warns against spending too much time trying to find the perfect word for every experience – for a person who’s prone to overthinking or rumination, the feelings wheel could just lead them to more of the same. “There can be too much of a good thing. Ideally, you want to think about using it to label and sort through your experiences, and say to yourself: ‘OK, what I actually felt was disappointed. I’ve made my meaning of that moment, and now I can put it away.’”

Emma Dibdin is a writer and mental health professional based in London

Cop31 draft text is attempt to ‘draw out parties’ to find agreement, president of talks says

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:54:42 GMT

Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”

The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.

The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.

“We’ve got to start with a broad document, concentrate on getting agreement with some difficult issues, then refine it down over the coming days,” Bowen told the Guardian in an interview.

Alden Mayer, a senior associate at the E3G thinktank, said putting out the draft text at this stage was a gamble. “But it would also be a gamble to wait until later in the week. They have decided to take the ‘full monty’ approach, knowing that many of the 144 paragraphs will not survive the week,” he said. “The question is where does the presidency think the sweet spot is on the various contested issues.”

The wording on fossil fuels echoes a pledge made by all countries at Cop28 in Dubai to “transition away from fossil fuels”, which had no timetable or work programme attached, but is likely to be attacked by oil-producing countries that have hardened their positions since then.

There are also provisions to address the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris agreement and a target to derive 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, a key priority for the host nation, Turkey.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, called the text “an overgrown garden. There are lots of encouraging green shoots but there are also a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out.”

He welcomed the fleshing out in the draft of a previous promise to triple finance to poor countries to help them adapt to the impacts of extreme weather. “If that language remains in the final version, it would suggest countries are starting to listen to the needs of the vulnerable,” he said.

after newsletter promotion

The “cover decision” is one part of the expected outcome of this Cop, and some countries – chiefly Russia, Saudi Arabia and the Arab group and some allies – have objected to having one. Cover decisions have been used in most of the 30 previous Cops, taking in resolutions that were difficult to fit into the other formal negotiating strands.

Within the other strands at Cop31, there are still major disagreements among developed and developing countries. Poor nations are unhappy that no new finance is likely to be forthcoming at this Cop.

“Climate action roadmaps without climate finance lead nowhere,” said Siphesihle Mvundla of groundWork, an environmental justice nonprofit in South Africa. “The global south is spending 225 times more repaying debt than they receive in climate finance from the very countries who owe them a climate debt.”

The text contains items likely to be subject to trade-offs among parties. For instance, language calling for “carbon dioxide removal” was attacked by campaigners who see it as a “false solution”, but it is unlikely that some fossil fuel-producing countries would agree any text without such a reference.

Bowen also said fossil fuel-producing countries did not bear more responsibility than consumer countries in tackling the climate crisis. “There are two types of countries in the world, fossil fuel exporters and fossil fuel importers, and we’re all in it together. The idea that everything [is for] fossil fuel exporters is not one I support,” he said. “We’re all part of this process, and just dealing with one and not the other is not realistic.”

He refused to commit Australia, which is one of the world’s biggest producers of coal, to a phaseout of fossil fuel exports, as campaigners and some countries are calling for, but said Australia had a plan to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions and was adjusting for a world in which all countries did the same.

“I accept the logic that all countries will need to reduce emissions, and that means they’re reducing their use of fossil fuels, and that will impact on Australia’s exports, absolutely,” he said. “That’s why we’re preparing our economy for that change.”

Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human?

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:22:51 GMT

The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspective

There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing.

There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking about their parents. There are refugees en masse, shorn of any traits or qualities at all, discussed purely in terms of whether or not the host state can accommodate them, and how long they should be allowed to stay in any given place.

But the refugee as a complex human, a mixture of strength and trauma, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs – this is a story I don’t feel I’ve heard much recently. Very few talk a lot about refugees as individuals, with personalities – and yet at the same time, the universalism of the experience, the fact of the status forced upon you and never chosen, is also etched away, or simply ignored.

So the refugee in the mainstream imagination toggles between hero, villain or victim – except it’s not quite that simple. People find it slightly harder to frame the child refugee as anything other than a victim – so instead, the status of “child” is endlessly contested, the tabloids popping up intermittently on a slow news day with rumours of 36-year-olds pretending to be teenagers.

The male refugee, meanwhile, is being steadily erased altogether, as an idea. If you were to get your discussion points from GB News, you would think there was no such thing as a man displaced by war, or hunted down by an authoritarian regime – there are only “fighting age men”, who should be at home, fighting; or predatory men, who arrive here via Europe in order to commit crimes under the cover of their “different culture”. A male refugee can be angry, but only as part of his antisocial, problematic persona, never legitimately. A female refugee can’t be angry at all, even if her home has been destroyed and her children have been killed. She can only be sad.

Seize the Summit follows Shaqayeq (from Afghanistan), Adnan and Safa (both from Syria) and Tania (from Ukraine). Damon said afterwards that the film wasn’t about war and displacement, it was about nature and recovery; but the thing that struck me most forcefully about it was how enragingly life-changing an injury can be. Safa doesn’t make it to the top of Kilimanjaro: she was the victim of horrific burns injuries that have compromised her breathing. Adnan was shot by a sniper and lost the use of his body from his chest down. He doesn’t make it to the top, either; his hero’s journey isn’t really about the mountain, it’s more about his struggle to accept help. He has spent the decade since his injury at age 14 trying to build a life in which he doesn’t need anything, and yet he won’t see any part of a mountain again unless others carry him up it, and his realisation of that is almost unbearably poignant to watch.

Ronan Toal, a human rights barrister speaking on the panel afterwards, said in passing that the Somali word for claiming asylum was “surrender”. That’s another notion that gets lost when the refugee isn’t described as fully human: how exquisitely painful it is to throw oneself on the mercy of anyone; how painful any of us would find it.

If, as a refugee, you’re not allowed a personality, it must be quite hard to feel like a whole, legitimate person in the new society where you’re forced to build a life, right? Yeah, pretty hard, Hanya agreed, being from Gaza. “The one thing you’re definitely not allowed as a refugee,” she said, “is a sense of humour.”

Seize the Summit doesn’t gild the experience of war – it is definitely not fun. Yet the mountaineers spend a lot of time laughing, which is not a heroic, strength-in-the-face-of-adversity story. It’s a human being story.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:05:58 GMT

While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged

Cop31 live – latest updates

Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.

While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.

The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.

The report from Unesco and University College London was launched at the UN climate summit in Turkey on Monday, revealing the results of tests on 15 of the world’s most popular AI models.

Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”

When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.

Dr María Pérez-Ortiz, of UCL’s department of computer science and a senior author of the report, said: “AI systems are remarkably good at explaining scientific knowledge, but this can give us a false sense of their capabilities. Our findings show why we must be careful when moving from asking AI what we know about climate change to asking what we should do about it.”

AI models also had a language problem. Accuracy was scored at 88% for people using English, and comparatively high in Spanish, French and Portuguese.

Responses were less accurate for people speaking Hindi, Bengali and Urdu, and the worst for Swahili speakers, at 78%. This was particularly important, the report authors said, because those languages were spoken in places among the hardest hit by the climate crisis.

The report was published on the same day Turkey, the Cop31 host, launched the AI Antalya pledge to make AI “part of the climate solution” with datacentres that are “sustainably” powered.

Julie Cerqueira, of the Natural Resources Defense Council, said AI’s rapid growth was “raising a new set of environmental and existential concerns around the world”.

She said the pledge was an important start but “more work is needed, and it needs to move quickly to keep up with the industry’s rapid-fire development and goldrush mentality”.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, said AI that “spreads disinformation, undermines science, divides societies and concentrates wealth” would damage the public trust the industry would rely on to grow.

“Communities are already pushing back against datacentres, concerned about their water, their energy bills and their environment. So public support is already sinking in deeper underwater,” he said.

French football head Philippe Diallo to fight Infantino for Fifa presidency

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:27:30 GMT

Diallo confirmed by Uefa as its chosen candidate

He accused Infantino of seriously damaging football

The French Football Federation president, Philippe Diallo, has been confirmed as Uefa’s surprise late choice to run for the Fifa presidency. The search for a Uefa-backed candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino was taken to the wire, with Wednesday the deadline for those planning to contest the Fifa election in March.

“At a meeting held today and chaired by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, the national associations represented on the Uefa executive committee and the Fifa council invited Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), to stand as a candidate in the Fifa presidential election in March 2027 and unanimously pledged their full support,” a statement said.

Diallo emerged as the favourite after plans to enlist a decorated former player or manager did not reach fruition. Uefa said the 63-year-old had accepted the invitation and that his candidacy was due to be ratified by the FFF on Tuesday.

Diallo strongly criticised Infantino in September, saying he had “seriously damaged the image and unity of football”. He continued: “His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.”

It is unclear whether the move to back Diallo will spell the end of the campaign begun by Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association, to challenge Infantino. Tashima, a Fifa council member, has influential backers within Uefa but its hierarchy appears to feel Diallo has a greater chance of wooing voters in other areas of the world.

Diallo is expected to win the backing of the vast majority of Uefa’s member associations and there are hopes he could pick up votes from Francophone members of the Confederation of African Football, which has been steadfast in its support for Infantino.

There are concerns that having multiple challengers to Infantino will strengthen his position and play into the hands of a campaign that will present the incumbent as the unity candidate after months of in-fighting.

Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, has been reluctant to endorse an alternative candidate, despite opposing Infantino, with some federations arguing that a boycott of the election would send the strongest message regarding the need for governance reform.

Diallo getting Uefa’s backing represents a marked departure from its original approach, in which it sought to coalesce behind a more high-profile figure who had made their name on the pitch or in the dugout. There had been late hope that Arsène Wenger, Fifa’s chief of global development, would throw put himself forward, but it would have required a major change of heart from him. Former players such as Mikaël Silvestre and, belatedly, Didier Drogba are understood to have expressed interest that never came to anything.

Diallo is a career administrator who has worked in French football since 1992, chairing the clubs’ lobby group Union des Clubs Professionnels de Football (UCPF) for almost 30 years before joining the FFF in 2021. He was elected president two years later in what was regarded in France as a shock victory, having initially stepped up in an interim capacity. Diallo joined Uefa’s executive committee in the same year.

Germany’s head coach, Jürgen Klopp, has said he would welcome a new president. “The general consensus is that a change might make sense. But what would interest me even more in this context, from a football perspective, is that we never thought things could get any worse after Sepp Blatter, and yet someone actually managed to make it worse.

Russell Brand: Open Secret review – ​a real tribute to the journalists and victims who brought him to justice

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:27:12 GMT

This Netflix documentary offers a fascinating look at how Brand’s behaviour wasn’t simply tolerated; it was actively celebrated

Last week was quite the week. Coming within a few days of each other, the sentencing of Russell Brand and the allegations about David Walliams have felt dizzying. As well as all the elation that justice has been served in relation to Brand, and the admiration for the women who saw that it was, there’s also an underlying sense of exhaustion about the sheer grubbiness of it all.

With this in mind, the thought of watching a feature-length documentary about the Sunday Times and Channel 4’s investigation into Brand might feel like willingly dunking your head into a toilet. However, Russell Brand: Open Secret is absolutely worth an hour and a half of your time. Not only is the film a tribute to Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, the journalists who spent years meticulously drawing the net closer to Brand – and, needless to say, to his victims – but it does a tremendous job of putting the whole sorry affair into a broader cultural context.

Because, at the time of his greatest fame, Brand’s behaviour wasn’t simply tolerated; it was actively celebrated, not least by him. We see clips of his standup that consist of him either dry-humping the air or delving into the seats to flirt with his audience. We see him signing cleavages and being followed around, Pied Piper-style, by crowds of young women. We see him reflect on the end of his BBC career, after the Andrew Sachs scandal, by boasting that he did worse things every single day. There is a clip of a podcast where he jokes about having raped someone.

And at the time, people couldn’t get enough. The tabloids crowned him “shagger of the year” three times in a row. Almost every single newspaper rapturously reviewed My Booky Wook. Whenever he put his voice to a cause, everyone involved fell at his feet, giddy at the attention that someone with his platform and fame could afford them.

Throughout, we hear testimonies from those involved in the Times’s investigation. Tellingly, his ex-girlfriend Jordan Martin wrote a book about the abuse she suffered at Brand’s hands. Even though she worked in PR herself, she couldn’t interest the press in her story. It might have been an open secret, but it was one that the establishment (and Brand’s lawyers) seemed motivated to ignore.

Obviously, the details of the allegations remain horrific. A number of his accusers speak up here – some on camera, some represented by actors – but they all follow a pattern of entitlement and power imbalance, of a man being told that he can’t have something and taking it anyway. For them to recount their experiences over and over again – to the press, to the police and now to a documentary crew – must have required a colossal amount of strength. But their willingness to put a human face on such traumatic stories makes the case against Brand undeniable.

The documentary isn’t only interested in what Brand did, though. It looks at how he repeatedly managed to find new audiences willing to forgive, overlook or simply ignore his behaviour. In the quarter of a century since he became famous, Brand’s career has surged and ebbed with bizarre regularity. He found fame on MTV, only to be sacked for dressing as Osama bin Laden on 12 September 2001. He was embraced by the BBC, only to be rejected after Sachsgate.

His film career ended, it is implied, because his reputation for sexual assault became too loud to ignore. So he moved back to the UK and involved himself in politics, until he realised that kneejerk Covid conspiracies got more views and found himself beloved by the right. Then, as the Sunday Times investigation came to light, he miraculously found Jesus. When it’s all threaded together like this, it is hard to see Brand as anything other than a drifting grifter willing to throw himself at anything that would keep him famous. Or, as standup comic Nish Kumar, who is interviewed here, puts it: a “moral vacuum”.

But perhaps the last few manoeuvres had a bigger purpose. The film moots that, by positioning himself as the voice of the truth, Brand was attempting to outplay the media. And so it came to pass. The night before the investigation was published, Brand uploaded a nauseating video where he told his viewers that the allegations were part of a coordinated attack designed to silence his criticism of mainstream media. Indeed, this was the exact line his lawyers used when they tried to stop the investigation’s publication.

Perhaps, given the mainstream media’s enthusiasm for making him a star in the first place, Brand had a point about its tendency to reach a consensus around its treatment of particular stars. But in the end, this was the very same institution that exposed him. There is something enormously satisfying about that.

Russell Brand: Open Secret is on Netflix

Miaow! What your cat is really trying to tell you

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:17:30 GMT

They only make this noise when humans are around – and, as you may have noticed, it is one of the bossiest sounds in the animal kingdom …

Name: Miaow.

Age: Evolved over millennia.

Appearance: A cat not taking no for an answer.

I guess cats have been miaowing since there were cats. They have been doing it only since they were domesticated. Cats don’t miaow at each other. The miaow is for your benefit.

You mean a miaowing cat is trying to speak human? After a fashion. It has been suggested that the cat’s miaow mimics a newborn baby’s cry, forcing humans to take notice.

Does the cat want something, or is it just being annoying? According to a new study, published in the journal Animal Behaviour, the cat wants something.

How did they prove that? The 38 cats in the study were presented with a transparent box inside which was food that was visible but not accessible – what animal behaviourists call an “unsolvable task paradigm”.

Sounds a bit mean. The feline subjects were shown the boxes under two conditions: human in the room and human absent.

And? And cats miaowed more – more than four times as much – when the humans were there.

No kidding. When no human was present, the cats tended to sit still and stare at the door.

Any other bombshell findings? According to the researchers: “Miaowing predominantly occurred while cats gazed at humans. Behaviours directed towards humans, including gazing and gaze alternation between them and the box, occurred significantly more frequently than zero.”

I think we can all see what the subject cats are driving at here. The leader of the study, Naila Fukimoto, said the behaviour was “suggestive of an intentional attempt to attract human attention”.

The cats are saying: “Open the wretched box.” It’s too early to jump to conclusions, but all the science points that way.

Can I just say that, as a cat owner, I did not need a 38-cat study to tell me that. Of course, further work is needed to support these findings.

I’m not sure it is. Any more cat research out there confirming the bleeding obvious? A 2019 study showed that cats do know their names, and just choose to ignore you when you call them.

If you ask me, the cats of this world could do with a little tough love. Your cat hears you, and he doesn’t care.

Do say: “Give a cat a fish, and it will eat for a day.”

Don’t say: “Teach a cat to fish, and it will continue to miaow at you until you bring it a fish.”

Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:14:37 GMT

Pattinson is a character actor whose talent for inscrutable appraisal may mean a new era for 007. Will this more willowy, classy Bond leave sexism in the shadows?

New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson Share your thoughts on the casting Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond

If it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality.

And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily gym regimen to bulk up. I like the taller and more willowy Bond that Pattinson represents, the Bond from whose frame the tux hangs gracefully, the Bond with elegant abandon who’s a former British Naval officer, not a former US Navy Seal, the Bond who with a crinkly-eyed reptilian grin can style out waking up with a hangover after too many whisky-and-sodas at the baccarat table.

But I like to think also that Pattinson could convert the diversionary cuff-shooting gesture of consulting his Rolex, to delivering a single lethal punch to the enemy’s unguarded solar plexus. (Although fisticuffs will be for the lower order of henchpersons; the Pattinson 007’s final confrontation with the primo villain will probably involve more hi-tech weaponry.) Pattinson could be a Bond to combine Roger Moore’s insouciance with the chill of Michael Lonsdale’s portrayal of plutocrat-villain Hugo Drax.

At 40 years old, Pattinson’s Bond will be a more worldly and mature agent, and his entire career has arguably been leading to this moment – establishment schooling at Hogwarts (rather than Fettes) as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire all the way through to the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves’s 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows – like Bond, used to working in secret.

He didn’t play Batman for Christopher Nolan, but for Nolan he interestingly played the slightly seedy British intelligence insider Neil in Nolan’s 2020 sci-fi Tenet and the unscrupulous Antinous this year in The Odyssey – both not good guys, character roles, both showing Pattinson’s class as well as his presence. Yet perhaps his most intriguing pre-Bond or proto-Bond outing might have been the alienated super-rich guy cruising the New York streets in his stretch limo in David Cronenberg’s Cosmopolis. Like Bond (or a future Bond) that was someone developing a tough, invulnerable carapace.

Yet for all the saturnine, even serpentine presence, Pattinson’s 007 could well be the one to find something other than the traditional cliched machismo and sexism in Bond in his relationship with female characters and indeed female colleagues – perhaps we might even see Bond’s feminine side. It’s an exciting bit of (long-delayed) casting.

Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:03:38 GMT

Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact

The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA

A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline.

The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.”

Nine years later, Flying Lotus, real name Steven Ellison, contributed to Grand Theft Auto V by curating the radio station FlyLo FM. He mixed wonky left-field rap, blistering Chicago footwork and, naturally, his own jazz-inflected beat music. Upon the game’s release in 2013, he got all his friends over to his home in Los Angeles, jacked a random vehicle, and got the station pumping. “It was just, like, ‘Am I fucking dreaming right now?’” he recalls.

FlyLo FM is emblematic of how the GTA soundtracks have evolved from aural capsules of distinct historic periods and locales such as 90s California and 80s Miami, into teeming, total documents of the sprawling, multi-faceted zeitgeist of the eras in which the games are released: not so topographically specific, but astonishingly extensive. Go back and listen to the soundtrack of GTA V: it is the sound of the 2010s.

And now, GTA VI is set to canonise the sound of the 2020s. Cruising around Leonida, a super-sized reimagining of modern-day Florida, players will blast tracks by the likes of Swedish rapper Yung Lean and Texas superstar Travis Scott. These big names sit alongside stations cranking out lilting reggaeton, melodic afrobeats, and grooving amapiano, genres that have exploded in popularity in the 13 years since the last Grand Theft Auto.

“After a while, there becomes a reputation to uphold,” says New York Magazine music critic Craig Jenkins of the encyclopedic breadth of these soundtracks. “There’s an expectation now.” More than that, Jenkins sees the GTA soundtracks as a major “flex” from Rockstar, in an era when many video game companies are cutting back – a pointed reminder of its singular financial and cultural clout. “Nobody else either has the juice or wants to go to the trouble of making it happen,” he says. “It costs so much to license anything these days.”

But licensing real-world tracks for in-game radio stations isn’t how the Grand Theft Auto soundtracks started. The audio team at DMA Design (before it became Rockstar North, the maker of GTA today) were experimenting with different song styles, and crediting their compositions to fictitious artists. Then, one of the game’s composers, Colin Anderson, had an epiphany: they could group these tracks according to genre, and package them as radio stations. So frequencies dedicated to icy east coast boom-bap rap, blaxploitation-era funk and hardcore rave became the sounds that made the first game’s New York analogue, Liberty City, come alive.

Anderson and his colleagues devised a simple test for judging whether the radio station idea was a success or not. “If players treated the tracks we’d recorded as if they were by real bands, and if they started stealing particular cars just to keep listening to particular stations, then we would have done what we set out to do,” he explains. Anderson remembers his vision quickly being vindicated: critics were effusive about the music of these made-up artists, and some players deliberately took longer to finish missions, so they could listen to their favourite songs.

Grand Theft Auto 3 marked a major turning point: fake artists were out; real musicians were in – the likes of dub originator Scientist and Detroit rapper Royce da 5′9″. But they were cult figures. With Vice City, Rockstar stepped up its soundtrack ambitions, securing prominent features from major acts such as Hall & Oates and the king of pop himself, Michael Jackson. Who can forget cruising down the Miami-inspired neon strip of Vice City listening to the future-funk shuffle of Billie Jean, feeling like the most famous Miami gangster of all time, Tony Montana?

Canadian R&B star the Weeknd has credited Vice City as a formative experience. “It really opened my eyes to a lot of 80s music,” he said. The underground Dutch producer Kai Hugo, who has released dreamy, 80s-inspired house music under various monikers including Palmbomen, discovered italo-disco through the game. When Soulwax asked him to be part of their Grand Theft Auto V radio station years later, he was taken aback. “To have my music included in the game, it felt quite special – kind of a full-circle moment,” he says.

“I’m certain that almost the entire millennial cohort can trace at least some aspect of their music taste to the GTA games,” says Jenkins. But it’s not only millennials who have embraced GTA: gen Z rappers, especially, reference the series in their lyrics (see Juice Wrld’s emo-rap anthem Wasted) and music videos (Croydon rapper Pozer’s Habits). For those wishing to bring listeners into their own violent, street-level worlds, GTA is an evocative hook.

The influence of GTA on musicians is one part of the feedback loop. Another is the material impact it has had on them. Dutch producer Hugo relocated to Los Angeles with his GTA cheque. For Romana Gonzalez, AKA R&B singer Nite Jewel, who scored a GTA V sync for her dreamy synth-pop anthem Nowhere To Go, the money enabled her to become an independent musician again. “I didn’t have the capital at the time to go back to my label, and Grand Theft Auto really made it possible for me to do that,” she says.

Think of the GTA soundtracks as a kind of cultural trickle-down economics: in the case of GTA V, which had the biggest entertainment launch ever in 2013, raking in more than $1bn in its first three days on sale alone, the wealth was spread among a broad group, including the soundtrack contributors. But Gonzalez, who recorded Nowhere To Go exclusively for GTA V (in response to a tight, 48-hour turnaround request from soundtrack supervisor Ivan Pavlovich), does not own the copyright for that track – Rockstar does. So even though it is her most popular song on Spotify by some margin (over 8m plays), she makes only a modest residual income from it, and the bulk of her fee was on work-for-hire terms: a one-off payment upon completion of the music.

“When you look at the royalty statement, is that fair? Well, yes and no,” says Gonzalez. “It’s Grand Theft Auto, it’s Rockstar’s brand. It would be nice if it was different, but at the same time, I’m not complaining about the amount of money that I continue to see from that sync in 2026.”

For the artists involved in Grand Theft Auto, that long-tail consistency is a major boon. Thanks to GTA Online, the online multiplayer portion of GTA V, which has eclipsed the base game in both revenue and popularity, Gonzalez has remained in players’ minds for over 13 years. When she played a gig in Oxted, a small commuter town Surrey, it was Nowhere To Go that received the most rapturous response. “The reach is insane,” says Gonzalez.

The frontman of indie-rock band Wavves, Nathan Williams, is unequivocal about the impact hosting a station and recording music for GTA V had on his career. “I was on the cover of Spin magazine, I’ve played Lollapalooza, I’ve had multiple Pitchfork best-new-musics,” says Williams. “All these things move you a little bit but none of them really do anything long-lasting. But people still come up to me at Wavves shows and say, ‘I discovered your band through GTA.’”

Even in the early 2010s, the name-making impact of Grand Theft Auto was clear. During outreach for FlyLo FM, Ellison recalls having to do very little convincing of artists to take part. “You can pretty much get anybody to do whatever you need,” he says. Case in point: California rap star Tyler, the Creator, who was just starting to crest thanks to Yonkers. “I’d been trying to work with Tyler for forever. And as soon as I said GTA, I got a track the next day. It was the fastest turnaround,” laughs Ellison.

The Grand Theft Auto games thrive on their sense of cool – their ability to tap up, and tap into, both mainstream and underground culture. Every featured artist, even those such as Tyler, the Creator, who only had a single track included on the soundtrack, can claim to have contributed to this sensibility. And it is one that remains rare in the world of video games: where many franchises look inwards for inspiration, Grand Theft Auto looks out. And whether out of sheer madness, hubris, creative genius, or bottomless riches (likely all of the above, in truth), its makers attempt something no other studio would dare: to roll up practically all of culture into a single work of interactive art.

Flying Lotus puts great stock in GTA being part of this history. “You know, I’ll always be able to say I was part of the biggest game ever,” he says. “That is, at least until 19 November.”

Grand Theft Auto VI is released on 19 November

New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:01:42 GMT

Daniel Craig’s successor in the franchise is confirmed after a long casting process, making Pattinson the seventh actor to play the role of 007

Share your thoughts on the casting Peter Bradshaw: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter to Bond via Twilight and the arthouse

Robert Pattinson has been announced as the successor to Daniel Craig, becoming the seventh actor to play the role in an official Bond movie.

The news was revealed on the official James Bond social media accounts account on Monday. All earlier content was abruptly wiped from 007 on X and Instagram just before 3pm GMT and a repeating message typed out: “Identity confirmed.”

The film studio then released a first photo of the actor in Bond’s trademark tuxedo with a press release confirming the news and saying Pattinson’s casting will “usher in a new era for one of cinema’s most celebrated characters”.

In a statement Pattinson said: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime … To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

The announcement came after a drawn-out casting process, in which Pattinson was understood to be on a five-strong shortlist, which included Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. On Friday suggestions emerged that Pattinson had been offered more favourable contract terms than his rivals, fuelling rumours that he was the strong favourite for the role.

Craig’s final film as Bond was No Time to Die, released in 2021 after being delayed due to the Covid pandemic. The narrative for the 25th film in the series lent the franchise a sense of closure, with Bond apparently dying before a title card promised: “James Bond will return”.

Craig made five Bond films in total, starting with Casino Royale in 2006. During his tenure the franchise became a box-office record-breaker, with 2012’s Skyfall alone taking $1.1bn globally.

Pattinson, 40, is due to appear in the next Bond film, the 26th in the franchise (although two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983, take the total to 28). The as yet untitled project will the first to be shot since Amazon-MGM Studios purchased the rights to the series for more than $1bn in 2025 from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, heirs to original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.

Harry Potter producer David Heyman and Spider-Man producer Amy Pascal will oversee the franchise, while the Dune trilogy’s Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight is writing the script.

Pattinson has demonstrated his versatility across a wide variety of roles, earning a reputation as an actor with broad enough appeal to support major blockbuster films while retaining artistic credibility with offbeat and unlikely choices. He first came to notice in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and achieved superstardom opposite Kristen Stewart as vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight film series. He appeared in films directed by David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis, Maps to the Stars), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse) and Lynne Ramsay (Die My Love), and returned to franchise film-making with The Batman in 2022.

The first actor to play Bond on the big screen was Edinburgh-born Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No. So successful was the film that Connery returned to make four further films over the next five years, which are considered by many to be some of the franchise’s finest: From Russia With Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball and You Only Live Twice. Bond creator Ian Fleming’s preference for the role, the English actor David Niven, starred in the non-canonical Casino Royale (1967), while the Australian model George Lazenby joined for one outing, 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, before Connery rejoined for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).

Roger Moore then lent the series a more ironic spin for his seven films between 1973 and 1985, which include The Spy Who Loved Me, Moonraker and Octopussy. The role then went to British actor Timothy Dalton for two films in the late 1980s; a six-year gap preceded Irish actor Pierce Brosnan’s debut in 1995 in GoldenEye. He shot four films as 007 before Craig’s tenure began.

The official James Bond films have so far made a total of $7.8bn, making the franchise the fifth highest-grossing in history. Proceeds from merchandise and sponsorship deals are estimated to far exceed that figure.

Catherine Shoard will be in the comments from 5.30pm today to answer readers’ questions about the casting.

Though Trump is giving him the cold shoulder, Netanyahu is pulling out all the stops to cling to power. And he just might

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:00:46 GMT

The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice

It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet his final downfall remains far from certain.

As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary lengths to cling to power, using every dirty trick in his well-thumbed handbook while calling for a “government of national unity” (excluding Arab parties). And the perception he has been hung out to dry by a similarly electorally humbled Donald Trump, his biggest ally, may also prove over-optimistic. Besieged Palestinians in the West Bank and in hungry, flooded Gaza, and the bombed and battered people of Iran, have good reason to be fearful.

Netanyahu’s bad-loser machinations ape those of Trump after Joe Biden expelled him from the US presidency in 2020. They include wild and unsubstantiated claims of electoral fraud involving Palestinian-led parties, whose unexpected haul of 19 parliamentary seats on a huge turnout has given them a potentially decisive say over who may form and lead the next government. He’s also parroting familiar, unfounded, non-specific allegations of foreign meddling. Investigators have found no evidence to justify these slurs – but, like Trump and Maga, Netanyahu and his extremist populist-nationalist allies and media backers keep repeating the lies anyway.

After sidelining the Arab-Israeli parties, Netanyahu’s “secondary goal is to incite the masses who heed his words to march on the Knesset next Tuesday [17 November] – the day of the speaker’s replacement – and prevent the plenum from convening. Or also to signal to outgoing coalition MKs to blow up the session,” warned Haaretz columnist, Yossi Verter. Such predictions are rightly ringing alarm bells over the future governance of a country that claims to be the Middle East’s only democracy. In dismaying prospect is Israel’s very own 6 January 2021, the notorious date of Trump’s failed Capitol Hill insurrection.

Netanyahu’s racism, never wholly concealed, has grown overt, blatant and repulsive. Any coalition that included, or was supported by Arabs, would be a “government of national suicide … with those who seek to destroy the state of Israel and establish a Palestinian state on its ruins,” he said in a recorded statement. The unmistakable implication was that all Arab-Israelis – about 21% of Israel’s total population – should be regarded as actual or potential Hamas-sympathising terrorists. “The fire and flames in the streets of Paris and Brussels will pale in comparison to the fire we will see in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa. Israel simply will not survive,” he said.

Despite his calamitous, unaccounted-for failure to prevent the 2023 Hamas attacks, the prime minister continues to claim only he, and he alone, can keep Israel safe. After witnessing another panicky, almost hysterical Netanyahu speech at last week’s Knesset swearing-in ceremony, Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the main opposition “change” group who has been given first chance to form a government, condemned his behaviour as shameful and hateful. “I became even more convinced that he is unfit to continue in office for even one more minute,” Eisenkot said. “We must act urgently to establish a national emergency government. The continuation of his rule divides Israel and endangers its security.”

Worries about more war to come are supported by reports that Netanyahu has not given up on his hopes of resuming attacks on Iran, thereby creating a new security crisis, boosting his own position and postponing a change of government. Eisenkot has pre-emptively warned him against such a move in a formal letter, urging him to “demonstrate national responsibility [and] exercise caution and restraint in making dangerous moves … Do not violate the people’s trust in government institutions and the decision-making process”. Eyal Zamir, Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, and other generals are said to have told US counterparts before the election that they believed Netanyahu was planning to draw Washington into a third military confrontation with Tehran in two years.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Swingeing Republican defeats in the US midterm elections, attributed in part to the unpopular and costly Iran war, appear to have jolted Trump into dropping any idea of renewed conflict – for now. He has also faced a backlash from within his own party, including from the vice-president, JD Vance, who specifically blamed the Iran war, and Trump’s unquestioning support for Netanyahu and Israel, for the poor results. Polls show that over time, moderate Republican and independent US voters are growing less supportive of Israel, while some younger Republicans also acknowledge the Gaza genocide and unrelieved Palestinian suffering there and in the West Bank.

Yet Trump remains highly unpredictable. He is already shrugging off the negative midterms verdict on his agenda, and is plainly determined to declare victory over Iran, one way or another. Last week Vance was summarily dismissed from his Iran negotiating role, with Trump insisting talks with Tehran were at an end. The US continues to exert military and increasing economic pressure on Iran, notably through an air, land and sea blockade. And the global oil price crisis persists. Sooner or later, the Tehran regime, fearing collapse or internal revolt, may feel forced to retaliate. If that happens, it will be Netanyahu’s opportunity. He may even artificially hasten a new confrontation, once again sucking in hapless Trump.

Take a step back from all this and consider the bottom line. The fact that Netanyahu remains in power as of now, and is still in with a chance of continuing as prime minister if opposition coalition negotiations stumble, self-destruct or are sabotaged, is extraordinary, unacceptable – and deeply shocking. Over many years, he has done incredible damage to Israel’s international reputation, not least in the US, and by his unending, grossly disproportionate war-making in Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Iran. He faces arrest by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes. At home, he is on trial for corruption; he is overseeing unprecedented terrorist settler violence aimed at illegally annexing the West Bank; and he stands accused of undermining Israel’s democracy through his judicial overhaul, attempts to muzzle broadcast media, cynical election manipulation and brazen lies.

Netanyahu is a disgrace to Israel and democratic governance everywhere. It’s time to say “enough”. Even though his defenestration will not, by itself, resolve the bigger issues, it would greatly help. He must be stopped. And this rare, post-election opportunity to stop him once and for all – to unequivocally, permanently eject him from office and from power – must not be missed, messed up or fumbled. “Bibi” must answer for his criminal conduct and misdemeanours, personal and political. If, as has happened before, he is allowed to wriggle free, not only Israel and Palestine but the entire world will pay a terrible price.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator
