‘George Michael came out of his coma talking like Jill’: Julia Davis and Rebecca Front on their squirm-inducing comedy Nighty Night

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:24:31 GMT

‘When Jill and Glen are in bed, that was Steve Coogan’s bed. He was rarely there so we didn’t bother washing the sheets afterwards’

It all started with the character of Jill Tyrell. I’d done Human Remains [a black comedy about oddball couples] with Rob Brydon and was trying to write something of my own. I remembered this woman from Human Remains called Beverley. She was in her 50s, from the West Country and did home hairdressing. She told a client: “The ammonia will burn your ears a bit, Joyce, that’s completely natural.” Bath and Bristol are embedded in my history, so I thought I’d develop that. I made Jill two decades younger and gave her husband Terry cancer, which she uses to her advantage.

I’m drawn to writing about unhappy couples and extreme, cuckoo-in-the-nest women. Nighty Night is like a West Country Fatal Attraction. People I’d met while doing office jobs inspired me. Once I asked to borrow a pen and this woman said: “I don’t feel comfortable with that because you might lose it, so I’m going to say no on this occasion.” I found that rude officiousness bizarre and funny. That fed into Jill. Abigail’s Party and Ingmar Bergman films were influences, and I also loved those 90s thrillers like Single White Female or The Hand That Rocks the Cradle.

Those were the glory days of comedy commissioning. I met BBC Three controller Stuart Murphy with one script and did a Jill impression. He went: “Let’s do it.” I cast friends and people I admired: Ruth Jones, Rebecca Front and Kevin Eldon. Poor Kevin, chained to the bed in a nappy.

We needed a romantic male lead – someone like Colin Firth or Greg Wise – so I offered them the role of Cath’s husband Don, the object of Jill’s obsession. They turned it down, obviously. Angus Deayton swooped in and saved the day. Mark Gatiss played Jill’s other love interest, Glen Bulb. He came up with Glen’s twitch himself. We were terrible for corpsing. I met Mark on the worst film ever made, Sex Lives of the Potato Men, and giggled all the way through – partly hysterics due to fear of the script.

Jill’s a sociopath and narcissist, but playing her was liberating. Therapeutic, even. When she goes jogging in lingerie, we filmed it in this village cul de sac. I trotted around in my bra and knickers while this local woman was out walking her little dog. She kept making rude remarks about me via the dog: “We don’t like that lady, do we?” We shot other scenes in Steve Coogan’s house. When Jill and Glen are in bed, that was Steve’s bed. He was rarely there, so we didn’t bother washing the sheets afterwards.

I did ballet until 14 and secretly wanted to be a dancer, hence Jill dancing a lot. I even had lessons from a pole-dancer. I’m surprised we got permission to ride a horse into church for Terry’s funeral but I fibbed that I was an experienced rider. I was scared it would start rearing up. Luckily it was fine, then I dismounted and did a dance to Alone by Heart. Soft rock suited Jill’s cartoonish flamboyance.

I wanted the theme tune to be Rain by the Cult but Steve suggested this jaunty Ennio Morricone piece. I was a bit resistant but it’s weirdly uplifting. A counterpoint to the horror.

Nighty Night divided people. Some would tell me it was sick or offensive. Others found it funny, which reassured me that we struck the right balance. I just thought it was ridiculously silly. I didn’t realise it had become a cult show until much later. Just recently, a guy stopped his bike to tell me he uses Nighty Night to test out new boyfriends and see if the relationship is going to work. I’d heard about gay clubs doing dress-up nights, so finally went along to one last month. Me and Mark judged the annual Miss Jill Tyrell contest at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern. Incredible.

Apparently Kylie watched the show while going through cancer treatment and loved it. I found that very moving. Cancer has touched my life, too. Nighty Night is me finding a way to deal with that terrifying thing. When George Michael was in a coma with pneumonia, he came round talking in a West Country accent. Turned out he’d been obsessed with Nighty Night and often did Jill impressions. It’s unbelievable it had gone into the recesses of his mind. I put Faith in the opening scene of [twisted romcom] Sally4Ever as a little tribute, hoping he was listening up there.

We still talk about doing another series. Jill might be working in cosmetic surgery nowadays, botching ops. Maybe she’s a mother too, which is a scary thought.

I did an episode of I’m Alan Partridge with Julia and we hit it off. Suddenly these scripts arrived. I made the mistake of reading the first two episodes and knew I had to do it. It meant cancelling a family holiday, which didn’t go down well.

I based my character Cath on these nice suburban mums from my childhood. Absolutely lovely but with a steely edge. Her passive aggression contrasts with Jill’s chaos. Her lines still get quoted back at me: “Let’s settle up now or it’ll just get nasty” when splitting the bill or “I don’t like it, Cath” when opening a present. Deep down, we all want to be more Jill. “Hiya Cath!” became a catchphrase. Fight attendants often say it as they hand me a drink. “Hiya Cath! Can I have a selfie?”

Physicality played a big part because of Cath’s multiple sclerosis. Initially I was anxious that MS didn’t become the butt of the joke and or to minimise what’s clearly a serious condition. I had long chats with a colleague of my husband’s who had MS and learned a lot about it. She showed me the sort of limp you might have. Even though Nighty Night is a comedy, I took it seriously. It actually made things funnier because Cath’s got all these disabilities and Jill doesn’t give a shit. It’s just another way to torment her. The more realistically I could portray MS, the better that dynamic became.

In series two, the script said: “Cath runs naked into the sea.” I told Julia I wouldn’t do the naked bit. They ended up getting a body double – an extra who was roughly the right size and shape. I even taught her the limp. I went into my local dry cleaners the day after it aired. The owner gave me a knowing look and said: “I saw you on TV last night.” I thought: “Not in that way, you didn’t.”

When the show aired, my parents didn’t know what to make of it. I said: “Don’t watch it as a sitcom, it’ll confuse you. Watch it as a comic thriller and it’ll make more sense.” A normal-looking woman came up in the supermarket and said: “Oh my God, that Jill Tyrell speaks to me!” I remember looking at her and thinking, in what way?

Nighty Night was outrageously funny and ahead of its time. It has a huge gay fanbase, which we never saw coming. Only recently, I was recording House of Games with Danny Beard, who won Drag Race. The first thing he said was: “Hiya Cath!” We ended up doing a TikTok together. I’d definitely be up for a reunion. I can’t imagine that Cath and Don would still be together. He’s probably been through several other wives. Cath could be celebrating her unique woman-ness via kundalini yoga.

Nighty Night is available on BBC iPlayer

As an oncologist, I’ve received my fair share of thank you notes, but nothing like this

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:00:20 GMT

Every year I receive a letter from the daughter of a patient I treated. It’s an act of unbelievable grace in a job that often feels thankless

Many years ago, in early November, I received a note.

It read: “Dear Doctor, Dad would have been 78 years old today. Of course, no amount of time would have been enough. We think of him and miss him every day.”

My patient’s daughter went on to write that, by talking to her dad every day, she was keeping his memory alive – and, partly, that meant connecting with the people who knew him. In the final few years of his life, this included me.

I was reminded of a man who had been a pleasure to know, right up to the visit that we both quietly understood to be his last. We had tried all kinds of treatments and trials, and his health was now steadily declining. I stressed the importance of good palliative care but, for the family, reeling in shock, it had felt like the “there is nothing we can do” speech.

Soon afterwards, he died peacefully, surrounded by his loving clan.

In 25 years of practice, I have received my fair share of thank you notes but nothing like this, on the birthday of a deceased patient. Touched by the gesture, I showed it to my kids and filed it away.

The next November, I received another note.

“Dear Doctor, Dad would have been 79 today. We remain ever so grateful for your care.”

I felt a catch in my throat.

Well, you know where this is going. Many seasons have passed but it’s November and, with it, another note.

“Dear Doctor, today we remember Dad and are reminded of your contribution to our lives.”

This annual gesture is the only communication from a daughter whom I have never seen again, save for the time shortly after her father’s death when she and her mother came with a gift. Unexpectedly unsettled by the waiting room that looked the same, minus their father and husband, they hurried out in tears, making me wish they had never come.

Between one November and the next, there is no request for a conversation, no demand for an explanation. She was close to her dad, so I imagine she has questions for me. Did I do my best? Have treatments advanced in the intervening years? Are other patients like her dad doing better? But there is nothing of the sort. And then, in November, this act of unbelievable grace that must surely pierce a tiny bubble of grief.

Oncologists are trained to help people navigate some of the most challenging times of life. When patients die, an essential consolation is believing that you gave them the best of your mind and manner. Indeed, this is an important aspect of sustaining the energy to care for other patients.

Sometimes, the job can seem thankless.

My midwife friend, driving home from a long day in the labour ward, rues that no woman will remember her. I joyfully refute this every time. Which woman doesn’t remember her midwife? I have lost track of mine but not their acts of kindness.

Perhaps this is one of the more humbling aspects of working in medicine: the extraordinary asymmetry of remembering.

Over the course of a career, we see thousands of patients. Not uncommonly, patients themselves will say, “I don’t expect you to remember me, you’re so busy”. We can care about all our patients and remember some more vividly than others – that’s just human nature. But for the patient sitting across from us, we might be their only doctor or midwife. Which means that an ordinary encounter late on a Wednesday afternoon may be a defining moment in a patient’s life. To meet this recognition not with hubris but with humility is the calling of good medicine.

We tend to think of our work in terms of what we do: the diagnoses we make, the treatments we prescribe, the decisions we get right. I remember how much I coveted these skills as a trainee.

So it has been a revelation of a lifetime to discover that patients and families remember something quite different. A reassuring word, a slow explanation, the feeling of being listened to, or simply the sense that someone cared enough to stay a little longer.

I wonder how often we underestimate the significance of these small encounters. We are inclined to think that the important work happens in the consulting room, in the operating theatre or on the labour ward. Yet the things people carry away with them may be much less tangible. My midwife friend cannot know that she may one day feature in the story a woman tells her grandchildren about the day their mother was born.

And so it should be. We cannot work with the expectation of being remembered, any more than we can demand gratitude from our patients.

But it’s worth remembering that we might be.

If you had asked me years ago, I would have assured you that although I missed my patient, my role was over. But, for his daughter, it seems not. Every year, with one dignified note, she brings together the dad she misses with the oncologist who had the privilege of knowing him.

We never speak but, all at once, she reminds me that the work of medicine is not always triumphant. It can also be quiet, its impact reverberating long after the encounter.

Sometimes, without knowing it, we become part of the memory that people are trying to keep alive.

This is one of the great privileges of medicine – but, as I now see, no less a responsibility.

Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the Public

‘These men feel protected’: how Mexico’s first femicide squad is turning the tide on record killings

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 13:00:01 GMT

The female-led unit in Mexico City has cut gender-based murders from a historic high in 2021. Now, there are hopes to appoint specialist teams and prosecutors nationwide

Paz Rodríguez woke up about 5am at her home in Milpa Alta, a suburb of Mexico City, on 20 March 2021. She thought about her plans for the day: pick up yellow lilies and cacti from her mother’s house and sell them in the market. Later that evening, they would cook mole, a traditional Mexican dish, together.

She reached for her phone, which was flooded with texts from her sister, Oliviera Rodríguez. “Mum’s dog is barking a lot,” she had written. “I keep calling and she won’t respond.”

Rodríguez, worried, rushed to her mother’s house. “Mum,” she called through the slightly open door. “Mum,” she called again, but no one answered. She walked through the kitchen and saw gas cylinders, usually lined up against the wall, scattered across the floor. She felt something was wrong.

In the bedroom, Rodríguez found her mother lying face down on the floor, unresponsive. “There was so much blood around her body,” Rodríguez says.

Her mother, Melesia García, 72, had been attacked the night before. The police said that assailants broke in, raped and killed her.

“They did terrible things to her,” Rodríguez says. “I don’t understand why. My mother never hurt anyone.”

The siblings buried their mother in Oaxaca, where she had grown up in the mountains, among flowers and cacti.

García was one of the 1,022 victims of femicide in 2021, when intentional murders of women and girls hit a historic high in Mexico.

When a prosecutor told Rodríguez they were treating her mother’s murder as a femicide, she had never heard the term before. The prosecutor’s team were part of a femicide unit formed a year earlier by Claudia Sheinbaum, now president of Mexico but then the mayor of Mexico City.

Six years on from the unit’s creation, official data shows that Mexico’s femicide rate has started to fall, from 1,022 victims in 2021 to 736 last year.

Eduardo Guerrero Gutiérrez, director of Lantia Intelligence, a consultancy specialising in public safety and crime, said the decline can be partially explained by appointing professionals to key positions, such as the femicide prosecutor, to tackle violence. Before Sheinbaum took office, these positions were held by politicians “who didn’t take these issues seriously”, he says.

While independent research suggests the true number of femicides is higher than in official statistics, the unit still represents cautious progress on one of Latin America’s most intractable problems.

The femicide unit, which operates from the first floor of Mexico City’s police headquarters, is at the forefront of the battle against the killings. Femicide detectives come and go at all hours. LGBTQ+ flags, pink anti-violence posters and a photo of a missing girl with a short black fringe hang on the walls. A lilac room is dedicated to investigating trans femicides.

On a recent afternoon, a female officer, who wanted to remain anonymous due to the sensitive investigations, showed us a video of a man in a helmet, shooting a woman as she walked out of a building. The woman fell to the ground, and the man jumped on his bike and left. The officer pulled up another video and pointed out the same man taking off his helmet. She had found that image after watching hours of CCTV footage and mapping the man’s bike route. Now they are trying to locate him.

Not every case is as straightforward. She is also investigating the murder of a girl at home. Though she has been through every piece of footage available from nearby cameras and flagged suspects, she has not yet found the killer.

The officer is part of the intelligence team that uses digital evidence and technology to track down suspects. In a recent undercover operation, she located a possible perpetrator hiding in Tijuana through his TikTok posts, chatted to him, and set up a date. The detectives arrested him at the location where the suspect believed he was meeting a woman.

The idea for a specialised femicide prosecutor came from feminist activists in 2017, after the body of Lesby Berlin Osorio, 22, was found in a phone booth, strangled by the telephone cable. Her case became a symbol of violence against women in Mexico.

The Mexico City prosecutor investigating Osorio’s murder described her in a social media post as a college dropout who was “drinking and [taking] drugs”. Outraged by his statements, activists demanded a prosecutor who would take femicides seriously.

In March 2020, Sayuri Herrera Román, a prominent human rights lawyer and a longtime activist, became the country’s first femicide prosecutor.

“We believed that we, as a movement, had earned that prosecutor’s office and that space, and that we had to take it,” Román says.

When Román founded the unit, there were only eight officers and the office did not even have cabinets – files were just dumped in boxes on the floor, she says. Over the years, the team has expanded to 86 people, including a photographer, forensics experts, litigators and psychologists.

García’s murder was one of Román’s first cases. The unit usually takes six months from investigation to prosecution, but in García’s case, it took four years. Local people misled the team to protect each other, she says, and witnesses were too scared to come forward.

In 2022, Román became a special prosecutor to investigate crimes related to violence against women across Mexico. Brenda Celina Bazán Varela, a detective on her team who was already investigating García’s death, became the new femicide prosecutor.

Varela ordered a review of the biological evidence in García’s case using the latest scientific methods and ran it through the database, which linked the DNA samples with her neighbour and his friend.

“This case was very difficult for us, but in the end we managed to bring these two individuals to justice,” Varela says. Both men were arrested in 2025.

The femicide detectives usually arrive at a crime scene shortly after the local police and follow their own protocol: they photograph the body, collect fingerprints and anything that could be considered evidence. Forensic officers swab fingernails and the pubic area, even if there is no sign of sexual assault.

Last year in March, Mexico City’s chief prosecutor, Bertha Alcalde Luján, introduced a new protocol ensuring all violent deaths of women were investigated as femicides. “We understand that the violence is often part of a broader context,” Luján says.

Still, many women feel like the authorities are failing to protect them. Independent reports show that victims and their families are worn down by incompetent police, authorities’ unwillingness to take action, delayed investigations and pervasive impunity.

As the sentencing hearing approached for García’s alleged killers, Rodríguez started to hope that justice would be served in her mother’s case. But on 28 July, the judge acquitted both defendants. The verdict, reviewed by the Guardian, found DNA evidence from the vaginal swab linked to at least two men and matched one defendant’s family, but the judge decided not to rely on it as the samples were “not collected and stored properly” and needed further examination.

“Sometimes there is a very thorough investigation and there is evidence, yet the judge’s interpretation fails to recognise that violence,” Varela says.

Having a specialised unit can help cases reach the courts. This year, Mexico City’s prosecutor has recorded 33 femicides, 32 of which have reached the courts. In total, 63 femicide cases were tried in 2026, including cases carried over from the previous year, and nearly half ended in a conviction.

However, the unit is unique to Mexico City, while other states are neglected, says Chantal Flores, a Mexican journalist who has been covering femicides for years. So far in 2026, 518 women have been killed in femicides across the country.

Feminists are trying to convince the senate to adopt a bill, signed by Sheinbaum in July, that would standardise femicide investigations and appoint a femicide prosecutor or unit in every state, as well as increasing the punishment from 40-60 years to 50-70 years.

Rodríguez, now 45, plaits her hair and hangs it over her shoulder, as her mother did. She attends feminist marches, wearing a T-shirt with her mother’s picture that reads “Justice for Melesia”.

Since the judge released the two defendants accused of her murder, Rodríguez and her family say they have been harassed by the men’s relatives.

“These men feel protected by the system that should have punished them,” Rodríguez says. She now rarely leaves the house, and is trying to save enough money to move to Oaxaca, to be close to her mother’s grave and to feel secure again.

“I am still mourning,” she says. “The judge killed my mother one more time by letting the perpetrators go free.”

WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao

‘I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl buried in mud. I knew we had to do something’

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 12:00:59 GMT

Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan

Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall

This is Imran Lodhi’s story

Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.

In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.

I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.

We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.

When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.

Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.

The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.

We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.

One old woman started to laugh. I was surprised. I asked her: “It’s OK, we have food, but why are you laughing?” And she said: “I was just complaining, ‘Lord, that you left me with an empty stomach today.’ And suddenly you appeared.”

It was a very strange experience for her. For us also. People, when they are in tough conditions, are attached to their beliefs. And, when things like that come up, they establish a spiritual connection with the people who are helping out.

We posted on social media. We tried to mobilise. A lot of people contacted us who were from other parts of Pakistan. Money poured in and we kept expanding the team. From two or three villages, we started to cover the entire district, and then almost the entire region.

The government protocols were to not go into certain areas that looked dangerous or were not safe for a boat. Families were trapped, many, many kilometres into the water. There was no land in one village. Small wooden cupboards were hung on trees so stuff could be saved from the water. The immediate shelter was a big tree near them. The whole family was in the tree. The elders were lying on the branches. They somehow made a swing for the kids. They spent days in those trees.

A few villages were completely destroyed. Not a single home was standing. Everything was in shock, even the trees. One old woman who was living with her married kids was not ready to leave that rubble. She was so attached to that home that she felt like there was no life after it. She had a small cupboard in which she kept some small things to sell, for her independence. She was so concerned about that small cupboard. When I reached there, that cupboard was all broken.

One day I had a fever and my wife stopped me: “Don’t go out – you are not well enough to help other people.” But I still went out to a village to help people. When we reached there, I got news that the city we were living in – which I thought was safe – suddenly was a source of threat. There was water coming toward the city. Within hours, the water would be in the city. My family was there. And I was almost 100km away.

So I rushed back. But the road toward the city was cut off by the flood. There was no way I could go back to my family. I called my wife and I asked them to stay vigilant and look out for water in the city. I gave them some suggestions: how they could save themselves and evacuate. That was a very, very tough call.

Eventually, the city was saved. Next day, we took a boat to get past the road that was cut off. Sitting in that boat, I was thinking about my family. Once I reached the other side, I called some people to take me home.

When I reached home, I had a very strong fever and I spent that day at home. I tried to behave normally, but everybody knew I was not feeling well. I took one day off from community work.

The next day I wanted to stop. But the problem was, I was in the middle of that network. If I stop, this whole process will stop. This whole network of relief work will stop.

The next day, even with a high fever, I left for the field because I didn’t want that to stop. When I grew up, the community fabric was very strong. It was common practice that whenever people got sick, got in an accident, hospitalised, people would visit the person and share some money.

This was the kind of culture I observed happening around me.

I went back to those areas where the flood came. There was still some water standing so there were remains of that devastation. But there’s a very common sweet in that area we call jalebi. I can smell that sweet in those villages. I see shops open. I see farmers, labourers. I felt good watching people working again. It looked like life was coming back.

There was an annual poetry event happening three months after the flood. Saraiki culture is very rich, one of the oldest. I was consulted by one of my friends who is the organiser of that event. Should we suspend this year’s events or not?

I said you should never suspend the event. Let people believe the normalisation, let people believe in the spirit of survival. They organised the poetry event.

Jay Shah re-elected unopposed as ICC chair after board clears way for bigger IPL

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 11:53:36 GMT

Global cricket tournaments will avoid March to May

IPL expected to expand to 12 teams from 2028

Jay Shah has been re-elected unopposed as the chair of the International Cricket Council after a board meeting in Bali that has also paved the way for the expansion of the Indian Premier League. In announcing its major events schedule until 2035, the ICC has moved its global men’s tournaments to the second half of the year, creating a three-month period from March to May that is expected to be filled by the IPL.

In the past two years, the men’s T20 World Cup and Champions Trophy have been played in February and March. The Future Tours Programme governing bilateral series between ICC members has yet to be signed off, but sources involved in those discussions have indicated that no major series will be scheduled between March and May.

Reports in India last week said that Pune and Vadodara have been earmarked as venues for new IPL franchises that would take the competition to 12 teams from 2028 and coincide with the next media rights cycle. The Board of Control for Cricket in India dismissed those reports, but is believed to be exploring an expansion of the existing 10-franchise structure that would involve every team playing each other twice in the regular season, meaning 94 matches instead of 74.

In common with other major global leagues, increasing the number of fixtures for broadcasters is seen as the only way to maintain the IPL’s revenue growth after the 2024 merger of Disney and Reliance Industries to create JioStar, whose current domestic deal is worth $6bn over five years.

The ICC’s calendar changes have made an IPL expansion possible as all its global men’s events from 2028 to 2035 will take place in the northern hemisphere autumn, with the exception of the 2034 men’s T20 World Cup, which has been scheduled for June and July, and the World Test Championship final which will take place in June in odd-numbered years until 2035. That almost certainly means they will be held in England. The England and Wales Cricket Board has a hosting agreement with the ICC until 2031, which is likely to be extended to cover two more finals.

Confirmation of Shah’s extension means he will stay in post until December 2030, when he must step down under the ICC constitution. Shah was previously secretary of the BCCI and his father, Amit, is the minister for home affairs in India’s government.

“Serving as chair of the ICC is both a privilege and a responsibility, and I remain committed to working with our members to advance the interests of cricket across the world,” Shah said. “I have always believed that cricket’s greatest strength lies in its ability to bring people together.

The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 11:10:56 GMT

Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance

Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost. The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died.

Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community alive. No – she was prophesying 40 years into the future about the digital-age phenomenon of ghosting. The fact that this practice is widespread enough for there to be a word for it is proof of the long since disintegrated fabric of our society.

I think if you share any time or spit with someone, you should have the courage and common courtesy to let them know if you don’t fancy doing it again.

Back in the day – when you would meet potential partners through friends or extended community circles – dumping someone with neither word nor explanation would be unthinkable. You’d be shunned for barbarism. But so much of dating now is at a remove from our would-be communities, siloed away into these apps, so there is no one to hold us accountable. Late-stage capitalism has us all working so hard that it’s rare we make it out of the house or office to socialise. When we do, we’re less primed for chance encounters with new people because we’re busy focusing on the people we barely get to see.

Couple that with an app culture that filters out those who don’t meet our expected criteria and, of course, modern dating becomes less connected and more prejudiced (OkCupid stats show a majority of straight men exclude the option to date black women). We swipe and we judge. We lean into our biases and lean out of romantic risk.

A friend of mine swiped left to reject the man who is now her husband. On an app, his 2D profile fell flat. But when she later bumped into him in real life, she fell for the strange wonder of how his face moved. In the flesh, she saw his unique personal magic.

So, set your single friend up with another friend. Send them out on a date. Or go out dancing. Book a hall. Throw a party! If it isn’t affordable, let’s fight to make it affordable.

We need a renaissance of hall parties. Thrown for no reason. Other than our need to gather – in community, in our chosen villages – to satiate our desperate hunger for connection. Or, at least, to give us singletons a chance at the unsanitised magic of human partnership.

Not ready for the cold and dark? Maybe you need a ‘winter transition week’

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 11:00:56 GMT

A psychologist has recommended we all take time for slowness and rest, to prepare ourselves for the coming months. It’s a nice idea, but it may prove my downfall

How are you feeling about the rapid dying of the light? Are you already sluggish and glum, poleaxed by the “polar vortex” or seasonal lurgy? That might be because you’re doing winter wrong: according to health psychologist Kari Leibowitz, writing in the Washington Post, we’d all benefit from a “winter transition week”.

Leibowitz, the author of a book, How to Winter, based on her time living in the Arctic, explains: “I intentionally clear out my calendar … say no to extra obligations, try to cancel or postpone unnecessary meetings and make time for rest and slowness.” During this time, she also recommends stocking up on tea, getting out thick socks, eating soup and planning little treats.

My issue with this good, if hardly groundbreaking, advice is: how do you transition out again? Because a regime of “rest and slowness”, refusing all engagements, sipping soup while swaddled like a baby in blankets and indulging in little treats is sensible for a week, but it will become my entire life if I let it.

I love winter, but I’m on week five and counting (or rather coughing) of some gross bug, and have cancelled my social life so comprehensively that everyone I know has forgotten I exist. When I consider venturing out, I remember the footage of last week’s horrifying rail replacement bus queue at York station, where I live, and think better of it. It’s so damn cosy here: the fire is on; the freezer is stuffed with soup and cake; every soft surface has a blanket on it, and every hard one a candle. There’s no room for more tea in this house, Kari! I get hit on the head by warming cinnamon and ginger concoctions every time I open the cupboard!

What I’m saying is: I’ve wintered too hard already – I’m so hunkered down, you might as well pop me in the fridge with my hibernating tortoises – and it’s only November. Come February, a gentle transition week won’t cut it. I’ll need a full, muscular intervention: someone to confiscate my heated throws and woolly socks and drag me back into society. They’ll probably need a cattle prod.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Controversial efforts to suck carbon from atmosphere championed at UN climate talks

The Guardian Mon, 16 Nov 2026 06:00:34 GMT

Proponents and lobbyists make renewed push for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) to be included in final text of Cop31

Send us your climate questions for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

What happens when the world, as expected, hurtles dangerously past agreed temperature thresholds? At UN climate talks, countries are being urged to turn to technology to reverse this fate by sucking carbon directly from the atmosphere.

A renewed push by proponents of carbon dioxide removal (or CDR), where heat-trapping carbon dioxide is taken from the atmosphere and stored deep underground, in oceans or in products such as carbonated drinks, is seeking to gain recognition in the final text of Cop31, the climate summit currently under way in Antalya, Turkey.

A pavilion, called Think Negative, has been set up at the sprawling summit venue, where plans for a dramatic increase in carbon removal is talked up as a way to help bring back the world from imminent “overshoot” of internationally agreed temperature thresholds.

Meanwhile, a record 700 lobbyists at this Cop are advocating for a distinct but related process called carbon capture and storage (or CCS), where carbon is captured at the source of a polluting facility and put underground, according to the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). This is more delegates than from the smallest 50 national delegations combined.

CCS has less support from environmentalists over its costs, mixed track record, and potential to prolong fossil fuel reliance. But on Friday, for the first time, both CCS and CDR were included in a text that will inform the basis of a final deal at the climate talks.

The UN has acknowledged the world will soon surge past a 1.5C rise in global temperatures since the pre-industrial period, which will unleash ever worsening heatwaves, floods, droughts and other deadly impacts, as countries continue to release greenhouse gases by burning fossil fuels.

Even with reduced emissions the planet’s fever will not fall below this level for thousands of years without the sort of rapid removal of CO2 as envisaged by the CDR advocates, who want to create a new global agency to coordinate carbon removals. They have also pressed Turkey and Australia, which are jointly presiding over the Cop31 talks, to include CDR in the summit’s final outcome.

“CDR still sounds unreal to people but we spent a whole year trying to make it into the agenda of Cop31,” said Göker Avci, a decarbonization strategist at CDR Türkiye. “We spoke with the presidency about making it into the final decision and they have started to realize the potential.”

There are various forms of carbon removal, such as directly sucking it from the air, crushing up rocks that can lock away carbon or, more naturally, through protecting and seeding forests and mangroves.

CDR remains relatively small scale, with around 2bn tons of carbon removed a year, almost all of it via reforestation. Technological efforts to vacuum CO2 from the air has removed just 2m tons, with leading companies in this area badly underperforming and struggling financially. With a lack of investor cash, which is instead flowing to areas such as artificial intelligence, CDR remains nascent and under-resourced.

Despite this, countries have long relied on the theoretical promise of carbon removal in their climate plans. That promise will quickly have to become reality if the world is to bend the temperature curve back to safe levels, rather than just flatline it – the UN recently estimated that an enormous 320bn tons of CO2 will have to be removed this century in order to get back under 1.5C.

“CDR’s really been missing from the discussion and debate even though it’s been in all the models for decades,” said Injy Johnstone, a net zero expert at the Max Planck Insitute. “It’s the only solution that we have to actually balance out those emissions and return from the state of overshoot.”

“Really these efforts shouldn’t have to be led by the entrepreneurs kind of doing their thing on the ground, we have to get more vocal about it and actually also start to put in place these kinds of procedures,” she added about the attempt to set up an international framework for CDR.

Although CDR is still largely missing from the equation, environmentalists have warned about the risks of depending on it. Large, potentially harmful, changes to land use and the oceans would be needed to remove and store enough carbon, they argue, while the reliance on cleaning up the atmosphere removes pressure on reducing emissions in the first place.

“The focus should always be on cutting emissions now, it’s very dangerous to assume that we can put more emissions into the atmosphere and then assume we will have technology in the future to just remove them again,” said Rachel Kennerley, carbon capture campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law.

“These are hypothetical technologies and part of the problem we’re seeing here is that we’re seeing the normalization of this overshoot peak and return pathway. That return element is at the moment hypothetical. I mean, I think it’s impossible.”

CDR is often confused for carbon capture and storage (or CCS), where emissions are captured directly at the source and buried. Kennerley said that CCS is a “greenwashing exercise” used by large oil and gas companies to extend the age of fossil fuels.

But the two processes are similar in some aspects, given they both ultimately end up having to store large amounts of carbon underground. “I think they fulfill similar kind of diversionary roles from mitigation,” said Kennerley. “I think they’re both allowed for prolonging fossil-fuel use, basically.”

Kennerley added that the exceedance of 1.5C should be kept as small as possible with the elimination of fossil fuel use, with reforestation then slowly eating up the excess CO2 to the point, over many hundreds of years, the temperature dips back down.

But advocates claim the scale of the climate emergency is such that CDR will be the only viable option to bring down the temperature. “It’s the only tool we have,” said Johnstone. “We need this, we need this fast, and we need to be really seeing it on a scale that rivals the global energy industry in terms of its kind of footprint in the world.”

Few, if any, figures in recent history have caused as much legal, political, financial and reputational upheaval as Jeffrey Epstein. A convicted sex offender, Mr. Epstein was connected to many of the world’s richest and most influential people and institutions. He died in prison in 2019.

The public fascination with Mr. Epstein intensified after President Trump initially refused to release federal investigative records after pledging to do so. In late 2025 and early 2026, Congress and the Justice Department did release millions of pages of documents related to Mr. Epstein that have helped answer questions, though many mysteries remain.

The New York Times has been investigating Mr. Epstein’s finances, enablers and possible co-conspirators since his arrest on federal sex-trafficking charges in 2019. Based on our continuing reporting, here is what we know.

The most recent revelations about Mr. Epstein include:

One way Mr. Epstein kept finding new victims was by grooming young girls to bring other young girls, often their friends, to visit him. Very few of the women have talked publicly about doing so. Some had been labeled traffickers and conspirators. But that seemed wrong to Marina Lacerda, who was first brought by a friend to meet Mr. Epstein when she was 13 years old. Ms. Lacerdo talked openly with reporter Jen Percy about her experience, a story that she told over many hours of interviews this summer and that was corroborated by several other survivors and materials in the Epstein files.

Karyna Shuliak, 37, stands to inherit as much as $100 million from his estate, according to files released by federal authorities. A native of Belarus who met Mr. Epstein when she was 21, Ms. Shuliak has not been identified as one of his victims nor was she seen by federal authorities as a co-conspirator in his sex trafficking. He helped her in many ways, including her attaining U. S. citizenship and getting her into dental school.

Leon Botstein, who was forced to retire in June as the president of Bard College after revelations in Justice Department documents about his longstanding friendship with Mr. Epstein, resigned from all of his positions affiliated with the college on Oct. 7.

The resignation came as the House Judiciary Committee sent a letter to Bard leaders saying that while Dr. Botstein was president, he “likely enabled and possibly even participated in” Mr. Epstein’s abuse. In a statement, Dr. Botstein called the allegations in the letter untrue and said he submitted his resignation “to protect Bard from any distraction.”

Links to all of our coverage can be found here.

Mr. Epstein has been accused by prosecutors and victims of raping, abusing and trafficking girls and young women. It was a vast, yearslong operation that involved:

In the mid-2000s, federal and state authorities identified more than a dozen such teenage girls in Florida. In many cases, Mr. Epstein’s longtime companion Ghislaine Maxwell recruited them under the pretense that they would be masseuses for a wealthy man at his mansion in Palm Beach.

Federal prosecutors later accused Mr. Epstein of abusing and trafficking dozens of girls at his townhouse in Manhattan, as well as in Palm Beach, from at least 2002 to 2005. He lured some by posing as a talent scout for Victoria’s Secret.

After he served time in a Florida jail for soliciting prostitution from a minor, Mr. Epstein appears to have shifted focus from underage victims to young women. He was often surrounded by aspiring models from Russia and Eastern Europe, some of whom later said they felt trapped under his control.

Some have accused several of those friends and associates of rape, though the men deny it.

They have accused him of raping or abusing them, including when they were girls — allegations that in some cases date to the early 1990s. At least one of those women, Virginia Giuffre, has died by suicide.

The federal government repeatedly missed opportunities to fully investigate or charge Mr. Epstein, until 2019. The missteps and lost opportunities included:

In 1996, Maria Farmer called the F. B. I. to tell the agency that Mr. Epstein had stolen nude photos of her underage sister. It ignored the tip for roughly a decade.

In 2005, the parents of a 14-year-old girl told the Palm Beach police that she had been paid to give a sexual massage to Mr. Epstein. That set off a state and federal investigation. While the authorities identified dozens of underage victims, the Justice Department — including the U. S. attorney for southern Florida at the time, Alexander Acosta — negotiated a deal: Mr. Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting prostitution from just one minor.

The agreement also shielded any “potential co-conspirators,” including his female assistants, from prosecution. Though Mr. Epstein served his sentence in the county stockade, he was allowed to spend much of his jail time working from his office.

After being released early from his 18-month sentence, Mr. Epstein was welcomed back into elite society, attending parties, hosting dinners and continuing to do business with major financial institutions.

In the 2010s, a number of federal agencies, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, investigated Mr. Epstein, but he wasn’t charged.

In 2016, lawyers for some of Mr. Epstein’s victims urged federal prosecutors in New York to investigate him for sex trafficking. The prosecutors chose not to.

It wasn’t until 2018, after the newspaper wrote a series about the 2008 deal in Florida, that federal prosecutors in New York opened a criminal investigation. It culminated in Mr. Epstein’s being charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

Mr. Epstein did not grow up with wealth. He spent his formative years in an insular world, in Sea Gate, in Coney Island, which was then a mostly working- and middle-class Jewish refuge. But the picture of his boyhood we found contains the fuzzy outlines of his future self: From a young age, Epstein preferred the protective company of a tight group of brainy boys and fixated on girls.

As an adult, he amassed a nine-figure fortune through scams, fraud and the careful cultivation of billionaires and banks. His financial success involved:

Mr. Epstein’s first big break was landing a job at Bear Stearns in 1976. He eventually resigned after being caught improperly lending money to a client and violating rules around stock offerings, but he used the connections he forged there to jump-start his career as a financial trickster.

In the 1980s, Mr. Epstein, claiming to be a financial savant, engaged in a series of escalating scams.

In the late 1980s, a mutual acquaintance introduced him to Leslie Wexner, who ran the two retail companies. Mr. Wexner entrusted Mr. Epstein with full control over his finances before cutting ties with him around 2007. Mr. Wexner later said Mr. Epstein stole more than $100 million from him.

In 2012, Mr. Epstein began working for his longtime friend Leon Black, the co-founder of the private equity firm Apollo Global Management who said the money was for tax and estate planning work. Mr. Epstein also introduced Mr. Black to young women.

From the late 1990s through 2013, JPMorgan Chase, arguably the world’s most prestigious bank, serviced Mr. Epstein, despite employees’ concerns about his potential money laundering. In 2013, he switched to Deutsche Bank, which also ignored repeated red flags.

The combination of great wealth and a reputation for seeming to know everyone enabled Mr. Epstein to insinuate himself into the lives of important people in politics, business, the arts and academia. His strategy entailed:

As his fortune grew, Mr. Epstein made big donations to prestigious universities like Harvard and to individual scientists. The money led Nobel laureates and other leading intellectual figures to regularly socialize with and seek favor from him, and their presence helped grow his circle of influence.

Some of the doctors and others bent or broke the ethical rules of their profession, which allowed Mr. Epstein to offer perks to other acquaintances, like access to premier medical care, investment opportunities with hedge funds or a potential edge in school admissions.

Mr. Epstein’s vast Manhattan townhouse became the venue for regular dinner salons for an eclectic mix of artists, scientists, intellectuals, lawyers and businessmen. Visitors were greeted with photo arrays exhibiting Mr. Epstein’s ties to the ruling class.

One of his most valuable connections was to the former president. The relationship helped catapult Mr. Epstein into the public spotlight and secure his image as a whisperer to the rich and powerful.

Mr. Epstein also boasted extensive Wall Street connections to C. E. O. s (like James Cayne and Jes Staley); investment tycoons (like Glenn Dubin and Mr. Black); and powerful lawyers, like Brad Karp and Kathy Ruemmler. A secretive law firm would later try, and fail, to fix Ms. Ruemmler’s image. Ms Ruemmler told a House committee in July that Mr. Epstein “was a masterful liar.”

He had a long friendship with Stephen Hanson, a New York City restaurant mogul who performed an array of tasks for Mr. Epstein, including arranging jobs, visas and entertainment for women. And he collected high-profile friends and associates overseas, including Prince Andrew, the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak and top Norwegian politicians.

Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist, told a congressional committee in June that Mr. Epstein exploited information about his extramarital affairs “to pressure me to re-engage with him” after Mr. Gates had begun to sever ties with him.

Mr. Epstein was friends with Mr. Trump long before he became president, and he developed a relationship with Mr. Clinton during his time in the White House. Those relationships involved:

The two men became good friends in the late 1980s, hanging out together at casinos, Mr. Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate and other venues. A note and sexually suggestive drawing containing what appeared to be Mr. Trump’s signature was included in a 2003 book for Mr. Epstein’s birthday. Mr. Trump has denied writing the note.

Some of Mr. Epstein’s victims, including Ms. Giuffre, were recruited by Ms. Maxwell from Mr. Trump’s Florida club and residence, where Ms. Giuffre worked as a spa attendant. Mr. Trump said last year that he cut ties with Mr. Epstein in the early 2000s because he “stole” his female employees, although the relationship also deteriorated when the men fought over a piece of Florida real estate.

Shortly after Mr. Clinton was sworn in as president, Mr. Epstein made his first visit. Visitor logs show that he came back numerous times during Mr. Clinton’s first term, though it is unclear how often he met the president. In 1995, Mr. Clinton wrote a get-well-soon note to Mr. Epstein’s mother on a Post-it.

In 2002, after Mr. Clinton left the White House, Mr. Epstein flew him and others to several African countries. The trip was one of the first times that Mr. Epstein attracted significant media attention.

Mr. Epstein’s New York mansion showcased photos of him with each of them. When Mr. Trump became president, Mr. Epstein at times presented himself as someone who had inside knowledge about the administration, though it was most likely an act. Both Mr. Trump and Mr. Clinton have said they knew nothing about Mr. Epstein’s criminal activity.

Behind the scenes, the Epstein crisis was paralyzing the Trump administration to a far greater extent than the public knew. In their public statements, Trump’s advisers were full of bravado, dismissing the crisis. In reality, it was consuming the highest ranks of the administration.

Mr. Epstein’s inner circle and the financiers and banks that enabled him faced allegations of wrongdoing. But U. S. prosecutors charged only one person other than Mr. Epstein. The legal trail included:

She is the only person other than Mr. Epstein to face criminal charges in the United States. In 2021, she was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Some Republicans have expressed support for the idea that President Trump would pardon her.

In the months after Mr. Epstein’s death, federal authorities investigated a number of Mr. Epstein’s former personal assistants, who were accused by some victims of participating in his sex-trafficking operation. Prosecutors considered charging at least one, but they ultimately opted not to, perhaps because she said she was also one of Mr. Epstein’s victims.

Federal prosecutors apparently didn’t interview or subpoena Mr. Wexner, Mr. Black and Mr. Epstein’s longtime accountant Richard Kahn and lawyer Darren Indyke. A federal document described Mr. Wexner as a co-conspirator, though his spokesman denied that the government ever considered him one.

But the House Oversight Committee issued subpoenas to Mr. Black in June, and in September, held him in criminal contempt of Congress over not responding — a move that amounts to an official recommendation that the Justice Department bring federal charges against Mr. Black.

Federal authorities interviewed women who accused Mr. Black and Mr. Staley, a former top JPMorgan executive, of sexual misconduct — allegations that both men deny. Prosecutors relayed those accusations to officials in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which did not bring charges.

As part of their investigations into Mr. Epstein, federal prosecutors subpoenaed the two banks that provided him with the greatest financial support, JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank. The prosecutors appeared to have quickly decided against charging either institution with wrongdoing.

Police departments and prosecutors in some other countries recently have taken a more aggressive approach. In Britain, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince, and Peter Mandelson, a former top government official, have been arrested in connection with Epstein investigations. Neither has been charged.

We are tracking that fallout here.

Mr. Epstein spent 36 days at the now-shuttered Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City before he was found dead in his cell on Aug. 10, 2019. The medical examiner ruled his death a suicide.

For the most in-depth investigation yet into his death, we consulted tens of thousands of pages of newly released documents, obtained Mr. Epstein’s own notes handwritten in jail — never before made public — and interviewed dozens of people related to the case. We found abundant evidence that for weeks before his death, Mr. Epstein had written about and discussed the idea of suicide and attempted it at least once, and possibly three times.

The circumstances around his death include:

Mr. Epstein was found unresponsive with a cloth tied around his neck in his cell two and a half weeks before his death. He denied trying to take his own life, but he was psychologically evaluated and placed on suicide watch for barely a day.

The cellmate, Nicholas Tartaglione, said the note was written by Mr. Epstein. It was sealed by a federal court for years. The Times successfully petitioned the court to unseal the note in May 2026. It has not been authenticated but bears similarities to known writings by Mr. Epstein.

As one of the highest-profile federal inmates, Mr. Epstein was supposed to be under close supervision and to have a cellmate. But he was left alone in a cell on the evening of Aug. 9, 2019. Other inmates reported to jail authorities that he was despondent.

Guards were supposed to make regular rounds to check on prisoners. But on Mr. Epstein’s last night, the two guards on duty in his area stayed by their desks. The guards were criminally charged, but the charges were withdrawn as part of a deferred prosecution agreement.

Mr. Epstein was found unconscious early on the morning of Aug. 10 with a strip of orange bedding cinched around his neck. He was soon pronounced dead, in what was later ruled a suicide.

From virtually the moment his death was announced, there have been doubts and unfounded speculation about the circumstances. His brother, Mark Epstein, is among those who don’t believe he killed himself. The Department of Justice re-examined the death in 2023 and found no evidence of a conspiracy or criminality.

The phrase usually refers to the millions of Epstein investigation documents that Congress directed the Justice Department to release. But there have been more. Over the years, all three branches of the U. S. government have released records, and media outlets, including The Times, have obtained documents through leaks or public records requests. The materials include:

In August 2019, a federal appeals court unsealed one of the first main caches of Epstein-related files, part of a defamation lawsuit brought against Ms. Maxwell by Ms. Giuffre, one of Mr. Epstein’s most outspoken victims. The files included depositions, photos, flight logs and other materials that gave the public a powerful glimpse into Mr. Epstein’s crimes and network. The morning after the files were unsealed, he was found dead in his jail cell.

The trove of documents dribbled into public view in 2023 during a court fight between the U. S. Virgin Islands and the bank. Those files showed the chummy relationships between Mr. Epstein and senior bank executives.

In 2025, The Times obtained thousands of Mr. Epstein’s photos and documents, which showed the inside of his Upper East Side mansion — including surveillance cameras in his bedroom area — and some of his correspondence with men like Woody Allen and Mr. Black.

Bloomberg News published several articles based on thousands of emails from Mr. Epstein’s Yahoo account. Those emails and others were later posted for public perusal on a site called Jmail.

After taking office in 2025, Mr. Trump backtracked on his earlier pledges to release the government’s files on Mr. Epstein. That led to a political uproar. Congress then passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which required the administration to release its files. In December and January, the Justice Department released millions of pages of records.

The Justice Department said it decided not to release many other records, because they would identify victims or could jeopardize ongoing federal investigations. Other documents appeared to simply be missing. That has stoked speculation about a possible coverup.

The Justice Department blacked out the names of some government lawyers or potential co-conspirators. It failed to protect victims’ names and included nude photos of potential victims. The Justice Department’s internal watchdog is now investigating whether the department’s disclosures followed the law.

Measles Is Sickening More Pregnant Women and Newborns, Alarming Doctors

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

A new analysis underscores the severe consequences of a measles infection during pregnancy, including hospitalization and pregnancy loss.

By Teddy Rosenbluth

At least 13 babies have been born infected with measles in the United States past two years, as the highly contagious virus has surged across the country, scientists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported on Monday.

Their preliminary analysis, published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence, is the first to document how common congenital measles has become nationwide. The authors also identified 112 pregnant women infected with measles in 2025 and 2026, most of whom were unvaccinated. Nearly one-quarter were hospitalized for complications unrelated to labor, such as pneumonia and respiratory failure. One was admitted to the intensive care unit. Some also delivered preterm, and two lost their pregnancies.

“This is much worse than we thought,” said Michael Osterholm, a public health expert at the University of Minnesota.

Measles is especially dangerous for pregnant women, whose immune systems are temporarily weakened. They are more likely to develop severe complications and 10 times as likely to die from measles.

Doctors know relatively little about how being exposed to measles in utero affects children because, until recently, cases of congenital measles were exceedingly rare in the United States. Even before vaccines were available, it was nearly unheard-of for an adult woman to become infected because almost every American had measles during childhood.

“There are a lot of holes in our knowledge,” Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the committee on infectious diseases at the American Academy of Pediatrics, said, adding, “We’ve been lucky enough for the past several decades not to have to think about this.”

Researchers are now racing to understand the long-term consequences of these infections as the virus spreads across the country. This year, there have been more than 5,000 measles cases nationwide and 10 deaths reported by state health officials. This week, international health officials are expected to announce that the United States has lost its measles-elimination status.

“This is what happens when we when we get to the point of losing measles-elimination status,” Dr. Ratner said. “We start seeing these rare things more often.”

Several outside experts said they found it unusual that the C. D. C. scientists published in an outside journal, rather than in the agency’s own scientific journal. But they noted conflicts within the agency over how to respond to the nation’s measles crisis. This fall, the C. D. C. prevented its scientists from sending out an urgent alert on measles in pregnancy, The Washington Post reported. Under the leadership of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., the agency has also publicly challenged two measles deaths reported by state officials in Pennsylvania.

In “normal times,” said Dr. David Kimberlin, a pediatric infectious disease expert at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, a report like this would have been published in the C. D. C.’s journal. “But we’re not in normal times,” he added.

“There’s been a reluctance to accept that measles causes severe infections and death,” Dr. Ratner said.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

As cases of congenital measles have become more common, doctors have started to piece together a concerning picture of the condition.

Dr. Michelle Barton-Forbes, a pediatric infectious disease doctor who worked at the center of a large measles outbreak in Canada last year, was one of the first physicians to document recent cases of congenital measles in North America. One of the primary risks she identified was a neurological complication called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which can affect a child up to a decade after an initial infection. It is almost always fatal.

While this is considered a rare complication of measles, affecting roughly 1 in 100,000 of those infected, babies are at a much higher risk than older children or adults. Some researchers have estimated that one in 158 infants develop SSPE after an infection. This is because their immune systems are too weak to stop the virus before it can “sneak into the brain,” Dr. Barton-Forbes said. In infants, the neurological complication may also develop much sooner; it has been reported in babies just a few months old, she said.

Dr. Barton-Forbes said she planned to follow the patients she diagnosed with congenital measles to see how many went on to develop SSPE. She also planned to monitor how many developed other infections as a result of “immune amnesia.” This complication — which occurs when a measles infection wipes out the immune system’s memory and leaves it more vulnerable to other illnesses — may become more common as large measles outbreaks become the new norm.

Unfortunately, Dr. Kimberlin said, “congenital measles is one that we’re probably going to be learning more about.”

Teddy Rosenbluth is a Times reporter covering health news, with a special focus on medical misinformation.

Trump Administration Moves to Close A. I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Nvidia C. E. O. Resigns

Advertisement

Supported by

The rules have been a topic of fierce debate in the administration and would cut back on a booming data center business serving Chinese companies.

By Ana Swanson and Tony Romm

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A. I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders.

The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole allowing China to sidestep a ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A. I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. Chinese firms have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Whether to close the loophole has been a significant source of contention within the Trump administration.

The new rule is intended to make it harder for Chinese firms to remotely access the chips. It will require overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran.

Data centers are also required to perform strict checks on their customers to determine if they are linked to those countries. And the U. S. will now require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said.

The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U. S. chips to train advanced A. I. models, the administration said in a news release.

The plan to crack down on China’s ability to access the coveted A. I. chips comes as President Trump is scheduled to travel to Asia. He will travel to the Philippines and then to China for an economic summit, where he is expected to meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping and discuss the war in Iran, nuclear nonproliferation and trade. The data center rules could create a new source of friction between the countries, at a time when Mr. Trump has been trying to keep a fragile trade truce with China intact.

Share prices of chip stocks tumbled Monday. Nvidia fell nearly 4 percent. Intel fell nearly 7 percent, and Micron more than 6 percent. Indexes that track these stocks fell too — the Philadelphia Semiconductor index sank more than 4 percent, and the broader, tech-heavy Nasdaq slumped, too.

The formerly obscure issue of chip sales to foreign data centers was thrust into the spotlight in recent weeks with the revelations about Megaspeed, a Singaporean data center firm created by a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, who was ousted as Nvidia’s chief executive last week. U. S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. (Chinese officials have denied that Ms. Huang is their spy.)

Firms like Megaspeed have legally been able to operate data centers in Southeast Asia that remotely serve Chinese clients. That means Chinese companies that are blocked from buying advanced Nvidia chips directly can simply rent them through Southeast Asian firms.

Nvidia and its proponents contend that the sales help create jobs in the United States and ensure that companies around the world are reliant on American technology.

But some officials in the Trump administration and in Congress increasingly appear to believe that Chinese access to these data centers has undercut U. S. export controls and allowed China’s artificial intelligence ecosystem to flourish. Some worry this could give Beijing an economic edge, as well as a military one.

That scandal has turned China’s access to advanced A. I. computing power into a subject of debate at the highest levels of the administration, with the Commerce Department, which oversees the regulations, clashing over them with other parts of the government.

The debate has set Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees chip policy, at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U. S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, who have all pushed to reinstate broad restrictions on data centers in recent months.

Mr. Lutnick had pushed for a leaner version of the rules on foreign data centers, one that would be less onerous for Nvidia and its customers.

The announcement on Monday said that the new rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” — both agencies that have pushed for more stringent rules.

Chris McGuire, a former Biden administration official who is now a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said that the line was “completely unprecedented.”

“That implies that Commerce was dragged kicking and screaming over the finish line to publish the rule that the White House wanted,” he said.

Those tensions spilled out into the open on Friday, when Mr. Bessent blamed Mr. Lutnick’s department in a TV interview for failing to sanction Megaspeed, saying that other departments had pushed for the measure but that the Commerce Department “has the pen.” Mr. Bessent added that Nvidia should be “held accountable” if it did not do enough to prevent illegal diversion of chips to China.

Both Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick are traveling alongside Mr. Trump this week as he visits the Philippines and meets with Mr. Xi in China.

When asked about Mr. Bessent’s comments on Monday, Mr. Trump said there were just “two different views.”

“One view is, you don’t want to insult China,” the president said, adding: “The other view is, just go down and dirty and do what you have to do. You can’t say either is wrong or right.”

The president said that Mr. Lutnick might have delayed actions against Megaspeed, but that he was doing it because “if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China.”

“I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” he said.

Mr. Trump also renewed his political support for Mr. Huang, saying that Mr. Huang had “learned a big lesson” and that the president “would not mind” if he were restored as the chief executive of Nvidia.

While the new rule on data centers appeared to be fairly stringent, analysts said that its enforcement would be up to the Commerce Department, and it remained to be seen how the department would put it in place.

Mr. McGuire said that, if enforced, the rules would be transformative for Southeast Asian data center businesses, also called neoclouds. “This effectively kills the business of neoclouds like Megaspeed that exist to provide remote access to large amounts of A. I. compute to China,” he said.

Neocloud stocks listed in the United States were hit hard on Monday, with CoreWeave and Nebius both slumping more than 6 percent.

In its news release, the Commerce Department said the rule was “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.”

The move would bring America’s rules on remote access of data centers into alignment with its rules on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology, the department said.

The rule also restores a previous provision that the Trump administration stripped away last year, which will cut down on China’s access to chip manufacturers like TSMC and Samsung. Since TSMC and Samsung use U. S. technology in their chip making, Chinese companies seeking to use those companies to make advanced chips must first apply to the United States for license.

Just before leaving office, the Biden administration issued global rules on chip sales, including restrictions on Chinese firms remotely accessing data centers. Trump officials said they would no longer enforce the rules after Mr. Trump won another term, and in May 2025 they officially rescinded the restrictions.

Since then, various draft versions of the rules have gained momentum in the government, only to be shot down by opponents.

It remains to be seen whether the new rules will trigger blowback from China. In a telephone briefing on Friday, a senior administration official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as part of the ground rules of the call, said the administration had been discussing potential measures on remote access and did not expect countermeasures from China in response. The moves would close loopholes in existing measures to counteract both smuggling and remote access of data centers, and the Chinese have stated publicly that they are not involved with smuggling, the official said.

Asked about the scandal with Megaspeed and Nvidia, another senior administration official on the call said the situation would not have any bearing on the trip. Export controls are national security matters and are not up for negotiation with the Chinese, the official said.

Aruni Soni contributed reporting.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.
