Chase Bank Reports ‘Technical Issue’ Disrupting Transactions

The New York Times November 16, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

Chase was among several U. S. banks whose customers reported technical issues on Monday.

By Michael Levenson

Chase Bank, which serves more than 86 million customers at 5,000 branches across the United States, reported that it was having trouble processing transactions on Monday.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” the bank said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

Some Chase Bank customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their A. T. M. cards or complete transactions at branches on Monday.

Customers at several other major banks, including Wells Fargo, U. S. Bank and Bank of America, also reported problems on Monday, according to Downdetector. com, a website that tracks user reports of outages. Users also reported issues with the online payment platform Zelle.

U. S. Bank said in a statement that its “systems are not directly impacted.”

“However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” it said.

Zelle said it was “not down.”

“Zelle is operating as it should,” it said in a statement, which noted that customers who use the platform access their money through their own bank accounts. “An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” it said.

Wells Fargo and Bank of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The banking issues were reported days after a global outage at Microsoft disrupted communications and work at schools, government agencies, hospitals and offices around the world. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to fail, officials said.

There was no indication that the bank issues on Monday were related to the outages at Microsoft. But the recent F. A. A. ground stop, which was related to an equipment problem with federal systems, added to the sense of gloom in social media chatter about troubles with modern technology.

The Microsoft outage, which started Thursday and was resolved on Saturday, affected some of its most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot. Microsoft said the outage had been caused by a “technical issue” and not a cyberattack or A. I. agent.

The F. A. A. ground stop, which was lifted hours after it was issued on Friday, created a cascade of flight delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend. Government officials attributed the disarray to a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas.

Michael Levenson covers breaking news for The Times from New York.

Challenging Consensus, Scientist Says Photos Show Epstein Was Killed

The New York Times November 16, 2026

The Epstein Files

Advertisement

Supported by

Investigations have found most evidence in Jeffrey Epstein’s death points to suicide. Michael Freeman, a forensic scientist who studies homicides, got rare access to the autopsy file and disagrees.

By Shaila Dewan and Leo Sands

Michael Freeman says he had one thought when he first saw a photo from Jeffrey Epstein’s autopsy: “Wait a minute, that doesn’t look like a hanging mark.”

The noose had not left a smooth, consistent line on Mr. Epstein’s neck that slanted to a peak, as in a textbook hanging. Instead, the mark was deep, ragged and branched into a Y-shape on one side.

Dr. Freeman, a forensic scientist who studies bias and error in death investigations, spent a year examining Mr. Epstein’s autopsy file, which was given to him by the dead man’s brother.

He is seeking to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal, but has been rejected so far. On Monday he presented them at the Middle Temple, a London legal society, where he argued that Mr. Epstein’s injuries are most plausibly explained by homicidal strangulation. He also asserted that injuries on the body suggest there was a struggle, contrary to the medical examiner’s findings.

“The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” he said.

The totality of the circumstances surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death in a federal detention center in 2019 points overwhelmingly to suicide, and several investigations have failed to produce evidence that anyone other than Mr. Epstein had a hand in it. Dr. Freeman’s analysis, parts of which he floated in a New York Times investigation earlier this year, may rekindle long-smoldering debates about his death.

Forensic pathologists who have seen some of the autopsy photos, though not the entire set, have agreed that the mark on Mr. Epstein’s neck was atypical for a hanging. Some of those experts said the images could still be consistent with suicide, but they cautioned that the injuries alone could not tell the full story, and that a cascade of institutional failures would make it difficult to ever conclusively determine what happened.

The New York City medical examiner’s office, which performed the autopsy, said this week that it “stands by its determination” of suicide.

Much information that medical examiners would normally use to determine a cause of death was unavailable; the examiner was not permitted to inspect the cell, for example. That has left the autopsy photographs as some of the only concrete evidence.

After being asked by a journalist to look at the hanging mark, Dr. Freeman asked Jeffrey Epstein’s brother, Mark, whether he could see the complete file. As next of kin, Mark Epstein was one of the few people who had access to the autopsy. He shared the file with Dr. Freeman last November.

Mark Epstein said in an interview last week that he had shown the materials to other experts who asked to see them — but whom he declined to name — and that the results had been inconclusive. “They were all hemming and hawing,” he said.

Shortly before Monday’s talk, Mr. Epstein posted the autopsy photos online for all to see.

Dr. Freeman said in an interview that he had no idea who might have killed Mr. Epstein, nor did he care. He was focused only on what he called oversights in the death investigation and autopsy report. “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” he said.

Jeffrey Epstein, a wealthy financier and convicted sex offender, is far from a typical subject for Dr. Freeman. As a consultant and scholar, he has argued that medical examiners too often ignore the most plausible cause of death in favor of one that excuses deadly force by the police or reinforces racial stereotypes.

He is not a board-certified forensic pathologist, the highest credential for medical examiners in the United States, but he has doctorates in epidemiology and forensic medicine and teaches forensic medicine at two universities. Dr. Freeman, an American, is also a fellow of the Faculty of Forensic & Legal Medicine at the Royal College of Physicians in the United Kingdom and the editor of its journal.

In one case, Dr. Freeman argued on behalf of a Black teenager charged with murder in Mississippi after a stillbirth, after tests found trace amounts of a cocaine byproduct in the baby’s blood. The umbilical cord had been wrapped around the infant’s neck, and the state had the country’s highest infant mortality rate. The charges were dropped.

In 2020, Dr. Freeman co-wrote a landmark metastudy on excited delirium, a term often used to explain deaths in police custody. His methodology and conclusions were hotly disputed, but they propelled a widespread rejection of excited delirium as a valid diagnosis or cause of death.

More recently, he consulted in the prosecution of a police officer who killed George Floyd in Minneapolis, using statistical probability to counter defense claims that drug abuse or heart disease had caused Mr. Floyd’s death. Dr. Freeman was also part of a panel of experts that identified dozens of deaths in police custody in Maryland that had been misclassified as natural or accidental.

Forensic pathology is sometimes said to be more art than science, and disagreements among experts are common. Medical examiners point out that they must defend their opinions in court, but Dr. Freeman is among critics who have complained that there are too few safeguards against bias and error.

For his Epstein investigation, he teamed up with two other skeptics, Itiel Dror, a cognitive neuroscientist whose real-world experiments have repeatedly embarrassed forensic practitioners, and Anders Eriksson, a forensic pathologist who led a Swedish government review concluding that “shaken baby” prosecutions had been based on flawed reasoning.

They are continuing to seek a publisher for their analysis. In the meantime, Dr. Freeman prepared his talk on Monday, which received a flurry of advance news coverage.

The talk was to be held at the University College of London, where reservations quickly reached capacity. But on Sunday, the school suddenly announced that it would not take place, citing “well-being implications for our students.” The talk was moved to the Middle Temple and those planning to attend were told they would have to watch it online.

In 2019, the medical examiner who performed the autopsy, Dr. Kristin Roman, faced limitations. There were no photos of Mr. Epstein hanging or with the strip of cloth around his neck. The piece of cloth sent to the medical examiner was not the one that had been used as a noose. The prison employee who found the body initially declined to speak to authorities.

Still, Dr. Roman told federal investigators that she had no doubt it was a suicide. There were no signs of a struggle and the body was “pristine,” she told them, with no bruises and no debris under the fingernails.

“This doesn’t look anything like a strangulation,” she said in a statement she gave to federal authorities.

Dr. Roman has since retired from the medical examiner’s office.

When the jail employee who found the body finally spoke with investigators two years after the fact, he recalled that Mr. Epstein’s rear end had been suspended about an inch off the floor.

Dr. Freeman used the employee’s description to reconstruct the hanging, creating 3-D computer models based on Mr. Epstein’s physique and the autopsy photos. He then used illustrations to argue that strangulation from behind was a better explanation for Mr. Epstein’s injuries, including what he said were fingernail marks above the ligature line, an abrasion at the base of the neck, and a deep, fresh hemorrhage in the left shoulder muscle.

He faulted investigators for not testing Mr. Epstein’s fingernails for DNA.

Dr. Freeman delivered the presentation in the master treasurer’s office of the legal society, with his co-authors and Mark Epstein sitting nearby. Toward the end, he showed a QR code linking to the autopsy photos.

“You will be able to see them for yourself, so that this is no longer an issue of one person makes one statement and then everybody has to believe it,” he said, adding, “This is a time for people to make up their own mind.”

Afterward, he turned to those in the room. “I tried not to sound like a kook,” he said, laughing.

If you are having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or go to SpeakingOfSuicide. com/resources for a list of additional resources.

Shaila Dewan is a Times reporter covering criminal justice — policing, courts and prisons — across the country.

Leo Sands is a correspondent for the Breaking News Hub of The New York Times based in London.

Grammy Awards 2027: The Full List of Nominees

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Grammy Awards

Advertisement

Supported by

The artists, albums and songs up for honors at the 69th annual ceremony were announced Monday. The show will be held on Feb. 7 in Los Angeles and air on ABC and Disney+ after decades on CBS.

Raye is the top nominee for the 69th annual Grammy Awards, with 11, tying a record set by Beyoncé at the 2025 ceremony for most nominations for a female artist. The “Where Is My Husband!” singer will contend for record, song and album of the year, in addition to songwriter of the year, non-classical, and competitions across pop categories for the song and for her album, “This Music May Contain Hope.”

The British singer-songwriter, born Rachel Keen, joins Rosalía (nine); Ella Langley and Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers (who each have seven); and Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and Olivia Dean (six) as the top nominees.

In an announcement Monday morning, the Recording Academy revealed nominees for the 2027 Grammy Awards in 100 categories, the largest field since 2011. New among them are five awards: R&B collaboration or duo/group performance, traditional pop vocal performance, traditional folk album, best Latin song, and best Asian pop music performance. The K-pop supergroup BTS said in July that it would not submit “Arirang,” its latest album, in an apparent protest of the Asian pop category. “We hope music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided into region or language,” each member said in statements posted to their social media accounts.

Albums and songs released from Aug. 31, 2025, to Aug. 28, 2026, are eligible; the winners will be determined by nearly 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy, among them performers, producers, engineers and songwriters.

The ceremony, which is scheduled for Feb. 7, 2027, at the Crypto. com Arena in Los Angeles, will be broadcast on ABC and stream live on Hulu and Disney+ as part of a new deal between the Recording Academy and Disney. Previously, CBS had aired the ceremony for more than 50 years.

Here is a complete list of the nominations.

Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Revive University Research Cuts

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The justices left in place a lower-court decision to block the administration from cutting millions in grants to University of California researchers over perceived ties to diversity initiatives.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a request from the Trump administration seeking to revive cuts to tens of millions of dollars in research grants to the University of California.

The court’s rejection of the case leaves in place a lower-court ruling that found the Trump administration had most likely violated the First Amendment when it terminated the grants over perceived connections to diversity initiatives.

The announcement by the justices came on a routine orders list and gave no reasoning, as is typical. No dissents were noted.

The decision was a blow to President Trump’s pressure campaign against one of the country’s largest and most prestigious public university systems. The University of California has been a major focus of the president’s critiques of the country’s universities for much of his second term. The 10-campus system has about 560,000 students and employees and receives about $17 billion in federal funding each year.

Matthew J. Tragesser, a Justice Department spokesman, said in a statement that the administration would continue its court fight to cancel the federal research grants and advocate “the executive branch’s lawful authority to administer federal funding programs.”

Erwin Chemerinsky, the dean of the law school at the University of California, Berkeley, who argued on behalf of the researchers, said he was “obviously delighted” that the justices had declined to hear the case and that courts had upheld that “the government cannot cut off grants based on the perceived viewpoint of the research.”

Rachel Zaentz, a spokeswoman for the University of California, said in a statement that the decision “preserves an important victory for the U. C. researchers whose critical work and federal grants were targeted.” She added that it supported “the principle that research funding decisions should be based on merit, not politics.”

In early 2025, three federal agencies terminated grants awarded to researchers in the university system, citing executive orders issued by Mr. Trump. Six researchers from the University of California sued to challenge the cancellations. They had received multiyear research grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, the National Science Foundation and the National Endowment for the Humanities that the administration said it would be canceling.

In May, a three-judge panel from the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit concluded that “because the agencies’ termination of grants was aimed at the suppression of viewpoints with which the government disagrees,” the cancellation “likely violates the First Amendment.”

The Trump administration then asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, arguing that the agencies’ decision to terminate the grants represented the sort of ordinary policy shifts of a new administration.

In urging the justices to take the case, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserted that “changes in administration invariably bring changes in policy and spending priorities” and that “presidents often direct agencies to review and terminate grants that no longer reflect the government’s priorities.”

Lawyers for the researchers pushed back, claiming that the administration had violated the First Amendment by “terminating already awarded grants to faculty and researchers at the University of California based on a perception of the viewpoint expressed in their research.”

In a brief to the justices, the lawyers asserted that federal agencies had identified grant proposals with “what they regarded as ‘dangerous ideas’ based on keywords in their titles and then abruptly cut off their funding.”

Federal agencies had explained in court filings in the case that they had used keywords related to diversity, gender and vaccine hesitancy, among other search terms, to determine whether research grants might collide with policy aims of the Trump administration.

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.

Connections Coach

News Analysis

The history of the sprawling corporate combinations is rich, colorful and mostly disappointing. Could a SpaceX-Tesla merger be a success story?

Credit... Richard Borge

Supported by

By Steve Lohr

No one could accuse Elon Musk of thinking small. And the vision he described last month of merging his two companies SpaceX and Tesla is characteristically ambitious: a digital conglomerate of unprecedented scale, spanning rockets, satellites, electric cars, robots and social media.

Mr. Musk is not alone as a digital-age corporate empire builder. Other tech giants are also now sprawling, multi-industry enterprises.

Alphabet’s businesses range well beyond Google search and cloud computing to include video streaming, self-driving cars, drone delivery service and drug development. Amazon has e-commerce, cloud computing, video streaming, a movie studio, robots, warehouses and delivery services.

But a SpaceX-Tesla merger would eclipse the others in its striking array of different businesses, forming a mega-conglomerate worth about $3.5 trillion.

Conglomerates of the past were typically driven by purely financial considerations, like the 1960s merger frenzy on Wall Street, or to diversify a company in order to make it better able to weather economic cycles and international competition, like General Electric.

But today’s conglomerate impulse has a different source — a drive for technological supremacy by broadening a corporation’s market reach and gaining an upper hand in the global A. I. race.

“These big companies are trying to deploy digital technologies, and increasingly artificial intelligence, across industries,” said David Yoffie, a professor at the Harvard Business School.

Mr. Musk acknowledged that the logic of a SpaceX-Tesla merger was a corporate move to seize the A. I. moment. The A. I. businesses at SpaceX include its Grok chatbot and A. I. software models, its data center-building unit and its Cursor A. I. coding assistant. Tesla would bring self-driving cars, robotaxis, humanoid robots and A. I. chip design.

During a SpaceX investor call last month, when Mr. Musk disclosed the two companies were exploring a merger, he said there was “a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” the stage at which A. I. surpasses human intelligence.

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest person, is chief executive and the largest shareholder of both companies. So special committees of independent directors at both companies will weigh whether to go ahead.

Corporate conglomerates in America have a rich, colorful and mostly disappointing history. The 1960s saw an explosion of deal making to build the fast-rising conglomerates of their day like ITT Corporation, Litton Industries, Gulf and Western Industries and Ling-Temco-Vought.

These companies were agglomerations of unrelated businesses. ITT (International Telephone and Telegraph) began as an communications company operating outside the United States, but it came to own Avis rental cars, Levitt home builders, Sheraton hotels, Scott’s fertilizer, Wonder Bread and Morton’s frozen foods, among others.

Wall Street was hot. So the currency of acquisition — the buying company’s stock price — was inflated. Debt was cheap and the accounting was creative.

Sleight-of-hand financial deals were the order of the day. One of its foremost practitioners was James Ling — “Jimmy Ling, the merger king.” He started an electrical contracting business in Dallas. Over the years, in deal after deal, he acquired companies in steel manufacturing, meatpacking, car rentals, military aircraft, car rentals, an airline and resorts. At its peak in 1969, LTV, as the company was known, ranked 14th in the Fortune 500.

But the 1960s bull market on Wall Street ended abruptly as inflation rose. LTV’s stock price plummeted, Mr. Ling was ousted and LTV went through a string of bankruptcies.

Still, even after the 1960s conglomerate bubble, there were multi-industry companies that thrived. The leading example grew out of the power generators to lightbulbs conglomerate formed in 1892, when Thomas Edison’s Edison General Electric Company merged with another company.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, General Electric enjoyed two decades of prosperity under the leadership of Jack Welch. G. E.’s revenue jumped nearly fivefold, to $130 billion, during Mr. Welch’s tenure. The value of its shares on the stock market soared from $14 billion to more than $410 billion, making G. E. one of the most valuable companies in the world.

In 2000, Fortune magazine named Mr. Welch the “Manager of the Century.”

G. E. seemed proof that a well-run industrial conglomerate could enjoy the advantages of size, funding, shared research and expertise. Like the digital giants of today, G. E. executives spoke of critical industrial technologies — physics and materials science — that could be applied to different industries. A gas turbine power generator, they explained, was essentially a big jet engine bolted to the ground.

But under Mr. Welch, G. E. diversified beyond industrial businesses into finance and commercial real estate. G. E.’s leaders viewed the company’s greatest asset as its management excellence, which they figured could be applied to any business. The money to be made on Wall Street looked easy compared to manufacturing.

For years, the buildup of that business paid off. The company’s finance arm, GE Capital, accounted for up to half of corporate profits in some years and became the largest nonbank financial institution in America. But the 2008 financial crisis hit the division hard.

In 2021, G. E. announced it was splitting into three companies: GE Aerospace, for jet engines; GE Vernova, for power generators and wind power; and GE Healthcare, for medical imaging equipment. The breakup was completed in 2024, as the once-iconic American corporate behemoth bowed to changing times and fortunes.

Studies of conglomerates over the years have found that the stock market value of the combined corporation is typically worth 10 to 15 percent less than if the businesses were stand-alone companies, known as the conglomerate discount. The benefits of combining businesses — the much-praised “synergies” — are overwhelmed by the complexity of managing varied operations and the difficulty of getting a clear picture of the performance of individual businesses.

Skeptics of a SpaceX-Tesla deal point to those challenges. “Shareholders can already own both companies, and this transaction would have all the drawbacks of a conglomerate,” said Baruch Lev, a professor emeritus of accounting and finance at New York University’s Stern School of Business.

Mr. Musk is an experienced corporate acquirer and he has proved skeptics wrong in the past, though a SpaceX-Tesla tie-up would be his largest deal by far. But the merger is not just about corporate size, it is a bet on the “A. I. synergies” that Mr. Musk hopes will result. Much will depend on how much shared A. I. technology and knowledge can be spread across the varied businesses, yielding cost savings and competitive gains, better products and services.

Some analysts say an A. I. conglomerate may well enjoy advantages as the technology is increasingly widely adopted. A combined SpaceX and Tesla, they say, will have greater power to develop, buy and build the technology and deploy it across industry after industry.

They cite the increasing collaboration already between SpaceX and Tesla, led by the giant SpaceX computer chip plant in Texas, announced earlier this year, which will cost at least $55 billion and in total spending could reach $119 billion. Both companies will use the chips manufactured in Texas, with Tesla-designed semiconductors made there as well.

“In this A. I. economy, where computing capacity rules the world, putting SpaceX and Tesla together makes a lot of sense,” said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, an investment research firm.

Steve Lohr writes about technology and its impact on the economy, jobs and the workplace.

By Zachary D. Carter

Mr. Carter is the author of “The Price of Peace: Money, Democracy and the Life of John Maynard Keynes.”

It wasn’t too long ago that Silicon Valley was celebrating the greatest invention in economic history. A dazzling new medium called cryptocurrency had arrived — at once an extraordinary investment, a government-proof digital money and perhaps a way to bring world peace. It would end global poverty and cure inflation. The possibilities were endless — until the public face of the crypto revolution landed in federal prison and the American president began winning his family millions through Trump-branded crypto schemes.

Cryptocurrency still exists, though few take seriously the grandiose promises of yesteryear. As the public’s enthusiasm for digital currency faded, some of its most prominent boosters began showering praise on another shiny object: The artificial intelligence universe is just lousy with crypto players. A. I. “is our alchemy, our Philosopher’s Stone — we are literally making sand think,” trumpeted Marc Andreessen, whose firm has been one of the most influential crypto and A. I. players over the past decade.

Of course, the extreme prognostications about artificial intelligence aren’t exactly like the woo-woo crypto hype of 2020. A. I. already has some genuinely useful applications in software development. It might even blow up the world! Maybe that’s why Silicon Valley’s hype machine has been so successful at turning the economy into a massive one-way bet on delivering a still undefined type of “superintelligence” to the globe. Last year, according to the St. Louis Fed, nearly 40 percent of American economic growth came from the A. I. build-out.

These days, however, excitement is mutating into anxiety. A major A. I.-themed hedge fund collapsed over the summer. Days ago, shares of the A. I. chip giant Nvidia plummeted upon the abrupt resignation of its megawatt chief executive amid allegations of extramarital affairs with a Chinese spy and two women who reported to him. Whatever technological changes may lie in store, the bigger picture is starting to look a lot like a movie we’ve seen before — wild promises and warnings, unusual financing arrangements and the collapse of highflying adventurers. One of our newest industries is following a highly familiar script: The A. I. build-out has become so dependent on the riskiest lending practices of Wall Street that Silicon Valley itself might now be better understood as a wild, unregulated division of the banking sector.

If you haven’t seen this movie, it usually ends in a mess: the 2008 financial crisis, or the collapse of railway mania in 1840s Britain that spurred an industrial depression, or the Panic of 1873 that caused a global catastrophe so bad they called it the Great Depression until that other one came along.

When financial history repeats, fatalism can be hard to resist. It is genuinely disheartening to see people pitch and fall for farcical nonsense, time after time. But our present is not simply repeating the recent past — in important ways, the cycle is getting worse.

Since the 1980s, the United States government has been subjecting more and more of the national economy to the risks of runaway finance. When any financial mania ends, the public shoulders the costs. Crushed stock markets erase savings and ravage job prospects. And when the government has to deploy taxpayer dollars to bail out, say, a major bank that got in over its skis, there’s less money around to fill the potholes, pay for the bus drivers or fund struggling schools. Almost everything working families rely on in daily life gets worse after a financial crisis, and the effects linger for decades in the form of lost earnings and family lives turned upside down by unemployment.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Or at least, it doesn’t have to be this bad. About 90 years ago, the economist John Maynard Keynes observed that monetary markets are inherently preoccupied with stories about the future. We save money to spend it later; we spend now to build and attain the things our future selves will appreciate. Keynes realized that attempts to calculate the future value of an investment accurately would require a level of certainty about the future that human beings do not possess. Sometimes things just happen — strange wars, senile presidents — you never know. Financial judgments are thus inevitably susceptible to the “animal spirits” of human psychology, carrying “only a little more” scientific precision than predictions about “an expedition to the South Pole.”

But Keynes insisted that while there may be no perfect economic system, there are degrees of dysfunction. The more a nation’s economy — be it based on manufacturing home appliances or on developing software — is absorbed by the vagaries of its financial functions, the more prone it will be to financial calamity.

At a time when valuations for A. I. firms like Anthropic are rising into the trillions, the American government is pouring gas on the fire. President Trump has been heralding massive A. I. spending as the economic future, before championing the coming of a “Supreme Intelligence” (since modified to “Super Intelligence,” his preferred term of art). Mr. Trump loves a soaring stock market and understands that the stock market is currently running on A. I. spirits — more than a third of the entire value of all U. S. equities is now subsumed under A. I. stocks. By late summer, tech stocks accounted for more than half the value of the S&P 500.

Not every stock market crash ends in a Great Depression, but the 1929 crash did. That experience persuaded the American government to implement a strict legal separation between financial activities and the rest of the economy — you couldn’t run a manufacturing operation that was also a bank. You couldn’t even run a bank that was also speculating in the stock market; these businesses had to be independently operated and regulated in order to isolate financial contagions, and to protect other economic sectors from the risks inherent to finance. And between the 1930s and the 1970s, this program basically worked. The catastrophic cycle of boom and bust that had plagued the American banking sector since the Civil War came to an end.

In the 1980s, however, President Ronald Reagan ushered in a fundamental redesign of the American economy. There hadn’t been a serious bank crash for decades, and Reagan was convinced that post-Depression regulations and other government red tape were to blame for the rampant inflation and grim productivity that dogged the 1970s. The marching orders were clear: Decentralize government oversight, and unleash the power of American profit.

These changes were not merely legal — they transformed the culture of the economy. For decades, bank executives had been the helpmates of heavy industry, living by the “3-6-3” mantra: borrow at 3 percent, lend at 6 percent, and hit the golf course by 3 p. m. Now they were to be masters of the universe, commanding the American economy from the skyscraper on down, disciplining bloated industry and complacent labor with the relentless drive for lower costs and higher profits. The earth-toned images of crime families and crooked cops that had dominated the late 1970s sharpened into the slicked-back icons of best sellers such as “The Bonfire of the Vanities” and “Liar’s Poker” and the director Oliver Stone’s “Wall Street.”

By the end of the 1990s, it seemed like nobody could imagine an economy pushed onward by anything other than the wolves of Wall Street. When Bill Clinton reviewed his presidential achievements in his 2004 memoir, he didn’t even mention two major financial deregulation bills he had signed into law with overwhelming bipartisan support. Finance was fundamental; financialization was just how the world worked.

The dismantling of Depression-era firewalls has predictably been accompanied by banking crises. As the 1980s turned to the 1990s, over a thousand ordinary savings and loans failed — roughly a third of the entire sector. Private equity firms had seized on new Reagan-era rules to turn these local lenders into dumping grounds for ultra-high-risk debt.

A decade later, executives at previously staid banks like Wells Fargo, Citigroup and Bank of America were enjoying new abilities to cross state lines and storm into the insurance and securities businesses. Once regional operations exploded into multisector international behemoths whose byzantine exposures were all but impossible to track, let alone manage. Even General Motors, the nation’s largest auto company, began exploiting various legal avenues to transform itself into one of the nation’s largest mortgage lenders, a move facilitated by a 1997 Utah state law allowing the company to operate its own full-fledged bank. It was an open mockery of the wall between finance and commerce that had been built after the Depression. Federal regulators looked the other way — until the financial crisis. By 2010, the U. S. Treasury had devoted $17.2 billion to rescuing G. M.’s bank, and $49.5 billion to save General Motors. Congress authorized hundreds of billions of dollars to help save the rest of the nation’s financial system, with trillions more in emergency lending from the Federal Reserve.

All of these debacles resulted in privileged insiders’ reaping enormous rewards while ordinary Americans were called in to clean up the mess. Banks dependent on public support paid out billions of dollars in bonuses to their top executives. The national unemployment rate hit 10 percent.

Financialization changed American institutions and altered the national culture of work and reward. Today, roughly one in four young men in America trades stocks on a daily basis; a similar percentage of young men gamble on a daily basis. Most of them, according to a conservative think tank, “feel like failures.” The, ahem, traditional sports betting industry in the United States scored record revenues of nearly $17 billion last year — never mind the growth of the indistinguishable activity at new sites called prediction markets, which are moving $24 billion a month globally.

Dudes have more time to trade these days: Between 1980 and 2000, the United States lost about two million manufacturing jobs. Mr. Clinton didn’t just deregulate finance; he attacked domestic industry by signing the North American Free Trade Agreement into law and welcoming China into the World Trade Organization. As a share of the U. S. economy, today’s financial sector is roughly triple the size of its post-World War II nadir — but even this figure is difficult to estimate, because so much financial activity has been subsumed into the tech world itself, with trillions of dollars in investment now hanging in the balance.

Everywhere you look in 2026, multitrillion-dollar tech companies are storming into the financial world. Meta and Apple now move funds for digital shoppers around the world, while Amazon and Apple pitch credit cards. Nvidia, the country’s largest computer chip manufacturer, is also a major lender to the A. I. industry and its insatiable hunger for cash, approving $500 billion worth of partnerships with big banks and private equity firms. Nvidia doesn’t just make and sell the chips that power the A. I. revolution. It also invests in the data centers that power the technology, and is partnering with OpenAI and other A. I. developers to provide hundreds of billions of dollars in additional financing for still more A. I.-related projects.

Nvidia is even in talks with insurance companies to insure these loans against default. This should sound familiar: In the early 2000s, big banks turned to the insurer A. I. G. to protect themselves against losses on risky mortgage bonds. But when home prices crashed, A. I. G. collapsed, risking the viability of Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and others. Insurance did not alleviate financial risk — it loaded an extra layer of financial risk atop the market, amplifying dangers rather than reducing them.

Whether Nvidia can, in fact, secure an insurer remains to be seen. But the impulse is revealing. By operating as a lender, Nvidia is already injecting the instability of Wall Street directly into what has become the most economically critical manufacturing operation in the country — as a matter of standard corporate policy. How fitting that the executor of many of Nvidia’s aggressive financial moves, the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has just been named its interim chief executive; the company’s financial maneuvers may be as critical to its future as its physical products.

Nvidia isn’t propping up the sector alone. A multitrillion-dollar sub-industry of “private credit” — a term of art for loans made beyond the purview of traditional financial regulations — has ballooned at the nation’s largest banks and private equity firms. And this shadow market just happens to specialize in hard-to-value projects related to A. I. and data centers.

The candle is burning from both ends. Wealthy individuals are increasingly relying on tech stocks as collateral for loans that are propping up our economy — loans to buy real estate, or cars, or even more tech stocks. A tech blowup could thus easily disrupt lending to other sectors of the economy: Mess with either the A. I. build-out or its increasingly fragile financial underpinnings, and both will be in trouble. They are already in many respects the same entity.

In other countries, innovation isn’t so heavily focused on A. I. China is investing in A. I. too, but it is accompanying its computer push with $2.2 trillion a year in green tech investment that is about strengthening manufacturing prowess rather than pure processing power. China has been developing better solar panels, more powerful wind farms, more efficient batteries and a new generation of electric vehicles. These innovations have their own stories to tell about the future, but there is an important difference between promising to improve something that already exists — say, a car, an effort that adds jobs — and vowing to change the technological foundation of all work without a plan. In the United States, the bulk of A. I. spending goes into building data centers with temporary local benefits; once they’re built, the construction jobs are gone, while the tax incentives deployed to get them constructed drain resources from state and local governments.

It is folly to hope the Trump administration will do anything to avert an A. I.-driven financial crisis. The administration is not only encouraging the tech industry’s leap into the turbulent waves of finance; it is helping car manufacturers get back into banking, too. In January, about 17 years after our government was forced to bail out G. M.’s bank, the Trump administration approved applications from Ford and G. M. to open new banks, headquartered in Salt Lake City.

This is probably going to hurt all of us, and managing the fallout from a crash is as much art as science. How we ought to structure the economy going forward, however, has been clear since the Great Depression: Don’t let big business merge with big finance. Our government needs to hold big tech and big finance accountable for operating deeply uncertain businesses with vast public consequences. We need smaller, simpler tech companies that support American industry rather than dominating it.

A. I. optimists tend to spend a lot of time talking about how the technology will cure cancer or end poverty — an acknowledgment that A. I. is a means to other advances that actually matter to people. If you follow the money, however, Silicon Valley is far more focused on generating more computing power, in the belief, held by some, that it will give A. I. superhuman abilities that will fix all of our problems. Not everyone agrees with that belief. Major A. I. executives can’t even agree on what A. I. is. (Most do seem to agree that they should not be liable for crimes committed with their new tools.)

Better computers can help with all kinds of things, but you can’t cure cancer with data centers alone. As with the pandemic-era crypto boom, A. I. has let its stories about the future run so far ahead of economic reality, the ultimate project starts to look like sweeping economic change for the sake of sweeping economic change. There are better futures to bet on.

Living in a state that surprised everyone on Election Day, I think you are expressing exactly what people voted for. We want America back. The country that once stepped away from royal centralization in favor of the People. That may sound naive but it is exactly where we are.

I wish I thought the recent election indicated a realization that our values were off track. I'm afraid for many people it just reflected their unhappiness with gas prices. Some people have (somehow) been surprised at the ugliness of this administration's "immigration control" efforts, and reckless use of war as distraction, but we have a disappointingly large number of people who would overlook any stupidity, until it affects the price of gas.

Zachary D. Carter is the author of “The Price of Peace: Money, Democracy and the Life of John Maynard Keynes.”

James Talarico Has the Rarest Political Virtue

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By Frank Bruni

Mr. Bruni is a contributing Opinion writer who was on the staff of The Times for more than 25 years.

On the morning after his astonishing 12-point win in one of the most closely watched Senate races in decades, James Talarico, a newly minted Democratic superstar from a newly blue Texas, visited a patch of red. He went on Fox News.

He could have been walking into the lion’s den as a show of mettle or simply to gloat. Before Election Day, he’d been mocked on the network as James “Tala-freak-o,” and here he was, a freaky and fantabulous victor getting the last laugh.

But when I watched his conversation with the anchors Dana Perino and Bill Hemmer, I didn’t get the impression that he was there to celebrate his own triumph. What struck me, as it has over the past year, was Talarico’s reserve and restraint.

He urged people not to listen to him — or any other politician — too closely, because words are easy and actions count more. He not only complimented President Trump on securing the nation’s Southern border, but also eschewed too much talk of prosecuting officials in the Trump administration. “I am not interested in retribution,” he said. He told Texans who hadn’t voted for him that he’d be working hard for them nonetheless.

I might dismiss all of that as pretty blather if it weren’t so consistent with his tone over time. And I wouldn’t linger over it and thrill to it if it didn’t reflect a faint pattern I detected in many Democrats’ successful midterm campaigns. I saw shoots of humility on a political landscape that has been largely barren of it over recent years.

A lack of humility explains a whole lot about our dysfunction and divisiveness, which we won’t repair without a resurgence of it. We’ve been at one another’s throats in part because we’ve been unhumble — and thus unable to acknowledge that there might be good reason for someone’s divergent opinion, that it’s not necessary to win every argument, that the public good matters as much as our private satisfaction and that a healthy democracy requires compromise, forgiveness, grace. We’ve had unhumble governments, and that has intensified partisanship and exacerbated its toll.

It was a kind of arrogance that, perversely, opened the door to Donald Trump — perhaps the most arrogant presidential candidate and then president we’ve ever had. A centerpiece of his pitch to voters in 2016 and then again in 2024 was that an entrenched and snotty political elite thought it knew better than they did, made no effort to understand the feelings and struggles of Americans in the parts of the country between the coasts, and imposed its ideas — about social justice, globalism, gender roles, language and more — in an oppressive, censorious fashion. There was enough truth to that indictment that Trump twice won the presidency.

But while he could call out others’ sanctimony, he couldn’t recognize or purge the nuclear-grade version of it in himself. His self-consumption and self-regard drove his rejection of the 2020 election results, and many of his supporters, with his encouragement, joined his rebellion, to the point of storming the Capitol and bloodying police officers. While their thinking can rightly be labeled conspiratorial, it can just as accurately be called unhumble. They decided that they held the truth, no matter all the proof to the contrary. They couldn’t accept that their preference for one presidential candidate over another could possibly put them in the minority.

Trump, of course, has spent his second term in the presidency elevating his wants and his wounds above anyone and anything else. His tariffs are less a sound economic strategy than a bludgeon with which he can bonk potentates who perturb him. He exhibits more interest in gilding his lair and putting his stamp on monuments than on fulfilling his pledge to ease Americans’ financial anxieties.

Humility? Don’t make me laugh. In his recent interview with Ross Douthat for “60 Minutes,” he conceded that he wouldn’t be able to summon a smidgen of it even if that were the postmortem terms of passage to paradise. He told Douthat that he would refuse to forgive the likes of James Comey, Nancy Pelosi and other leaders who, in his estimation, wronged him.

The lessons of the Democrats’ midterm rout won’t be wholly clear until more time has passed and more evidence gathered, but it seems to me that many voters were rejecting not just Trump’s megalomania and narcissism but many politicians’ failure to step far enough outside their own egos and interests to hear and heed the people they’re supposed to be serving. Democrats flourished because their approach was such a down-to-earth one. Such a practical one. So different from Trump’s bluster. So focused on voters’ everyday lives and anxieties.

It reflected — and modeled — a kind of humility.

In her successful bid to become the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since 1990, Gina Hinojosa downplayed her most progressive cultural positions, acknowledging that many Texans disagreed with them. That was shrewd, even necessary, strategy. But it was humble as well — the acceptance of a world that didn’t and needn’t conform exactly to her liking. In her victory speech, she thanked Gov. Greg Abbott, the incumbent whom she defeated, for his offer to help her with her transition into office, and promised all Texans: “I will listen when you disagree. I will admit when I am wrong.”

On Roy Cooper’s way to winning the Senate race in North Carolina and flipping a seat in the chamber from red to blue, he spent less time touting his considerable accomplishments during decades in public office than in promising economic relief for distressed Americans. His past took a back seat to voters’ present and future.

I’m not saying that he or Hinojosa or any of the Democratic Party’s midterm stars are meek creatures, loath to have their say or get their way. People tend not to run for office unless they venerate their own instincts, relish their own voices and bloom in the spotlight. Talarico’s victory tour didn’t end with Fox News. It continued with “Saturday Night Live.”

He’s allowed a little showboating, given the balance of his behavior. In an article for MS NOW, Eugene Daniels recognized how hard and earnestly Talarico worked to repair a breach with Black voters during his campaign. It was a tale, Daniels wrote, “of old-school pounding the pavement, modern campaigning via influencers, and yes, money. But it’s also a story of the power of that rarest of political traits: humility. It could turn out to be the story of the 2026 midterms.”

If so, it should include Talarico’s answer, before Election Day, to a question about whether he was the one to turn Texas blue. “I’m not interested in turning Texas blue,” he said. “I want to win this seat so that I can fight for all 31 million Texans whether they’re Democrats, independents or Republicans.” He added that “the best color for Texas is purple” because “when you have a purple state, when you have competitive elections, it forces every politician in both parties at all levels to stay on their toes.”

On their toes, not their pedestals. What a freaky thought.

It would have been politically foolish of Talarico to state on Fox News that he wants retribution. Let's wait and see how he votes. I give Talarico tremendous credit for going on Fox News. I hope more Democrats are as bold in 2027.

I have heard Talarico speak and am very impressed. However, there is a difference between retribution and justice. Justice is there to repair harms and prevent future abuses. I would not want the pursuit of justice to keep the dems from progressing with their work for the people but without justice Republicans will keep on lying, breaking the law and grifting.

People need to remember that you can forgive but you don’t have to accept the actions of the transgressor. You don’t have to let the Republicans keep walking over everyone else and continue their bad behavior. You always love the child while correcting their actions. We need a correction here so I hope the Democrats do investigate and not turn a blind eye to the corruption. Like a parent, you can set limits and hand out consequences but do that without hate.

In The Guardian, Arwa Mahdawi recounted an alligator’s unwelcome appearance in — and removal from — a North Carolina bagel shop: “The gator insists he did nothing wrong and is the victim of a schmear campaign.” (Thanks to Susan Dawkins of Clyde, N. C., and Hillary DeFrancesco of Santa Fe, N. M., for nominating this.)

In The Athletic, Candace Buckner recalled the big-spending ways of Jim Irsay, the former owner of the Indianapolis Colts, who died last year: “Irsay didn’t leave his children with crushing debt. He left them with something far worse: An N. F. L. team without a franchise quarterback.” (Wendy Rosenthal, Plainsboro, N. J.)

In his newsletter, Jim Bob Moore found fault with Democrats for not having more success in Texas earlier: “Democrats spent the better part of twenty years waiting for demographics to deliver a blue Texas, as if destiny were a precinct captain. The census kept its end of the bargain. The ballot box didn’t, because nobody had given people a reason to show up.” (Mauri Moore, Seattle)

In The Financial Times, Robert Armstrong appraised Talarico: “His standard costume of crisp white shirt, blue blazer, dark trousers and carefully brushed hair evoked a loyal son dressed to visit his mother on Easter Sunday — all that was missing was the bouquet of tulips. There were cowboy boots involved, but those are a regional obligation.” (John Jacoby, North Andover, Mass.)

In The Washington Post, George F. Will excoriated JD Vance. “His 2026 campaigning, frenetic and futile, lowered the tone everywhere, left wreckage in his wake and underscored this: He represents a potential four-year prolongation of the nation’s slog through a sewer of scabrous rhetoric serving odious politics,” Will wrote. (Tom Fiedler, Asheville, N. C., and Sherri Kimes, Palm Springs, Calif., among many others)

In The Bulwark, Mona Charen deemed Marco Rubio little better than Vance: “He may not have personally bitten the heads off the chickens, but he enjoyed the meal.” (Mimi Bluestone, Brooklyn)

In The Times, Carlos Lozada considered the contortions to be performed by some of Trump’s collaborators after the voting on Nov. 3: “Welcome to the Nov. 4 Club, made up of Republicans who insist that they’ve finally had enough or that all along they were privately concerned, personally appalled, secretly dismayed or whatever euphemism best elides the abdication of principle for expediency.” They have their work cut out for them. “It’s a tricky move, to apologize for being an apologist,” Carlos wrote, but what are they to do? “One day you’re riding the Trump train; the next, you find yourself tied to the tracks.” (Sandra Cirincione, Flanders, N. Y. and Michelena Hallie, Amenia, N. Y., among many others)

Also in The Times, Matt Labash identified a peculiarity of the president’s political disposition. “One thing we do know about Mr. Trump is that however much he depicts the Democrats as Marx-loving pinkos, he himself is a lifelong karmic socialist: forever committed to redistributing blame,” Matt wrote. (Jo English, Menlo Park, Calif., and Jason Miller, Ann Arbor, Mich., among many others)

And Maureen Dowd captured the tension between Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer on the set of the 1939 movie “The Women”: “Things came to a delicious head when Crawford read lines with Shearer while engaging in her cacophonous hobby, knitting. Norma genteelly asked Joan to put away the clacking knitting needles, but the whole point was needling Norma, so Joan didn’t.” (Dan Tannenbaum, Phoenixville, Pa.)

In The New Yorker, Anthony Lane recognized an oddity in the art world: “Nowadays, it is not uncommon for single paintings awaiting sale to go on tour like rock stars.” One of them, he added, “traveled to Hong Kong, London, San Francisco, and Singapore before being hawked at Christie’s in New York” and “now resides in Saudi Arabia, although, for all we know, it could be hanging out at the Chateau Marmont and running up a bar tab for the ages.” (Jack Weiner, Hoboken, N. J.)

In his newsletter, Ron Charles ogled the trees: “Every autumn, they drop their leaves on us like incendiary Post-it Notes, little missives of mortality too lovely to believe.” (Katie Sasser, Portland, Me., and Stacy DeBroff, Boston)

And in her newsletter, Clara Parkes explained what a certain glimpse of a certain river means as she drives by it: “This view tells me I’m getting closer to home — that, very soon, I’ll be pulling off the main road and onto a smaller one that leads to a smaller one yet. If I had a tail, here’s where it would start to wag.” (Linda Warner, Belgrade, Maine)

To nominate favorite bits of recent writing from The Times or other publications to be mentioned in “For the Love of Sentences,” please email me here and include your name and place of residence.

I admired the 2025 documentary “Predators,” which explored the moral murk and collateral damage of the hugely popular Dateline NBC series “To Catch a Predator,” in which the network star Chris Hansen and his crew used actors posing as children to lure would-be molesters into homes where Hansen lay in wait, ready to expose them on camera. So I was excited to see the new movie “Primetime,” a fictionalized take on those sting operations starring Robert Pattinson as Hansen. But it’s a needlessly stylized and melodramatic production that obscures the most interesting ethical questions. “Primetime” is now streaming for a rental fee.

My Times Opinion colleague Bret Stephens and I shared our instant reactions to the midterm results in this online interchange. Then, last week, we wondered what happens when a peacock of a president becomes a lame duck.

Parting Songs: For a blast of pleasantly straightforward radio-ready fare, “Dust,” by Broods. For an equally approachable indie track, “Agnes,” by Glass Animals. For a sonically fanciful (and oddly hummable) indictment of sexism in the music industry, “Castle,” by Halsey.

I often hear people say they’re grateful for how their dogs coax them outside. They’re glad for the motivation to turn away from the television or the computer, toward greener pastures and fresh air.

But Regan doesn’t simply tug me into nature. She gives me a heightened experience of it. Sensations that might wash over me mesmerize her, and I find myself pausing, concentrating, figuring out what holds her rapt and then appreciating it to a degree I otherwise wouldn’t have.

Her ears lift and stiffen. Why? I focus and then I know: She has identified the rustle of muscle against brush, coming from a few dozen feet to our left, where, I now see, several large deer are trudging through the forest. Or she has detected the whistle of wind through the maples and magnolias, faint enough to go unheard — but not by Regan. And, as a result, not by me.

We’re now deep into autumn, and that’s clearly an olfactory buffet. Her nose twitches curiously, eagerly, joyfully. She treats each fallen leaf as some message from the gods above, to be decoded by sniffing and sniffing and sniffing some more. I’m impatient at first, but then I relax, and I let my own, inferior nostrils take in the smells around us. I’m reminded of the singular perfume of November air, which carries the oxymoronic sweetness of decay. I’m put in mind of football, of Thanksgiving, of fireplaces rekindled after many months of neglect.

Winter isn’t far off. I’m hoping for some snow (no guarantee in this area of North Carolina). And that’s not only because of how pretty the neighborhood looks under a fresh blanket of it. It’s also because of how it elates Regan. She uses her snout to plow it, her tongue to lick it. She rolls sideways through it, as if it’s flour and she’s a self-coating cutlet.

I watch her and realize just what a fluffy, frosty marvel this rare visitor is. And I’m happier than I’d be if I were greeting it alone. Sometimes wonder comes more easily to dogs than to us. That’s the millionth reason to relish their company.

Frank Bruni is a professor of journalism and public policy at Duke University, the author of the book “The Age of Grievance” and a contributing Opinion writer. He writes a weekly email newsletter. Instagram Threads @FrankBruni • Facebook

As he prepared for a visit to China, the president played down the fallout from Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman officials have identified as an intelligence asset for Beijing.

By Shawn McCreesh

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Monday that he was open to seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the head of Nvidia, his latest public expression of support for the tech executive who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U. S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I would not mind; I would not mind that,” Mr. Trump told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House as he departed for a trip to Asia, including a stop in China.

“I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another,” he added.

The president’s remarks were his first in days on a scandal that has engulfed the chip-making giant at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom and raised questions about his handling of a potential national security threat. His backing of the former Nvidia chief added to a growing chorus from tech leaders who say Mr. Huang’s departure threatens to set the United States back in the A. I. race.

The president cast doubt on whether Alice Huang, the woman with whom Mr. Huang had a relationship, was actually a spy.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” Mr. Trump said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all.”

When a reporter pointed out that Mr. Trump’s own secretary of state had warned him that intelligence officials believed she was, the president pleaded ignorance.

“Who told me that?” he asked.

“Secretary Rubio,” the reporter replied.

“I haven’t heard that,” Mr. Trump said. “I haven’t heard that.”

The president has repeatedly defended Mr. Huang since the revelations.

Last week, Mr. Trump called Mr. Huang before he stepped down and urged him to keep fighting for his job, The New York Times reported.

Mr. Trump was warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang, who intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

On Monday, the president repeatedly downplayed the severity of the Nvidia fallout, and he insisted that national security had not been put at risk. “I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” he explained.

Mr. Trump plans to meet with President Xi Jinping of China during his trip, as part of a trilateral summit that also includes President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. A White House spokeswoman has said they plan to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran.

There could also be progress on the creation of a system for the United States and China to alert each other about A. I. national security issues, but the Nvidia scandal may have made that more difficult.

Mr. Trump’s exchange with reporters on Monday was his first public appearance since Wednesday. In the intervening days, the controversy over Mr. Huang’s demise had reached into the president’s cabinet, pitting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC that his department had been pushing Mr. Lutnick’s department for months to crack down on the flow of U. S. technology to China.

The president attempted to gloss over these divisions.

“Different viewpoints,” he said simply. “One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

He added that Mr. Lutnick was “doing a very good job.”

The president has continued to express sympathy for Mr. Huang. He told reporters last week that he was concerned with how the technology executive was holding up amid the controversy.

“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right,” Mr. Trump said then, adding: “I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement, and I believe he’s suffering greatly. More so because of his family, his wife who he loves and his family, but he is definitely suffering.”

On Monday, Mr. Trump said: “Jensen obviously has good things going. He has a family situation, which is a rough deal. And what he wants to do is sell chips.”

Shawn McCreesh is a White House reporter for The Times covering the Trump administration.

Elon Musk Wants to Merge Tesla and SpaceX. Their Businesses Already Overlap.

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

For years, engineers have shuffled between Tesla and SpaceX, and the companies have worked on major projects together.

By Grace Kay

Nearly a decade ago, Elon Musk gave Tesla’s design team an unusual assignment: Build a sports car that can fly.

Mr. Musk brought in a small team of engineers from SpaceX, his rocket company, to lend a hand. Led by Bill Riley, SpaceX’s executive overseeing engineering on the rocket intended to land NASA astronauts on the moon, the team juggled their day jobs with outfitting a Roadster sports car with cold-gas thrusters, a technology more commonly found in rockets that has enough force to burst a human eardrum, according to three people familiar with the project.

This year, as engineers from both companies prepared for the car’s debut, they spent months putting it through its paces at SpaceX’s rocket testing facility in McGregor, Texas, the people said. In October, a driverless Roadster did a kick flip in midair, launching off a ramp more than 60 feet high.

This is “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company” Mr. Musk told the crowd.

The flying car demonstration offered a rare glimpse into how the world’s richest person has already created unusual cooperations between his two companies — which he now hopes to merge into a conglomerate valued at more than $3 trillion.

For years, Mr. Musk has quietly shuffled executives and engineers between Tesla and SpaceX to work on his passion projects, blurring the lines between the two, according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former employees, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential business matters. The arrangements highlight how Mr. Musk treated the huge companies as interchangeable parts of a single empire, long before shareholders have been asked to vote on combining them.

“It’s unusual because they have a common C. E. O. who is one of the wealthiest people on the planet,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management. “There’s nothing like this that’s happened. Even in the days of John D. Rockefeller, you didn’t have this kind of consolidation of wealth and power.”

Representatives for Tesla and SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The merger will require approval by independent committees from each company, and approval by shareholders.

Mr. Musk has said the companies’ work overlaps closely and he thinks a merger would be a “good idea.” But he has said he will not be a part of any special committee discussions, comparing the decision to “tap dancing through a minefield.”

Mr. Musk has rapidly consolidated his business empire over the past few years. In February, he merged his A. I. start-up, xAI, with SpaceX, bringing in engineers from the rocket company to lead key projects, including xAI’s data center build out and a reorganization of the start-up, according to five people with knowledge of the company. The acquisition took place less than a year after he merged the A. I. start-up with his social media company, X. The combined SpaceX, which went public in June, is valued at $1.89 trillion.

A merger of Tesla, which is valued at $1.54 trillion, and SpaceX would combine the electrical-vehicle manufacturer and its solar business with a government contractor with ambitions to send astronauts to Mars. The massive deal would wrap cars, rockets, satellites, data centers and A. I. into one company.

“The synergies are pretty obvious,” said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business. “There’s loads of conflicts of interest. They all get resolved with this merger.”

Some of the existing connections between the companies — most of which are paid for by the companies — have been detailed in contracts and public filings. In the prospectus SpaceX’s initial public offering, the company said it had bought about $890 million in Tesla products since 2023, including Cybertrucks and Megapack batteries to help power the company’s data centers. The filing also detailed how the companies share private jets.

Tesla has incorporated some SpaceX products into its offerings, including adding Grok, an A. I. assistant, as a chat feature in Tesla vehicles and incorporating SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service into its future vehicles. Tesla announced in January it had invested $2 billion in xAI as a part of a larger partnership between the two companies.

But much of the overlap can be traced to staffing.

The two companies have shared some talent for more than a decade. Charlie Kuehmann has served as vice president of materials engineering for both companies since 2015. And earlier this year, Tesla’s vice president of A. I., Ashok Elluswamy, the man responsible for leading Tesla’s self-driving software and work on humanoid robotics, began working simultaneously with SpaceX’s A. I. unit, according to two people with knowledge of his work. About one in 22 SpaceX employees list Tesla as a former employer, and the carmaker is SpaceX’s largest source of new hires, according to LinkedIn data from intelligence firm Live Data Technologies. Most came from the car maker’s engineering ranks, and the pace of hiring Tesla recruits has more than doubled this year, the data shows.

Existing staff at both companies have teamed up on projects in addition to the Roadster. Mr. Musk co-founded xAI in 2023 to compete with A. I. start-ups including OpenAI. Soon after, he announced the company had turned an old factory in Memphis into a giant data center called Colossus to help power the Grok chatbot.

Tesla engineers assisted with the project, which took 122 days. Some staff came from Tesla’s own A. I. data center in Texas, a site that helps power the company’s self-driving software, according to three people familiar with the project. Others came from Dojo, Tesla’s supercomputer project meant to compete directly with Nvidia.

In spring 2025, two engineers from Tesla’s Dojo supercomputer team both worked for both xAI and Tesla, according to internal documents viewed by The New York Times. One of them, Dan Rowland, went on to lead xAI’s data center team before leaving the company in August. Those data centers later accounted for $506 million in Tesla battery purchases.

Earlier this year, Mr. Musk moved an xAI project — to create a digital A. I. agent capable of replacing some white-collar workers — to Tesla’s Autopilot team, three people familiar with the project said. Tesla also hired a handful of xAI engineers to work on the A. I. tool, which was renamed Digital Optimus after the company’s humanoid robot, the people said.

Mr. Musk has said the project is part of Tesla’s $2 billion partnership with xAI, which he recently renamed SpaceXSI.

Mr. Musk has also pushed his companies to use the others’ technology. In July, Mr. Musk sent Tesla employees a companywide email asking them to use Grok as their primary A. I. model, according to a memo viewed by The Times. He told staff that the latest Grok model was lower cost compared with competitors like Anthropic, and asked engineers to directly email him with Grok feedback.

Tesla this year gave staff early access to new versions of the Grok chatbot and coding models for testing. SpaceX’s A. I. unit has been using data from Tesla usage to evaluate its A. I. models and hone them, according to internal communications viewed by The Times.

The companies are only continuing to grow closer. In March, Tesla and SpaceX said they were planning a $16.8 billion joint investment in a chip manufacturing facility in Texas. The project will build the chips that help power SpaceX’s A. I., as well as Tesla’s robotics and autonomous vehicle systems. In the months since, the names of dozens of SpaceX engineers showed up listed in Tesla’s internal organizational charts, according to documents viewed by The Times.

Some engineers at Tesla and SpaceX have considered a merger a foregone conclusion for years. Employees have used an internal chat channel dedicated to discussing Tesla’s stock to hype up a potential deal for months, according to three people familiar with the channel.

Mr. Musk has struck a more cautious tone.

“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” he said last month on a call with investors. “I think that would be overstating it.”

Ryan Mac contributed reporting.

I'm a New York Times reporter, covering Elon Musk's companies with a focus on AI and emerging technology from New York.
