The Blue Wave Lifted Democrats. But Not All Progressives Rose as High.

The New York Times November 16, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Newsletter

The performance gap with moderates narrowed, but progressive candidates underperformed by enough to keep the “electability” debate alive.

By Nate Cohn

Democrats have been debating whether the party should move to the left or the center for nearly a decade. This month’s midterm results were almost perfectly calibrated to make sure the debate rages into the next presidential primary.

On the one hand, Democrats won in a tsunami. They often did so with a populist pitch, and despite the calls for the party to move to the center. The new progressive activist left won more races than ever before, including its first big victory in a battleground state: Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed won a divisive race for Senate. Incredibly, in May, he even predicted his exact margin of victory: seven percentage points.

On the other hand, progressive candidates underperformed by enough and in enough races to keep the old “electability” debate alive and well. Many of the weakest Democratic results — those where the party fared relatively poorly given the national environment and the characteristics of the state or district — came in races where Democrats picked progressive candidates in contested nominating fights this summer.

Mr. El-Sayed’s victory is an example of this kind of underperformance. While he won and won comfortably, his victory was underwhelming if judged against how Democrats did elsewhere in the country. After all, Michigan usually votes about the same as the country; this year, Democrats are on track to win by 13 or 14 points nationwide. Mr. El-Sayed’s seven-point victory counts as a significant underperformance against that backdrop.

It’s important to note that many progressives fared well, even though many of the party’s weakest showings featured progressive nominees. In congressional races in Montana, Ohio and Pennsylvania, populists with a blue-collar background — like firefighters and union leaders — won in districts that voted for President Trump in the last election. Progressives also fared extraordinarily well, like Democrats of all political stripes, in districts with large Hispanic populations, including in key battlegrounds in California and Colorado.

And if one accepts a broad definition of progressive — which might include much of the mainstream of the Democratic Party, not just factional candidates of the progressive left — progressives didn’t merely perform well but may have also found a way forward for a divided party.

Democrats of all ideological leanings gravitated toward a distinctly progressive message, including embracing populist economics and opposing Israel’s conduct in Gaza, even while many tried to steer clear of “socialism” and the “woke” politics of the early 2020s. The appeal of this affordability-focused message was first demonstrated by the democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani in his New York mayoral campaign. But Democrats across the ideological spectrum — from Jon Ossoff and James Talarico to Mr. El-Sayed — can be said to have followed a similar blueprint.

Nonetheless, the party’s weakest results tended to come when Democrats nominated progressive candidates in high-profile primaries, where ideological differences were likely to be amplified. They also tended to come in states where Democrats appeared burdened by the perceived excesses or failures of progressive governance. In a blue tsunami, it did not ultimately cost the Democrats many elections — the races for Florida Senate and Maine’s Second District stand out as the likeliest candidates — but in a more competitive year the toll could have been more significant or even decisive.

The question of how well progressives or moderates fare is always fraught, and the answer can be highly sensitive to the way the analysis is conducted. This year, the Democratic Party’s extraordinary gains among younger, Hispanic and red-state voters — along with the G. O. P.’s relative resilience among older, white and blue-state voters — make it even more challenging. This analysis attempts to account for the demographic and political characteristics of a state or district, as well as the prior political strength of the Republican incumbent, if one is running.

Even when progressives clearly underperform, it’s not necessarily clear whether their ideology or policy views were the reason. After all, there are many progressive Democrats — like those who support Medicare for all or oppose aid to Israel — who are well within the mainstream of the Democratic Party and fare well in elections. Tammy Baldwin and Cory Booker (who overperformed Nov. 3 in New Jersey, by our measures) are examples of mainstream progressives with solid electoral track records.

Instead, the progressives who systematically underperform have tended to come from a narrower faction of the party: the new, activist left. This faction is clearly to the left of the party’s mainstream progressives, most obviously when its members embrace socialism and slogans or positions like “defund the police.” But they’re often different in other respects that can contribute to their electoral woes. They are “fighters,” not compromisers. They often focus on issues that animate activists, like Gaza and climate change, rather than bread-and-butter economics (though Mr. Mamdani’s affordability playbook helped ease this issue this cycle). And they run against the mainstream of the Democratic Party; in doing so, they signal to voters that they’re not just a little farther to the left, but different in kind.

All of these challenges make it harder to identify whether progressives underperform and, when they do so, exactly why. But at least in this year’s Senate races, a complicated analysis isn’t necessary to see that all six of the Democrats who substantially underperformed (by at least five percentage points) are progressives — and it includes all five of the progressives who prevailed in high-profile, contested nominating battles this summer: Mr. El-Sayed, Angie Nixon in Florida, Ed Markey in Massachusetts, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Troy Jackson in Maine.

Senate races in states with progressive Democratic candidates had smaller blue shifts than those in the rest of the country.

Note: Shift toward Democrats is calculated using 2026 Senate results compared with 2024 presidential results.

By The New York Times

The findings hold in a more sophisticated analysis that accounts for their opponents, control of state government and the demographics of their states. In some cases, the progressive showing looks better by this measure. Mr. Jackson’s underperformance, for instance, isn’t nearly as large after considering Maine’s relatively old and white population, let alone the strength of his opponent, Susan Collins.

Nonetheless, the same Democrats underperformed, and moderate or establishment-backed Democrats did not. The one moderate Democrat who seemed to be at risk of underperforming under similar circumstances — Chris Pappas in New Hampshire, who faced the former senator John Sununu after a competitive primary in a relatively old and white state — did not underperform at all by this measure and won by a wide margin. All other major Democratic Senate candidates ran ahead of Democrats nationally.

Senate races in which Democrats underperformed by two percentage points or more based on district demographics, prior election results and incumbency.

By The New York Times

By this measure, the biggest underperformer was actually Jeff Merkley in Oregon. As the only senator to endorse Bernie Sanders in 2016, he’s certainly a progressive. And despite winning easily, his roughly 19-point victory was a large underperformance: He won by less in Oregon than Roy Cooper did in North Carolina.

But it doesn’t necessarily follow that Mr. Merkley underperformed simply because he was a progressive, and it highlights some of the challenges involved in evaluating progressive candidates. He may have been weighed down by the unpopularity of Oregon’s Democratic governor, for instance, who won by less than 10 points. Of course, the Democratic government in Oregon is unpopular in part because of its handling of ideologically charged issues, like homelessness and public drug use, but it’s possible that another Democrat would have struggled in the Senate race.

This story repeats itself in blue states across the country. In general, Democratic candidates for Senate and House fared worse in states with relatively unpopular Democratic governments. Many of these states also happen to elect relatively progressive Democrats, including for Senate this year. Minnesota, where Ms. Flanagan is judged as an underperformer in our analysis, is another state where Democrats may have been burdened by this kind of problem.

Nonetheless, there’s an overarching pattern across the states where progressives underperformed, regardless of the popularity of Democratic government. Across these races, progressives struggled to match Kamala Harris’s 2024 support among older voters and white voters with a college degree, according to Times Voter Trends. These groups have trended toward Democrats over the last decade, but they appear to have major reservations about supporting more progressive Democrats. They usually opposed them in the primaries and in some cases may have done so in the general election.

The highest-income communities near Detroit, Boston and Minneapolis all swung to the right — in some cases voting more than 10 points to the right of the 2024 election result even in a year when Democrats ran 15 points better than Ms. Harris nationwide. So did areas dominated by older voters, like The Villages in Florida. This suggests that something similar is at play across these races — a backlash among affluent and older moderates — even if the reason for the backlash might not always be about the progressive on the ballot.

The story is even harder to tease out in the House, where establishment-backed candidates of varying ideological stripes won Democratic nominations in almost every vigorously contested race. The handful of progressive-backed candidates who did win in competitive races — based on endorsements from groups like the Justice Democrats or Mr. Sanders’s Our Revolution — were also a fairly idiosyncratic bunch. Some of the candidates even strain the usual definition of a progressive candidate, like those who do not support Medicare for all.

The group of progressive-backed candidates who didn’t support Medicare for all — usually blue-collar populists in working-class districts that voted for Mr. Trump — fared quite well. The more archetypal progressives — those endorsed by the progressive left and who did support Medicare for all — were relatively likely to underperform.

Two of the party’s three worst showings in the battlegrounds, by our measure, involved House progressive nominees. In one of those races, the Democratic candidate probably cost the party a seat.

Maine’s Second is the only district that flipped from blue to red (other than those affected by gerrymandering). The moderate Democrat Jared Golden decided not to seek re-election after he faced a primary challenge from a progressive (although he cited other reasons for exiting). In the end, the progressive, Matt Dunlap, was defeated. Remarkably, Maine’s Second has gone from being the most Republican district won by a Democrat in 2024 to the most Democratic district won by a Republican in 2026.

Democrats did not lose in Michigan’s Seventh District, a classic battleground where the party nominated William Lawrence, who until recently was a Democratic Socialists of America member. He won, but only by about three points in a district that Mr. Trump won by one point in 2024. By our estimates, this was an even worse underperformance for Democrats than in Maine’s Second. Mr. Lawrence ran behind Mr. El-Sayed in this district as well.

That said, there were two other progressive-backed candidates who fared better. One was Bob Brooks, a firefighter and labor leader who easily won a classic battleground district, Pennsylvania’s Seventh. He performed about as one might expect. Whether he modestly overperformed or underperformed depends on whether one accounts for his party’s overall strength in Pennsylvania (in general, House candidates tend to fare better in states where their party fared well at the top of the ticket; the analysis was conducted each way).

The biggest progressive winner of all was Randy Villegas, a professor who holds an overwhelming lead — 68 percent to 32 percent — in a redrawn California district that would have voted for Mr. Trump by around two points in the last election. The backstory here is simple: Hispanic voters make up a majority of the electorate, and Democrats made enormous gains among them nationwide and perhaps especially in California’s Central Valley. If Mr. Villegas paid any penalty for his progressive views, there’s no sign of it in the data. A second progressive in a relatively Hispanic district — Manny Rutinel in the Denver area — ran in line with expectations.

Beyond the contested nominating battles in competitive states, most progressives tended to fare somewhat worse than other Democrats, but not by much. There were clear exceptions — Representative Ilhan Omar in Minnesota is currently the only House Democrat who is performing worse than Ms. Harris did in 2024 — but in general the differences are modest at best. This finding has been echoed by other analysts in recent days, and it is somewhat of a departure from recent cycles, when progressives underperformed by larger margins even in noncompetitive races.

This might suggest that progressives made progress toward finding a more appealing message, perhaps in part because of the new focus on affordability. Or it may mean that this year’s blue tsunami washed over the usual ideological divides. With Mr. Trump’s approval rating in the 30s, perhaps many voters who might ordinarily consider voting for a Republican over a progressive Democrat didn’t feel they had a choice.

Nate Cohn is The Times’s chief political analyst. He covers elections, public opinion, demographics and polling.

Grammys Snubs and Surprises: Rosalía’s Arty Entry and Noah Kahan’s Exclusion

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Grammy Awards

Advertisement

Supported by

Madonna and Kahan were locked out of nominations in the top categories, the Womack Sisters were recognized and country’s gender divide showed up in an unexpected way.

By Jon ParelesBen Sisario and Joe Coscarelli

There’s an arty wild-card in the top Grammy categories. Rosalía’s 2025 album “Lux (Complete Works)” is nominated for album of the year; its track “Berghain” is up for song and record of the year. “Lux (Complete Works),” which was just named album of the year at the Latin Grammys, has lyrics in more than a dozen languages, a panoply of collaborators and arrangements that encompass orchestras, electronics and flamenco. Although “Berghain” is named after Berlin’s renowned dance club, its music is full-tilt operatic, with Rosalía backed by an orchestra and choir; she sings in German and Spanish and shares the track with Björk, who invokes “divine intervention,” and Yves Tumor, whose lyric would have to be bleeped on ABC. Rosalía’s nominations also include nods for other “Lux” songs that are closer to pop: “Sauvignon Blanc” (pop solo performance) and “La Perla” (Latin song). Alongside the pop hits that share the top categories, “Berghain” arrives from an alternate universe. — JON PARELES

Madonna’s 2025 album, “Confessions II,” was widely hailed as a high-concept sequel to her 2005 “Confessions on a Dance Floor” — a major statement after years of uneven albums. “Confessions II” is a loving, history-minded survey of club culture from someone who’s seen — and changed — it all. But the album was shut out of the top categories, and it doesn’t even get a chance at pop vocal album. “Bring Your Love,” shared with Sabrina Carpenter, is among the nominees for pop duo/group performance, but other “Confessions” tracks are relegated to the dance/electronic categories, which don’t usually appear in prime time. — PARELES

The Canadian bass-and-drums duo Angine de Poitrine didn’t exactly scream “Grammy bait” when their performance on KEXP went viral earlier this year. Wearing polka-dot costumes with bizarre, face-covering headgear, they looked like errant kids’ TV characters — at least until they laid into their stuttering, microtonal prog grooves. But Angine de Poitrine, up for best new artist and three other awards, captivated the not-so-small sliver of the music world that luxuriates in stuff like this, and nowadays also cherishes it as a kind of oddball antidote to A. I. slop. We used to think of the “real musicianship” contingent of Grammy voters as people who relished a really smooth jazz solo. Maybe this is a new acid test? — BEN SISARIO

When the Grammys split the best country album category last year into traditional and contemporary branches, the hot take was that it was a reactionary response to Beyoncé winning with “Cowboy Carter” in 2025. And perhaps it was. But did anyone expect it would end up as a gender divide? In its second year, the contemporary country album ballot is all women: Ella Langley, Kacey Musgraves, Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith and Megan Moroney (average age: 31). Traditional country album, on the other hand, is all men: Willie Nelson, Vince Gill, Cody Johnson, Charley Crockett and Charlie Worsham (average age: 57). Hey boys, try something contemporary. — SISARIO

The much-mocked best new artist category — which often translates as “new to us industry gatekeepers” — got a rule tweak this year, refining it as a place for those who “achieved a breakthrough into the public consciousness and notably impacted the musical landscape,” so long as they’ve only been submitted a maximum of four times (up from three).

In practice, that meant love for the New York rock inheritors Geese — on the band’s official third album — who achieved five nominations in all, with four in the genre categories. (Honestly, not many would have blinked at an album of the year nod for “Getting Killed.”) Also practiced and present: the pop singers Remi Wolf (on her third major-label album) and Slayyyter, something of a veteran in the SoundCloud underground whose mainstream coronation is now official with four total noms, including best new artist.

Audrey Hobert, the comedic TV writer-turned-weird-girl phenom (after songwriting with her bestie, Gracie Abrams), had one of the year’s true Cinderella stories with her assured debut, “Who’s the Clown?,” and should have been here, too. (Her brother, Malcolm Todd, was also a common bet; Stella Lefty, absent as well, probably spared herself further backlash.) But given how this stuff tends to go, next year still seems like an option. — JOE COSCARELLI

The Womack Sisters are an unexpected but welcome nomination for best new artist. Perhaps a familiar name helped. The three sisters’ uncle was the 1960s soul hitmaker Bobby Womack, and their parents, Cecil and Linda Womack, were songwriters who also recorded as Womack & Womack. Their maternal grandfather was Sam Cooke. “The Womack Sisters,” their debut album, leans into the 1960s soul heritage that Grammy voters have long rewarded, with vintage-style arrangements and close girl-group harmonies that don’t sound one bit Auto-Tuned. — PARELES

Since his Covid-specific smash single “Stick Season,” the Vermont singer-songwriter Noah Kahan has been a stadium-filling, guitar-strumming behemoth taking every correct step. Expectations were so high for his latest, “The Great Divide” — with many predicting an appearance in the album of the year category, if not song and record for the title track — that Kahan felt the need to tamp down emotions in a social media post last night: “Whatever happens tomorrow I love you all and I have done everything I’ve ever needed to do in my career because of YOUR support,” he wrote. “You guys are all I care about.” A nominee but not a winner for best new artist at the Grammys in 2024, Kahan received just one nod, for best contemporary folk album. His underdog status squeaks by. — COSCARELLI

In yet another weak field for best rap album — and amid Drake’s ongoing Grammy boycott, which this year kept his “Iceman” (to say nothing of “Habibti” and “Maid of Honour”) off ballots — there is one bona fide commercial breakthrough in Don Toliver’s “Octane,” as well as some shruggy picks (Wale, Rapsody).

But the feel-good nomination is for “Dillagence II” by the veteran rapper Busta Rhymes and the producer J Dilla, who died in 2006; neither has ever won a competitive Grammy. In a category that can sometimes feel like it rewards lifetime achievement (or name recognition), this isn’t a bad use of either. And it balances out the feel-weird moment that is Ye, formerly Kanye West, getting recognized for the deluxe edition of “Bully,” an album that is both filling stadiums worldwide, and absent from all critical and commercial discourse at the same time. — COSCARELLI

Jon Pareles, a culture correspondent for The Times, served as chief pop music critic for 37 years. He studied music, played in rock, jazz and classical groups and was a college-radio disc jockey. He was previously an editor at Rolling Stone and The Village Voice.

Ben Sisario, a reporter covering music and the music industry, has been writing for The Times for more than 20 years.

Joe Coscarelli is a culture reporter for The Times and a co-host of the Times podcast “Popcast.”

Raye, Rosalía and Ella Langley Top a Women-Led 2027 Grammys Field

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Grammy Awards

Advertisement

Supported by

Langley is the first straight-up country artist to contend for the top album prize in eight years, and Raye’s 11 nods lead all nominees.

By Ben Sisario

Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley, Phoebe Bridgers and Raye are among the top contenders for the 69th annual Grammy Awards, leading a nominee class that is dominated by young women.

Raye, a British singer-songwriter with a jazzy, R&B-throwback style, has the most nods this year, with 11. Rosalía, the Spanish singer who has filled arenas with boundlessly eclectic, multilingual music, has nine, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Among the other top nominees, the chart-dominating new country star Ella Langley and her collaborator Miranda Lambert, along with Rodrigo and Bridgers, have seven nods apiece. Bruno Mars, a longtime Grammy darling, has six, as do the R&B singer-songwriters Leon Thomas and Olivia Dean, the latter another retro-flavored British singer who won best new artist at the most recent Grammy ceremony.

Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande and the anything-goes New York rock band Geese are also in the mix in top categories.

They will face off on Feb. 7 in Los Angeles, in a show to be broadcast live on ABC and Disney+, a new media partner for the Recording Academy after more than 50 years with CBS.

The latest competition may not offer the same clash-of-the-divas drama that in recent years has occasionally pitted Swift, Beyoncé or Adele against one another. Nor does it have the intense political valence of the most recent ceremony, in February, when Bad Bunny took album of the year amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

But the lineup shows a fresh group of young artists, most of them women, who have found abundant critical and popular acclaim. Langley, 27, whose song “Choosin’ Texas” — a slice of old-fashioned Nashville songcraft that set a chart record this year — has become the first straight-up country artist to contend for the top album prize in eight years, when Kacey Musgraves took it with “Golden Hour.”

In addition to Langley’s “Dandelion” and “This Music May Contain Hope.” by Raye, 29, the contest for album of the year includes Swift’s monster hit “The Life of a Showgirl”; Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” her third LP in a row to be nominated; Rosalía’s “Lux (Complete Works),” which last week won album of the year at the Latin Grammys; and records by Bridgers (“Lost Weekend”), Dean (“The Art of Loving”) and Mars (“The Romantic”).

Five songs will compete for both record and song of the year: Dean’s retro-inflected “Man I Need,” Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” Rosalía’s “Berghain,” Rodrigo’s “The Cure” and Raye’s “Where Is My Husband!” (The record of the year prize goes to the performers and producers behind a single track; song of the year recognizes songwriters.)

Also up for record of the year are Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia,” Mars’s “I Just Might” and Tame Impala’s “Dracula,” featuring the South Korean singer Jennie. Mars’s “Risk It All,” Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me” and Swift’s “I Knew It, I Knew You,” a track from the film “Toy Story 5” that represented her return to country, fill out the song of the year ballot.

Langley is the only act up for all four top prizes, including best new artist. Her competition in that category includes Geese, Slayyyter, Remi Wolf, Don Toliver, Sienna Spiro, the Womack Sisters and Angine de Poitrine, a Canadian duo that drew attention as much for their prog-rock sound as for their masked appearance and carnivalesque, polka-dotted stage costumes.

Among Raye’s other nominations are best pop vocal album, where she will compete against Dean, Grande, Mars and Rodrigo; best dance pop recording, facing Madonna, Zara Larsson, Slayyyter and Tinashe; and songwriter of the year, non-classical.

In other contests, the nominees for best contemporary country album — a category that debuted last year, when the academy split the country album award into contemporary and traditional categories — are all by women: Langley’s “Dandelion,” plus releases from Musgraves, Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith and Megan Moroney.

Angine de Poitrine, the costumed Canadian duo, is up against the Rolling Stones, Foo Fighters, Jack White and Muse for best rock album, and faces Bridgers, Geese, Rosalía and Hayley Williams of Paramore for best alternative music performance.

And although Beyoncé, the winningest artist in Grammy history, did not release a new album over the last year, she was nominated in best R&B solo performance for “Morning Dew (Donk),” a bonus track on a recent reissue of her 2006 album “B’Day.”

Ye, the rapper, producer and recent industry pariah formerly known as Kanye West, is up for best rap album, for “Bully (Deluxe),” which will compete against Cardi B, Don Toliver, Wale and Busta Rhymes.

In 2022, Ye was up for five Grammys but was disinvited from performing, after exhibiting erratic and troubling public behavior, including a music video portraying the kidnapping and burial of a character who resembled the comedian Pete Davidson. Later that year, Ye made a string of antisemitic remarks, including saying “I like Hitler” on a podcast.

In 2025, Ye was nominated for best rap song for “Carnival,” and in January, he took out an ad in The Wall Street Journal apologizing for his history of antisemitic statements.

This year the Recording Academy will give out Grammys in 100 categories — the most in 16 years, after a steady creep of category additions and adjustments.

One controversial addition this year was best Asian pop music performance. After years of debate within the academy, it was intended to recognize the global popularity of K-pop and other brands of contemporary pop in Asia, and included a requirement for the use of “one or more Asian languages.”

But the effort came under fire soon after its announcement in June, when BTS, by far the biggest K-pop supergroup, said it would boycott the Grammys over the move. In identical statements, the seven members said, “We hope music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided into region or language.” Another chart-topping K-pop act, the Stray Kids, also withdrew.

That left the academy scrambling to defend its category, which for its inaugural year will include acts less well known to Western audiences, including the all-female Japanese metal band Babymetal, Bini, Ive, KiiiKiii, SB19 and the Japanese performer Lisa.

In addition to the Asian pop award, four more new categories will be awarded at February’s ceremony: best R&B collaboration or duo/group performance, best traditional pop vocal performance, best Latin song and best traditional pop folk album. (The existing folk album category has been renamed contemporary folk.)

Winners will be determined by nearly 16,000 voting members of the academy, who include performers, songwriters, producers and engineers. They considered nearly 25,000 recordings released from Aug. 31, 2025, to Aug. 28, 2026.

The voting body has been undergoing significant changes in recent years, with thousands of new members invited — including about 1,900 who are also eligible to vote at the Latin Grammys — and inactive older members quietly moved to nonvoting status.

An earlier version of this article misidentified an artist who is nominated for best Asian pop music performance. She is the Japanese performer Lisa, not the singer Lisa who is a member of the South Korean group Blackpink.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Ben Sisario, a reporter covering music and the music industry, has been writing for The Times for more than 20 years.

Robert Pattinson Named as the Next James Bond

The New York Times November 16, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

The announcement ends years of speculation over who would take over the role after Daniel Craig’s five-film run.

By Brooks Barnes

Reporting from Los Angeles

After seven years of rumors, wish lists and wild guesses, Hollywood’s most feverishly followed casting search is over: Amazon MGM Studios has chosen Robert Pattinson to play James Bond.

Pattinson, the 40-year-old English actor, will become the seventh man to play 007 in the official 25-film series. Pattinson is known for blockbusters like “Twilight,” “The Batman” and, most recently, “The Odyssey.”

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson said in a statement.

He succeeds Daniel Craig, who announced in 2019 that he would depart the role. Craig’s decision set off a frenzy of speculation among Bond enthusiasts, bookmakers and the British tabloids. Who could be trusted to step into the multibillion-dollar franchise? What kind of Bond would click with a new generation? Should Bond be Black? Or female?

At various points, the supposed candidates included Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Hardy, Regé-Jean Page, Tom Holland, Jacob Elordi and Theo James.

Pattinson was chosen over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. The five actors underwent screen tests in London in late October. The auditions involved stunts, dialogue and camera presence; they were overseen by Nina Gold, an Oscar-nominated (“Hamnet”) and Emmy-winning (“Game of Thrones”) casting director. Bond auditions can be revealing: Henry Cavill, who lost the role to Craig in the previous casting search, told Men’s Health in 2019 that he was asked to re-enact a scene in which Sean Connery’s Bond emerged from a bathroom in nothing but a towel.

James Bond is one of the most coveted — and unforgiving — roles in moviedom. When Craig was cast in 2005, taking over from Pierce Brosnan, detractors complained that he was too blond, too short and insufficiently suave. Carping fans have long been part of the Bond tradition, but the internet gave them a new megaphone. Craig’s “fleshy” ears and “potato” face were mocked on message boards. One group even created a protest website, CraigNotBond. com.

Craig went on to become one of the most celebrated Bonds, but playing a superspy with a license to kill took a physical toll. Over five films, he suffered injuries to his shoulder, calves, knee and ankle while shooting action sequences, at one point questioning whether he could continue.

The character also comes with a complicated cultural legacy, including what Helen Mirren has called his “profound sexism.” Nor is Bond’s appearance the only thing purists obsess over. Even minor adjustments to his martini order can be treated as grounds for an international incident: The product-placement Heineken he drank in “Skyfall” did not go down smoothly.

But this is no ordinary 007 handoff.

Amazon is attempting to reinvigorate a series that has been without a new movie since 2021, with the hiatus on track to become the longest in Bond history. In the franchise’s absence, a new generation of moviegoers has come of age with little attachment to the glamorous British spy, gravitating instead toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is also proceeding without the Broccoli family, whose expert stewardship of the franchise — over six decades — turned it into one of the most valuable properties in Hollywood history.

Amazon acquired a 50 percent stake in the Bond movies as part of its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM in 2022. Barbara Broccoli and her half brother, Michael G. Wilson, retained ownership of the rest — along with final say over creative decisions. In 2025, after years of behind-the-scenes tensions over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe, the tech giant wrested creative control from Broccoli and Wilson.

Albert “Cubby” Broccoli, her father and his stepfather, first brought James Bond to the big screen with “Dr. No” in 1962. The official series has since generated nearly $7 billion in domestic ticket sales alone, after adjusting for inflation. Some longtime fans have worried that the films will become more corporate and American in style, losing their distinctly British character. With so much at stake, Amazon recruited Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman who has become one of Hollywood’s most successful producers. David Heyman, the producing force behind all eight “Harry Potter” movies, is also helping to chart Bond’s future.

The 26th Bond film — not counting two made outside the official series, “Casino Royale” (1967) and “Never Say Never Again” (1983) — will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, whose credits include the Oscar-nominated “Dune” movies. Steven Knight, creator of the crime drama “Peaky Blinders,” is writing the screenplay. It’s an original story. “Casino Royale” in 2006 was the last Bond movie based substantially on an Ian Fleming novel. There are no more to adapt.

A release date has not been announced. Bond movies typically require six to seven months of filming alone, making a theatrical debut before 2028 unlikely.

Tess Felder contributed reporting from London.

Brooks Barnes is the chief Hollywood correspondent for The Times. He has reported on the entertainment industry for 25 years.

There’s a New James Bond, Again. How Did the Last Ones Fare?

The New York Times November 16, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

The casting of 007 inevitably stokes debate, and the immediate reaction doesn’t necessarily match the eventual reviews.

By Calum Marsh

Calum Marsh has seen every Bond movie and is a rare viewer who likes George Lazenby’s most.

Now that Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond, fans of the franchise will no doubt weigh in with their verdicts, sizing up the actor and drawing firm conclusions before he even has the chance to make a first impression as 007.

It won’t be the first time. Opining about Bond casting is an age-old pastime, and each actor who has played the world-famous British spy has faced skepticism upon being thrust into this particular spotlight.

And some Bond traditionalists are also wary over what direction the films, based on the novels by Ian Fleming, will take now that the franchise is controlled by Amazon MGM, which has said that it plans to take the series in new paths.

But hasty complaints and lasting assessments aren’t always the same, and history has been kinder to most Bond stars than the hair-trigger reactions would have suggested.

Here’s a look back at how The New York Times has viewed the previous Bond actors when they were cast and after the films made it to the big screen.

Before Fleming’s novel “Dr. No” was adapted for the screen, a London newspaper conducted its own search for the ideal actor to play the super spy, The New York Times recalled in a 1987 lookback for the film’s 25th anniversary. “A thousand readers sent suggestions, including a man named, appropriately enough, James Bond,” the article noted.

Sean Connery, the producers’ choice for the role, won Fleming’s approval, too: He described Connery, according to The Times, as “an absolute corker, a 30-year-old Shakespearean actor, ex-Navy boxing champion, etc., and even intelligent.”

Reviewing “Dr. No,” Bosley Crowther praised the film as a “lively, amusing picture,” and described Connery’s Bond as “an elegant fellow” who is “natty, naughty and nifty to the end.”

Years after Connery’s Bond era, which the critic Caryn James recalled as “a time many still consider the Golden Age,” she summarized Connery in the role as “smoother than a dry martini, faster than an Aston Martin, practically able to leap from tall buildings and land in a woman’s bed.”

Lazenby, who appeared in only one Bond adventure — “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” (1969) — rarely gets much of a second thought.

In his review, the critic A. H. Weiler was immediately dismissive of Lazenby, a former model and car salesman who was new to film acting. “He’s tall, dark, handsome and has a dimpled chin,” Weiler wrote. “But Mr. Lazenby, if not a spurious Bond, is merely a casual, pleasant, satisfactory replacement.”

Fifty years later, The Times noted that the film had “won increasing respect” for its direction, script, music and “mastermind criminal scheme,” but even Lazenby expressed some regret. “At the time, I thought I did a good job,” he said. “Now I know I could do it better.”

“The Saint is taking over as 007,” James F. Clarity proclaimed in The Times when it was announced that Moore, the star of TV’s “The Saint,” had been named Connery’s successor. (Connery, the piece added, had abandoned the part after it “made him rich and bored.”)

But the critic Roger Greenspun was left unimpressed by “Live and Let Die,” the eighth Bond installment and the first starring Moore. In fact, it was Moore’s presence in particular that Greenspun objected to in his review for The Times, dismissing the actor as “handsome, suave, somewhat phlegmatic,” and with “a tendency to throw away his throwaway quips as the minor embarrassments that, alas, they usually are.”

Moore was the oldest Bond actor when he last reprised the role, in “A View to a Kill” (1985). He was 59, and the reviews were not kind. “The effort involved in keeping Roger Moore’s 007 impervious to age, changing times or sheer deja-vu seems overwhelming,” the critic Janet Maslin wrote, deriding the movie as “a monumental chore.”

Dalton was first flagged as a potential Bond as early as 1969, but he declined on the grounds that he felt too young for the role. Nearly two decades later, he accepted the part.

A brief Reuters news item published in The Times in 1986 noted that Dalton, “who was born in Wales and whose physique and accent fit the fictional mold of Mr. Fleming’s dashing hero,” was a serious actor known for his theater work. A Times profile of Dalton, published in the lead-up to his Bond debut and written by Benedict Nightingale, reiterated the point, describing the actor as “a bit of a paradox,” like Bond himself.

The Dalton films were a little edgier than their predecessors, and reviewers noted the absence of light comedy that had defined many of the Moore escapades. Caryn James called “License to Kill,” Dalton’s second Bond flick, “familiar,” but noted that “Mr. Dalton’s presence adds a darker tone.”

Although Brosnan, best-known at the time for “Remington Steele,” did not appear as Bond until 1995, he had professed in an interview a full decade earlier that he had aspirations of succeeding Moore in the role. When he eventually made his debut as Bond in “GoldenEye,” at age 43, he told The Times that he would “be a fool to tamper with what makes James Bond work.”

In her reviewing of “GoldenEye,” Janet Maslin called Brosnan “the best-moussed Bond ever to play baccarat in Monte Carlo.” But he was getting on in years as the series continued.

In “Die Another Day,” Brosnan was nearing 50, and as the critic A. O. Scott noted in a positive review of the film, had “a thicker face and a stiffer gait than he did in his callow ‘Remington Steele’ days.” But, Scott added, Brosnan’s Bond “is curiously vulnerable, decidedly flappable underneath the cynical urbanity.” The writer also highlighted a quality most rare in Bond actors: “tenderness.”

In October 2005, the franchise unveiled Daniel Craig as “the first blond James Bond and only the second Englishman to star as Agent 007 in the movie series.”

The reaction was vociferously negative.

In an opinion article for the Times, Deborah Lipp lamented that Brosnan was being “forced out while still on top.” And a news article quoted one fan’s diatribe over the announcement: “My god, don’t the producers have any brains? Craig is not Bond material. Bond must be tall, dark and handsome. Or at least two of the three, and he isn’t even one!”

But Craig won the day. The critic Manohla Dargis wrote in a review that Craig “fits Fleming’s description of the character as appearing ‘ironical, brutal and cold’ better than any actor since Mr. Connery.”

Sarah Lyall wrote from London, “Now even the meanest-spirited, most Sean Connery-nostalgic critics in Britain seem to have been charmed out of their bad attitudes by Mr. Craig’s performance as a gritty, steely James Bond.”

This Cancer Kills Children in a Year. Research Has Been Stalled for a Year.

The New York Times November 16, 2026

Ryleigh Schecter, 5, in her bedroom at home in Twinsburg, Ohio. She was diagnosed this year with an incurable brain tumor.

Supported by

For 27 years, the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium worked to save kids with brain cancer. But just before 5-year-old Ryleigh Schecter was diagnosed, the government shut it down.

By Lisa Miller

Visuals by Lexi Parra

Reporting from Tampa, Fla.; Cincinnati, Columbus and Twinsburg, Ohio; Turkey, Texas; Bethesda, Md.; and New York.

When Ryleigh Schecter answered the front door to her home, she was wearing an oversized lavender bow in her hair that matched the stripes on her shirt. “Rainbow” is her favorite color, she told me as I sat with her and her parents, Amanda and Aaron, in their cozy living room in Twinsburg, Ohio. To prove it, she recited the colors of the spectrum in order, adding “pink, silver, gold” at the end. She is 5.

Eventually, the Schecters and I began to talk about the medicine she takes, and on cue Ryleigh sped to the kitchen and raced back with a sandwich bag full of Skittles. It contained only the red, orange and yellow ones. “I don’t like the purple or the green,” she explained.

Ryleigh takes two drugs every night, one designed to treat breast cancer. Her mother mixes them as if from a chemistry set and administers them orally with a syringe. Ryleigh hates them.

“The first one tastes disgusting, and the second one tastes medium,” Ryleigh told me.

What does the first one taste like? I asked her.

“Dirty water mixed together,” she replied. After each dose, Ryleigh eats a Skittle to wash away the taste. She likes orange best.

Seven months ago, Ryleigh was diagnosed with an incurable brain tumor called D. I. P. G. Her drug regimen is part of a clinical trial, the only slim chance of extending or saving her life. Through trials, scientists start to understand not only what helps a particular child, but how generations may be cured in the future.

A child with diagnosed D. I. P. G. will usually get six weeks of radiation five days a week. After that there is no proven treatment, no standard of care. The average time between diagnosis and death is nine to 12 months. Knowing this, parents will consent to anything. They will move. They will quit their jobs. They will sign forms acknowledging that under experimental treatment, their child may suffer painful or debilitating side effects. Yet even under the care of the most brilliant oncologists, the disease is likely to progress.

Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma usually strikes between 4 and 10 years old, with about 300 children a year diagnosed in the United States. It grows in the brainstem, which controls the primary functions of human life: breathing, balance, the heartbeat. There, it meshes with the tissue, “like sand in grass,” clinicians say. For these reasons, it is inoperable.

No one wants their child to become “a human guinea pig,” as Amanda Schecter put it to me, but when the choice is between that and nothing, there is no choice. Of course, the Schecters want to help science. But first they want to save their child.

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

When the Schecter family went looking for clinical trials, one avenue of hope had recently been closed. In August 2025 the National Cancer Institute, part of the National Institutes of Health, terminated the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium, long a cornerstone of the government’s pediatric brain cancer effort. When the government did not renew the consortium’s $4 million annual grant, eight ongoing trials were closed or paused. Described publicly as a consolidation to improve efficiencies, the closure was part of the Trump administration’s sweeping moves to upend the government’s approach to federal research funding.

The Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium — 16 elite pediatric hospitals in the country working together to test novel treatments for D. I. P. G. and other brain cancers — usually ran six to eight active clinical trials a year. Most were Phase 1 trials, a drug or therapy’s first step toward government approval. When the government defunded the consortium, researchers at its member hospitals were testing a promising immunotherapy and were about to test a laser therapy. For D. I. P. G., they were experimenting with a skull cap that sends electricity directly into the brains of patients; they were also testing a vaccine.

The D. I. P. G. trials were once available through the consortium at multiple sites within half a day’s drive of Ryleigh’s home, according to Kara Buente, who helps families like the Schecters find trials through her nonprofit, The Bella Project. Both were paused. Ryleigh does not have access to either of them.

The Schecters settled on a Phase 2 trial called TarGeT-A, led by researchers at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. Ryleigh is doing well. During my visit, she served us pretend breakfast and pretend ice cream cones with toppings, then gave us the pretend check. In September, she started kindergarten and Amanda went back to work as a school principal. More recently, when Ryleigh asked her mother if she would get braces like her brother, Hudson, “it was a gut punch,” Amanda said.

The Schecters can’t understand why the government would dismantle a productive collaboration when their crisis is urgent. “Like, up a creek without a paddle and not knowing what the next step is,” Amanda said to me.

The National Cancer Institute pulled the plug on the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium in a video call on Aug. 14, 2025. The news was “catastrophic,” Ira Dunkel recalled in an interview at a cafe on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, near Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where he works as a pediatric oncologist. At the time of the phone call he was also chair of the consortium.

Like everyone in academic medicine, Dunkel had been following the news of the Trump administration’s cuts to the N. I. H. budget, but he did not believe they would affect his work.

“I thought no political appointee or political person would want to be, like, shutting down research for children with brain cancer,” Dunkel explained, expressing himself carefully and in a soft voice.

A National Cancer Institute oncologist, Malcolm Smith, delivered the news. Smith and Dunkel had a long relationship, and Smith seemed to understand he was dealing a fatal blow, Dunkel told me. He knew “we were going to have to fire people and stop our studies,” Dunkel said. Smith would not tell him who made the decision or how it was made, attributing it only to “government leadership.”

When reached for comment, Smith said the conversation was “difficult, personally, for me.”

The $4 million grant was tiny in the scope of the $732 million that the N. I. H. spends annually on childhood cancer, but it was “hugely important,” Dunkel told me. In a Phase 1 trial, researchers test experimental treatments for safety in humans. Physicians and scientists within the consortium designed the medical aspects of their studies, but a team behind the scenes managed and administered the regulatory, operational and technological sides so they could be smoothly integrated among 16 research sites and available to patients nationwide.

Furious parent groups responded right away. About a month after the consortium was defunded, a bipartisan group from New York, including Representative Mike Lawler, Republican of New York, called on Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to reverse the decision. “We cannot afford to take this step backward,” the group said in a letter.

The next week, the Trump administration announced a doubling of funding, to $100 million, for its data initiative to speed childhood cancer research.

“For too long, families have fought childhood cancer while our systems lagged behind,” Kennedy said in remarks at the White House. “President Trump is changing that. We will harness American innovation in artificial intelligence to find cures for pediatric cancer.”

By the time I met with Dunkel nearly a year later, the National Cancer Institute had updated its web page to include an FAQ explaining the closure of the consortium. It was “not a cost-cutting measure,” the FAQ said. Enrollment in the consortium’s studies had slowed. To improve efficiencies, its work would be absorbed by a larger government-funded research network also committed to early-phase trials, but with a broader focus on all childhood cancers.

At the cafe, Dunkel made his rebuttal. Yes, enrollment had slowed. Experimental cancer therapies have become so targeted that the number of eligible patients within an already small population has shrunk. Yet from his point of view, the consortium was doing good studies and publishing them in “high-impact journals.” Besides, he said, who cares if multiple networks are devoted to finding cures for childhood cancers? Other networks had similar aims, but they did not have the consortium’s singular focus. “Even while all these groups were coexisting, there were more good ideas than the capacity to study them,” he told me.

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

Dunkel came across as a man still in grief as he tried to tally the losses.

Children in clinical trials often give samples during research: tumor tissue, spinal fluid, blood. Sometimes, to help speed science along, parents donate the samples after a child’s death. With the closure of the consortium, something had to be done with hundreds of human samples stored at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles. If the originating hospital wanted them, they were returned. If not, they were destroyed.

At St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Memphis, 27 years of research data on more than 2,000 children with rare brain tumors had to be archived. Under the consortium, any researcher with a hypothesis could have applied to look at its data. Without a vetting process or dedicated staff, that’s going to be “much, much, much more difficult to do in the future,” Dunkel said.

Finally, there was the loss of the trials themselves. On Nov. 3, after queries from The New York Times, the National Cancer Institute updated its web page again.

The paused trials are “planned to reopen to enrollment in late 2026 or early 2027,” it said. For parents who have been told their child has a year or less to live, the 15-month administrative delay is agonizing.

One of the paused trials was called PBTC-059. A Phase 1 trial led by researchers at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston, it was exploring the safety of CAR-T therapy in patients with a rare brain cancer called ependymoma. The therapy, in which a patient’s blood is engineered to boost its immune response, has generated huge excitement in the pediatric brain cancer community. CAR-T therapy has dramatically improved cure rates for the most common childhood leukemia.

Another trial, called PBTC-N14, was closed entirely. The first step after a brain-tumor diagnosis is often a brain biopsy, but these are invasive. Consortium researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering were exploring whether cerebral spinal fluid, collected without surgery, might provide the same genetic information and help guide treatment while sparing children harm. “Everyone thought it was a good study, and tried to answer a good question,” its lead investigator, Matthias Karajannis, told me. “But it did not finish answering that question.”

The consortium ended in September 2026, with the weekly video meeting. It had a funereal tone, Dunkel said.

The shuttering was “one of the very worst professional moments of my career,” Dunkel told me. “I felt the loss of hope and opportunity for the parents and the patients. The loss of progress in the field for everyone involved, the doctors and scientists as well as the patients.”

“I guess I never really thought that this was my fault,” he said, then paused. “But I did feel like as the captain of the ship, I let down a lot of people.”

In late August 2025, Keith Desserich received a call from Dunkel, who relayed the news. “I think he was on the verge of tears,” Desserich told me.

Together with his wife, Brooke, Desserich founded The Cure Starts Now in 2007 after the death of their 6-year-old daughter, Elena, to D. I. P. G. The families who volunteer with The Cure Starts Now, most who have had a child die from a brain tumor, collect donations by hosting 5K runs and bowling nights and direct the funds toward promising, early-stage research.

Since 2017, Desserich had been on the steering committee of the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium. A Cincinnati-based entrepreneur in his professional life, he believes in funding numerous small projects in the hope that one will develop into what he calls “the home run cure.” He estimates that since 2017, The Cure Starts Now has given between $2 million and $3 million in seed money to projects initiated by consortium researchers.

Desserich is a boyish man with a bullish demeanor. After losing a child in this horrific and random way, a parent feels constantly besieged, he told me. In the lingo of his nonprofit, a child struggling with D. I. P. G. is a “warrior” and their illness is a “fight.” I met the Desseriches in July when I traveled to Tampa to attend the annual meeting of their nonprofit. Standing at the head of a chilly hotel conference room, Desserich exhorted the 50 member families to redouble their efforts. The closure of the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium was an “earthquake,” he said.

“How are we able to continue this research even if the government is not going to do it?” he asked.

The families in Tampa wanted me to know this: The primary experience of having a child with D. I. P. G. is helplessness. Parents want to fix things for their children. When the consortium lost its funding, the parents in Tampa were angry and bereft all over again. It felt “like picking off a scab,” said Lisa Hill, whose daughter Lauren, a basketball star, was 19 when she died in 2015. After the golf outings and ATV races and silent auctions, after endlessly reciting the idiosyncrasies of their beloved children to elicit dollars from friends and strangers, “We close down research for things that don’t have a cure?” said Josh Hines. He and his wife, Jill, were in Tampa after losing their daughter, Harleigh, to D. I. P. G in 2023.

In Desserich’s view, Dunkel and the other leaders of the consortium were old fashioned: too trusting of government, too modest. He had been pushing them to expand internationally to boost the numbers of patients in trials and to better showcase their groundbreaking ideas with promotion and PR. “There was this resistance of, ‘Oh, we can’t do that. Government won’t like it,’” Desserich said.

In the summer of 2025, he started hectoring them. “Do we think we’re fine for renewal?” he asked Dunkel. “What happens if government gets fickle?” He found Dunkel’s optimism naïve.

Soon after the Aug. 14 call, N. I. H. officials invited Desserich and a number of other parents to a video meeting. They tried to clarify their rationale, but Desserich thought they appeared as surprised by the termination as he was. An N. I. H. spokesman said they had been considering the move for years.

The lost funding does not bother Desserich as much as the loss of the intimate collaboration. The consortium held a competition every five years to identify the hospitals doing the most relevant and rigorous work. These members were “the dream team,” as Desserich saw it. And patients’ families were reassured by the government’s imprimatur.

As part of its most recent website update, the National Cancer Institute announced it was committing “approximately $4 million,” the same amount previously allocated to the consortium, to the larger network, to build brain-tumor expertise and expedite more early-phase clinical trials. Desserich was underwhelmed. “I don’t care if we had $60 million, $100 million. You’re not going to be able to duplicate” the consortium, he said.

Baylie Barclay heard about the closure from Desserich. It was “devastating,” she told me.

When a clinical trial stops enrolling new patients, she said, scientific discovery slows down. And in the case of a child with D. I. P. G., “you don’t have any time.”

Since their son Paxton died from D. I. P. G. in July 2025, Baylie and her husband, Lane, have committed themselves to raising money for pediatric brain-cancer research from their home in Turkey, Texas, a village of 300 people in the state’s Panhandle. On the one-year anniversary of Paxton’s death, the Barclays hosted a 5K run to raise funds for The Cure Starts Now. Every one of the residents of Turkey attended that day, Barclay told me, and together they contributed $20,000.

Barclay, who is 30, now works out of Paxton’s former bedroom as a family support coordinator for The Cure Starts Now. Paxton was the middle child, and his family remembers him as wild, the life of the party, a Western boy who loved his cowboy boots and kept souvenirs from the day in his pockets: wire nuts, dead minnows, sticks and feathers. His family has a saying, which they’ve printed on T-shirts: Live Like Pax. When they wonder what Paxton would do, they go camping or wake surfing.

As Barclay works, she is surrounded by Paxton’s Legos and his Pokemon cards. She finds families with new diagnoses on social media and writes quick, personal notes. She connects families with services: information about trials, financial support to pay for travel and hotels near treating hospitals, and provides a listening ear.

Focusing on funding science research keeps Barclay connected to her son. Near the end of Paxton’s life, he was angry, exhausted and tired of being isolated in the hospital. At 8 years old, he had been through three clinical trials. One day, she was on the phone when he heard her say that his cancer was incurable.

“And he said, ‘There’s no cure?’” Baylie remembered, “and I was like, ‘Not yet.’” She said this calmly. “And that was the day I was like, I’m going to do more. He would not have wanted me to ever stop.”

So when Paxton died, the Barclays gave every part of him gathered during trials to scientific research. “Take his information,” the Barclays told the doctors. “Take anything left over. Take his blood tests. Use them. Please, take it and find the cure. Whatever you need to do.”

The D. I. P. G. community online is close-knit. The Barclays and the Schecters didn’t know each other, but Baylie and Amanda are now in touch through social media. When Ryleigh Schecter was diagnosed, Baylie Barclay sent the family “Warrior” T-shirts emblazoned with Ryleigh’s name. The Schecters wore them on vacation.

In its web pages updated this month, the N. C. I. describes its revamped pediatric brain cancer research effort in a futuristic light: the larger network will take on a revitalized and accelerated effort to discover novel treatments through clinical trials. With “administrative modernization” and “the application of Super Intelligence (SI),” the new organization will “generate meaningful research results.”

They make it sound so slick and simple, Amanda Schecter said. In her experience, a clinical trial is a matter of countless blood draws and a squirming child in an MRI machine. Recently Ryleigh’s oncology team asked Amanda and Aaron to give blood and saliva samples, and to sign consent forms to use the tissue from Ryleigh’s biopsies in the event that they don’t need it. This is for kids in the future, they told her, and the Schecters automatically said yes. But part of Amanda wasn’t really listening. Her mind was on Ryleigh, down the hall in another room. Amanda finds her own mental chatter exhausting: She desperately wants to hope but not too much. On her Instagram recently she shared a poet’s incantation.

“So scared of time,” the poem went. “So aware of time. So desperate for time. So grateful for time. All at the same time.”

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

Produced by Jeffrey Furticella and Umi Syam.

Lisa Miller is a Times reporter who writes about the personal and cultural struggle to attain good health.

Lexi Parra is a photojournalist for The Times, based in New York. She is a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

The Best Thanksgiving Is a Southern Buffet

The New York Times November 09, 2026

Seconds are encouraged at Eric Kim’s Korean American dinner and love letter to the South.

Seconds are encouraged at Eric Kim’s Korean American dinner and love letter to the South.

By Eric Kim

Published Nov. 9, 2026 Updated Nov. 9, 2026

The Philadelphia chef Amanda Shulman once showed me, after a meal at her restaurant Her Place, a scrapbook filled with menus of every dinner party she’d cooked at home. What a great way to honor not just the meals prepared but the memories created and time well shared, I thought.

I was entering a new stage of life and wanted to live more intentionally, earnestly, to show love to the people who most matter to me. So, at the start of this year, inspired by Ms. Shulman, I vowed to have more friends over for dinner.

If love is attention, then cooking must be its purest manifestation. Cooking is how I thank people and tell them how much I care. A tablecloth, a lit candle and a generous spread can say so much more than a handwritten letter.

I suppose, then, what follows — my Thanksgiving table — is an extension of that, a reflection of how I cook for those I love, and of my background, tastes and predilections.

I’m a Southern boy at heart, having grown up in Atlanta with casseroles and country-style buffets after church on Sundays. But my family roots are in South Korea, where jangs like gochujang, doenjang and soy sauce aren’t just culinary parlor tricks; they’re foundational.

A brown gravy, for instance, can gain immeasurable savoriness from a dollop of doenjang. If gochujang makes its way into the cranberry sauce, then so be it. I serve it all informally, in a love letter to the Southern buffet, where you want an eclectic mix of dishes that work together.

Some of these 10 recipes are more involved than others, but all are easy and will, I hope, teach you something new and inspire you to stretch a bit: to tackle a cooking project, perfect a culinary technique, maybe even dive into your first solo roast turkey.

I like to spread the work across three days. On the first day, I do the grocery shopping, start thawing the turkey, chop all the vegetables and make the pickles. On the second, I dry-brine the turkey and prepare the casseroles just before the point of baking, covering and refrigerating them. On the feast day itself, I roast the turkey, bake off the casseroles and prepare the fresh vegetable sides.

With this meal, I have just one rule: Everyone makes their own plate. I like to pile mine high, everything smothered in brown gravy, with room for seconds, thirds and pudding. My husband is partial to the squash macaroni and cheese, but the unanimous favorite among my friends seems to be the kale and cheese rice casserole. My hope is that you’ll find a new favorite in this collection, cook it for those you love and remember what matters most: standing side-by-side, catching up between sips of wine, working together toward a meal, like a last supper at the end of the world.

Drawing on quick-pickling methods from South Korea and the American South, this recipe makes three distinctly flavored and irresistibly crunchy pickles. For a proper Southern relish tray, set them out with crackers, olives and cheese, and enjoy with cocktails or the rest of the meal. (Don’t forget to tuck leftovers into turkey sandwiches.)

Recipe: Quick-Pickled Radishes, Cauliflower and Cucumbers

Roasting a whole buttered turkey alongside heads of garlic, dried chiles and tomato leaves you with a fantastic base for a Thanksgiving dinner. Those aromatics will not only infuse the pan juices that baste the turkey, but also tint it fire red. A dry brine is crucial here — most good turkey recipes call for this — as it seasons the meat through and through and helps it retain moisture even after a long roast.

Recipe: Roast Turkey With Garlic and Chiles

A great gravy starts with flavorful drippings and a good stock. Here, doenjang, the Korean fermented soybean paste, lends both high and low notes, while a splash of cream at the end rounds it out. If you can’t find doenjang, then white or red miso works in a pinch. Additional gamchil mat (the Korean word for “savory taste”) comes in the form of Worcestershire sauce, though soy sauce tastes great as well.

Recipe: Doenjang Cream Gravy

These smashed red potatoes might seem understated — tasting distinctively of, well, potatoes — but they’re key to extending the richer flavors on the Thanksgiving table. A flurry of thinly sliced scallions adds welcome freshness, and a cream infused with dried shiitake mushrooms, nutmeg and those scallion whites helps match gravy’s super savory depth.

Recipe: Scallion Smashed Potatoes

Traditional Southern cornbread dressing is a tender union of everything delicious and good in the world, and in this modern spin on sausage stuffing, it’s crumbled along with saltine crackers to soak up broth like a sponge, keeping things moist, not wet. (It even coheres the stuffing’s disparate parts without the need for eggs.) Fennel seeds, fresh sage and dried red chile amplify the spiced, comforting notes, while sweet-tart apples, first marinated in cider vinegar to set the red color, punctuate the dish with acidity and sweetness.

Recipe: Sausage and Apple Cornbread Stuffing

Kale replaces broccoli in this rustic spin on a classic Southern casserole, adding some necessary roughage to your spread. Leafy Tuscan kale cooks down in a thin sauce of milk, onion and nutmeg, then mixes with plump rice and white Cheddar. A final grating of Parmesan on top becomes crisp and toasty in the oven.

Recipe: Kale and Cheese Rice Casserole

Sliced orange squash gives classic macaroni and cheese a golden glow. Four cheeses — cream cheese for creaminess, Cheddar for sharpness, smoked Gouda for intrigue and Pepper Jack for a little kick — work together here to create an elegant but deeply comforting flavor, texture and look. Enjoy this mac gooey and warm, fresh out of the oven, or wait until it cools completely to slice into clean squares that can be griddled back to temperature or baked until crisp at the edges.

Recipe: Acorn Squash Macaroni and Cheese

A touch of soy adds oomph to stovetop vegetables, while a slick of butter leaves them looking glossy and vibrant. Be sure to cut your vegetables into small, narrow pieces so they cook evenly in the quick 10-minute burst of heat this recipe calls for. Roll-cutting the carrots is a great way to practice your knife skills.

Recipe: Soy-Butter Glazed Green Beans and Carrots

Canned cranberry jelly is a beautiful starting place for balancing bold Korean flavors. When melted down and mixed with gochujang, vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, the sauce becomes a savory, tangy accent on a Thanksgiving plate, uplifting roast turkey and even playing well with mashed potatoes. A smear of this is fantastic in a leftover turkey sandwich.

Recipe: Gochujang Cranberry Sauce

Instead of pie, a fluffy banana pudding scented with cardamom is light enough to linger over after a big feast. Make this the day before (and at least the night before) serving, so the vanilla wafers can absorb the cream and become soft and silky.

Recipe: Cardamom Banana Pudding
